notes.title: Introduction to Biology: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 1

Introduction to Biology

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. What biology is, why it matters, the scientific method, lab and field tools, the light microscope, and lab safety.

Study lessons 1.1 to 1.6 in order. Check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 1
  • Define Biology (lesson 1.1)
  • Explain why Biology is studied (lesson 1.2)
  • Plan a biological investigation using the scientific method (lesson 1.3)
  • Identify some common tools of a Biologist (lesson 1.4)
  • Utilize a microscope (lesson 1.5)
  • Execute general laboratory safety rules (lesson 1.6)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Biology: scientific study of life or living things (bios = life, logos = study).
  • Living things: cells, growth, reproduction, genetic transmission, energy use, homeostasis, evolutionary adaptation.
  • Scientific method: observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → conclusion → communication.
  • Hypothesis: testable proposed scientific explanation.
  • Magnification: how many times larger the image is than the real object. Resolution: ability to distinguish two separate points.
  • Total magnification = eyepiece × objective (example: 10× × 40× = 400×).
  • Carry a microscope by the arm with a hand under the base. Always start on low power.

notes.title: 1.1 Definition of Biology: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.1

Definition of Biology

What biology is, what "alive" means, and how biology links to other sciences.

Competency: define Biology

Key term Biology. The scientific study of life or living things. From Greek bios (life) + logos (study).
Key term Homeostasis. Keeping relatively constant internal conditions despite outside changes.

What does it mean to be alive?

Life is hard to define in one short sentence. We recognize living systems mainly by shared characteristics:

  • Composed of one or more cells
  • Can grow
  • Can reproduce
  • Transmit genetic information to offspring
  • Need energy to do work
  • Maintain relatively constant internal conditions (homeostasis)
  • Capable of evolutionary adaptation to the environment

What is a scientific study?

Biologists study living things using a scientific method. They ask questions, suggest possible answers, and test those answers through experimentation. They study structures and processes that can be observed and measured, directly or with tools such as microscopes.

Biology and other natural sciences

Biology merges information and tools from all natural sciences.

  • Chemistry: naturally occurring elements in organisms, chemical bonding, molecules, acids, bases, and related ideas
  • Physics: with chemistry, helps explain conversion of radiant energy into organic molecules in photosynthesis
Must remember
  • Biology = scientific study of life · bios + logos
  • Homeostasis = stable internal conditions

notes.title: 1.2 Why do we study Biology?: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.2

Why do we study Biology?

Biology explains the living world and improves medicine, food, farming, and the environment.

Competency: explain why Biology is studied

Humans have an inborn curiosity about nature. Studying biology helps us understand how living things work, how they function, and how they interact with the environment.

Why biology matters

  • Explains how animal and plant bodies work
  • Explains how ecosystems work
  • Advances in genetics and cell biology transform medicine and agriculture
  • Forensic biology helps investigate crime
  • Ecology helps societies evaluate environmental issues such as global warming
  • Supports treatment of diseases such as AIDS, tuberculosis, and some cancers
  • Biologists discover drugs used to treat human diseases

Applications in day-to-day life (textbook list)

  • Fermentation by yeasts, other fungi, bacteria, or their enzymes: wine-making, brewing, bread baking, cheese production
  • Antibiotics such as penicillin produced by mould fungi or bacteria
  • Industrial chemicals (example: citric acid, lactic acid) using bacteria or fungi
  • Sewage disposal: bacteria in filter beds help purify effluent
  • Discovery of DNA structure and forensic analysis of DNA from crime scenes
Exam tip

Give clear examples across medicine, agriculture, food or beverage processing, forensics, and environment.

notes.title: 1.3 The Scientific Method: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3

The Scientific Method

Biology is a science of inquiry. Clear steps make results testable and repeatable.

Competency: plan a biological investigation using the scientific method

Key term Hypothesis. A proposed scientific explanation (possible answer) for a question or set of questions. It must be testable. Several hypotheses may be possible for one problem.
Key term Scientific method. A series of steps that guide scientists through investigations so conclusions are based on observations and others can repeat the work.

Steps of the scientific method

  1. Observation. Careful noticing of a problem or event. Direct (sense organs) or indirect (tools such as microscopes). Observations lead to a question.
  2. Asking questions. Observations lead to inquiry.
  3. Forming a hypothesis. Propose possible testable answers.
  4. Testing the hypothesis. Use experimentation. Experiments must be duplicatable so other scientists can get similar results. If data do not support the hypothesis, propose a new one.
  5. Making conclusions. Ask whether the original hypothesis still fits. Keep it if yes. Reject and replace if no.
  6. Communicating the findings. Write what was done and the results. Submit to a scientific journal. Findings help teachers and students.

Order: observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → conclusion → communication.

Everyday example (torch)

Torch does not light when switched on. You form hypotheses (dead battery, broken bulb, and so on), test them, and conclude which explanation fits. Same logic as lab science.

Seed germination activity (textbook model)

  • Question: importance of temperature for seed germination
  • Germinate beans at room temperature, colder place, hotter place
  • Measure germination time and seedling length; draw a bar graph (X = time/day, Y = length); interpret and report
Exam tip

Hypothesis = possible explanation of an observation (not an unchanging law).

notes.title: 1.4 Tools of a Biologist: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.4

Tools of a Biologist

Lab and field tools for measuring, observing, and culturing.

Competency: identify common tools of a biologist

Some tools measure, some observe, some culture microorganisms.

Key terms Magnification. The number of times larger an image is than the real size of the object.
Resolution. The ability to distinguish between two separate points.

1.4.1 Laboratory tools

Key termHand lens. A convex lens in a circular metallic loop with a handle. Gives an enlarged image of an object. Higher magnification than the naked eye, but not enough for detailed cell study (need a microscope).
Key termMicroscope. Instrument used to observe objects too small for the naked eye. Magnifies the image so bacteria, fungi, and parasites can be seen.
Key termLight microscope. Uses a beam of light to view specimens. Simple = one lens. Compound = two or more glass lenses (most common in biology; can magnify up to about 2000×). Monocular = one eyepiece; binocular = two.
Key termElectron microscope. Uses a beam of electrons and electromagnets (not glass lenses). Higher magnification than light microscopes; used for extremely small organisms such as viruses.
Key termGlass slide. Supports the specimen under the microscope.
Key termCover slip. Thin square or circular glass sheet that covers the specimen on the slide. Protects from dirt and chemicals, protects the microscope, locks moisture so the slide does not dry, and improves the view.
Key termAutoclave. Equipment that sterilizes (kills microorganisms) culture media, contaminated materials, and bacterial spores using high temperature and highly pressurized steam. Needed when spores resist chemical disinfectants such as bleach.
Key termCulturing. Growing microorganisms in a controlled environment. Used in medicine (penicillin), food and beverage (wine, beer, cheese), biofuel, and more.
Key termIncubator. Device that keeps the temperature best suited for growth of different microorganisms.
Key termPetri dish. Flat dish with a slightly larger matching cover (glass or plastic). Used with gelling media such as agar; sterilized in an autoclave.
Key termCulture tube (test tube). Tube used to culture microorganisms with solid (gel) or liquid (broth) media; sterilized in an autoclave.
Key termFlask. Flat-bottom vessel with a long narrow neck for easy mixing without spilling and gentle heating with swirling. Large-volume culture with broth media for large populations of microorganisms.
Key termBalance. Used to make up solutions accurately and weigh specimens.
Key termDropper. Glass tube with a small opening and a rubber bulb. Controls how much solution is added to a reaction.
Key termTongs. Metallic scissors-shaped tool for lifting hot objects (crucibles, beakers, dishes, flasks).
Key termDissecting tool kit. Tools for dissecting animals (catheter, groove probe, scalpels, scissors, forceps, pins, and so on).
Key termDissecting pan. Pan that holds the specimen while it is dissected so internal organs can be studied.
Key termCrucible. Small ceramic or metal container that withstands high temperatures; used to melt elements.
Key termBeaker. Cylindrical glass container for making solutions, holding hot or cold water or ice baths, and so on.
Key termHotplate. Heats solutions and helps make agar culture medium.
Key termpH meter. Measures the pH (acidity or basicity) of substances.
Key termThermometer. Measures the temperature of substances.
Key termForceps. Hold or pick up small objects; many shapes and sizes.
Key termSpatula. Spoon-shaped tool for mixing substances into a solution, stirring, and scraping.
Key termWash bottle. Flexible bottle used to rinse lab materials; squeeze to adjust water pressure.
Key termBunsen burner (or alcohol burner). Produces a single open flame for heating and sterilization in lab experiments.

1.4.2 Field tools

Key termInsect net. Cloth or fine-mesh bag on a wire loop attached to a wooden or metal pole; used to collect insects.
Key termFishing net. Mesh net (sometimes called a fish trap) made from fibres woven in a grid; used for fishing.
Exam tip

Be ready to state the function of flasks, tubes, wash bottles, droppers, spatulas, dissecting pans, and field nets. Light vs electron: light uses light + glass lenses; electron uses electrons + electromagnets (higher magnification; viruses).

notes.title: 1.5 The Light Microscope: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.5

The Light Microscope

Parts, functions, magnification, and careful handling.

Competency: utilize a microscope

Light rays focus on the specimen. Light that passes through is focused by the eyepiece and objective lenses. Total magnification = eyepiece × objective (example: 10× eyepiece × 40× objective = 400×).

1.5.1 Parts and functions

Key termEyepiece (ocular). Top lens you look through. Standard often 10×; optional 5× to 30×.
Key termEyepiece tube. Holds the eyepiece above the objective. On some binoculars it can rotate for better viewing.
Key termObjective lenses. Main lenses that magnify the specimen at different powers (often about 4× to 100×).
Key termArm. Support that connects components so the microscope can be held and used properly.
Key termBody tube. Connects the eyepiece to the objective lenses.
Key termNose piece. Rotating mount that holds several objectives so you can change magnification.
Key termCoarse adjustment knob. Brings the specimen into general focus; moves the stage roughly and quickly.
Key termFine adjustment knob. Makes the image sharp; moves the stage only a little.
Key termStage. Platform where the specimen sits for viewing.
Key termStage clip. Holds the slide so it does not slip.
Key termAperture. Hole in the stage that lets light reach the specimen.
Key termIlluminator. Light source at the base (instead of a mirror); often low-voltage.
Key termCondenser. Lens under the stage that collects and focuses light onto the specimen; important for sharp images at high magnification (about 400× and above).
Key termDiaphragm (iris). Under the stage; controls how much light reaches the specimen (intensity and beam size).
Key termBase. Bottom support that holds the whole microscope.

1.5.2 Handling and using

  • Remove carefully from the cabinet
  • Carry upright: one hand on the arm, one under the base; do not bump it
  • Slide must be clean and dry
  • Centre the best region over the light hole
  • Always start on low power (4× objective), even if you need high power later
  • Focus with coarse knobs first, then fine knobs
  • To increase power, centre the region, then change to a higher objective
  • Use immersion oil only with the 100× oil-immersion lens; one drop only
  • Focus by moving lens and specimen apart, never closer into each other
  • Never touch lens surfaces with fingers
  • Lower the stage before removing the slide
  • Clean with lens paper and alcohol when done
  • Before storing: 4× over the stage, stage lowest, light off, cord wrapped, oculars toward the back of the cabinet
Must remember
  • Total mag = eyepiece × objective
  • Closing the diaphragm reduces light to the specimen
  • Several objectives = different magnifications for different detail levels

notes.title: 1.6 General Laboratory Safety Rules: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.6

General Laboratory Safety Rules

Protect yourself and others before, during, and after every lab.

Competency: execute general laboratory safety rules

Key term Safety. Being protected from harm or other danger; controlling recognized hazards to keep risk acceptable.

Lab safety means working carefully, fixing small problems early, and keeping safety in mind at all times.

  1. Follow the instructions. Read and listen to the full procedure. Know how to use every piece of equipment before you start.
  2. Know safety equipment locations. Fire extinguisher and first-aid kit must be ready. Know how to use them. Check they work. Learn lab safety signs.
  3. Dress for the laboratory. Lab coat, safety goggles, gloves, hearing protection if needed, long pants, long-sleeve shirt, closed leather shoes or boots (no sandals). Tie hair back. Use a disposable respirator when handling toxic chemicals. Dress for the experiment.
  4. Never eat or drink in the lab. Do not store food in the same fridge as experiments, chemicals, or cultures.
  5. Never taste or sniff chemicals or cultures. Some can be deadly. Label glassware before adding chemicals and read labels.
  6. Act responsibly. Never mix chemicals randomly to "see what happens" (explosion, fire, or toxic gas risk).
  7. Clean and store waste properly. Start and end with glassware, chemicals, and equipment clean and stored correctly.
  8. Handle chemicals properly. Respirator for toxic chemicals. Never let chemicals touch bare skin. Never leave containers open. All containers need labels. Never use unlabelled chemicals.
  9. Know what to do in accidents. For burns or chemical exposure, flood the area with cold tap water for several minutes.
  10. Keep safety and chemical hygiene as a constant priority for everyone in the lab.
Exam tip

Returning unused leftover chemicals to the original container is not correct handling. Goggles and coats protect eyes and body; tied hair keeps hair out of flames and chemicals.

notes.title: Characteristics and Classification: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 2

Characteristics and Classification of Organisms

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. This unit covers what living things share, how taxonomists name and group organisms, Ethiopian examples, dichotomous keys, the five kingdoms, and Ethiopian taxonomists.

Study lessons 2.1 to 2.7 in order. Use this page to check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 2
  • State the characteristics of living things (lesson 2.1)
  • Classify living things based on taxonomic principles (lesson 2.2)
  • Argue for or against the importance of classification (lesson 2.3)
  • Describe the system of Linnaean nomenclature (lesson 2.4)
  • Classify common Ethiopian animals and plants based on the taxonomic categories (lesson 2.5)
  • List the characteristic features of the five kingdoms (lesson 2.6)
  • Appreciate the works of renowned taxonomists in Ethiopia (lesson 2.7)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Living things share cells, energy use, response to stimuli, growth, reproduction, excretion, ordered complexity, homeostasis, and evolutionary adaptation.
  • Taxonomy is the science of naming, identifying, and classifying organisms. Classification groups things by similarities.
  • Hierarchy: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum (Division in plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
  • Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
  • Binomial nomenclature: Genus + specific epithet (example: Homo sapiens). Italicize in print. Underline when handwritten.
  • Ethiopia is a biodiversity hotspot and a primary centre for crops such as tef and noug.
  • Dichotomous keys identify organisms using paired choices.
  • Whittaker's five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Viruses are not placed in a kingdom.
  • Animals: invertebrates (no backbone) vs vertebrates (backbone).
  • Ethiopian taxonomists include Prof. Sebsebe Demissew, Dr. Mesfin Taddese, Prof. Ensermu Kelbessa, Prof. Silesh Nemomissa, and Prof. Abebe Getahun.

notes.title: 2.1 Characteristics of living things: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.1

Characteristics of living things

Movement alone does not prove life. A car moves and gelatin wiggles, but neither is alive. Use shared characteristics.

Competency: state the characteristics of living things

Life is hard to define in one sentence. Living systems share these properties:

Key termCellular organization. Living things are made of one or more cells. Unicellular organisms have one cell (example: bacteria). Multicellular organisms have many cells (example: plants).
Key termEnergy requirement (metabolism). Living things need energy for chemical work. Autotrophs (producers) make their own food (example: plants by photosynthesis). Heterotrophs (consumers) take food from others.
Key termResponse to stimuli. Living things detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
Key termGrowth. Permanent increase in size and mass by more cells, larger cells, or both.
Key termReproduction. Making more of the same kind. Unicellular organisms may divide into two. Multicellular organisms may reproduce sexually or asexually.
Key termExcretion. Removing metabolic waste products from the body.
Key termHomeostasis. Keeping internal conditions stable within limits (example: body temperature control).
Key termAdaptation and evolution. Populations change over generations so traits fit the environment better.
Exam tip

List several characteristics and give one short example for each. Do not use movement alone as proof of life.

Must remember
  • Cells + energy + respond + grow + reproduce + excrete + homeostasis
  • Autotroph makes food; heterotroph takes food

notes.title: 2.2 Taxonomy of living things: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.2

Taxonomy of living things

Organizing living things makes them easier to find, study, and relate to each other.

Competency: classify living things based on taxonomic principles

Key terms Classification. Grouping things based on their similarities.
Taxonomy. The science of naming, identifying, and classifying organisms.
Taxonomist. A scientist who studies taxonomy.
Identification. Recognizing organisms using characteristic features.
Nomenclature. The naming part of taxonomy.

2.2.1 Principles of classification

  • Biologists judge degrees of similarity and difference.
  • They use external and internal structure, where the organism lives, and genetic makeup for evolutionary relationships.
  • Greater physical similarity usually means a closer biological relationship.
  • Features used: morphological, physiological, molecular, behavioural, and/or ecological characters.

2.2.2 Taxonomic hierarchies

  • Aristotle (384-322 BC): early system. Plants as trees, shrubs, herbs. Animals by red blood or not. Problem: grouped very different flyers (birds, bats, insects).
  • Carolus Linnaeus (1707-1778): father of taxonomy. Orderly ranked hierarchy. First two-kingdom idea: Plantae and Animalia (did not separate prokaryotes/eukaryotes, unicellular/multicellular, or green algae from fungi).
Key term Taxonomic hierarchy. Arranging organisms into successive ranks (increasing or decreasing). Each rank is a taxon (plural: taxa).
Key termDomain. Rank above kingdom in modern classification.
Key termKingdom → Species ranks. Broad to narrow: Kingdom → Phylum (Division for plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.

Three domains

Key termDomain Bacteria. Prokaryotic. No nucleus. Cell wall with peptidoglycan. Unicellular or colonial. Divide by binary fission. DNA as a circular chromosome.
Key termDomain Archaea. Prokaryotic. Extreme environments. Cell wall without peptidoglycan. Unicellular or colonial. Binary fission. Circular DNA.
Key termDomain Eukarya. Nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Linear chromosomes with histones. Unicellular, colonial, or multicellular. Mitosis. Includes protists, fungi, plants, and animals.

Bacteria vs Archaea also differ in membrane chemistry, chlorophyll use (bacteria may photosynthesize; archaea do not in the same way), methane generation, and antibiotic sensitivity.

Key terms Species. Unique type of organism. Biological species: group that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
Prokaryotic cells. No separate nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells. Nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Exam tip

Know the order of ranks and the three domains. Linnaeus = father of taxonomy.

Must remember
  • Taxonomy = name + identify + classify
  • Domain to Species hierarchy
  • Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya (each with its own cell chemistry and structure)

notes.title: 2.3 Relevance of classification: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.3

Relevance of classification

Classification is useful for science, society, and the economy, not only for tidy lists.

Competency: argue for or against the importance of classification

Why classification matters

  • Identify harmful and beneficial organisms
  • Save time and energy when studying organisms
  • Understand relationships between organisms (living and extinct)
  • Framework for research (example: dinosaur bones with internal spaces like bird bones suggest a closer link to birds than to reptiles)
  • Useful in agriculture, forestry, and medicine
  • Can support the economy: new lumber, foods, medicines, energy sources

Example from the textbook: if one tree species has disinfectant chemicals (example: Shiferaw / Moringa, Moringa stenopetala), a closely related species may share useful substances.

Key reminder Species (biological). A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring. Members often look similar, though human breeding can create wide appearance differences (example: cats).
Exam tip

Be ready to argue that taxonomy helps medicine, agriculture, relationship studies, and discovery of useful species.

Must remember
  • Classification reveals relationships and practical uses
  • Related species may share useful chemicals
  • Biological species produce fertile offspring

notes.title: 2.4 Linnaean system of nomenclature: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.4

Linnaean system of nomenclature

One scientific name works worldwide. Local names change by language and region.

Competency: describe the system of Linnaean nomenclature

Carolus Linnaeus was a Swedish naturalist. In Systema Naturae (1735) he described and classified thousands of plants and also classified animals. He refined and popularized binomial nomenclature.

Key term Binomial nomenclature. Internationally agreed system: scientific name = genus name + specific epithet.

Why scientific names?

  • Maize has many local names (example: Bekolo in Amharic, Boqqollo/Badallaa in Afan Oromo, Baddela in Sidaamu Afoo, corn in American English).
  • Ethiopia has 80+ ethnolinguistic groups. Africa has thousands of languages.
  • Latin-form scientific names avoid confusion across languages.
  • Similar size, shape, colour, or behaviour can confuse common names. Scientific names reduce that risk.

Example: botanical name Zea mays for maize.

How to write a scientific name

  • First word: Genus (capital letter)
  • Second word: specific epithet (small letter)
  • Italicize when printed. Underline when handwritten.
  • Example: humans = Homo sapiens

A genus (plural: genera) is a group of similar species. The specific epithet may describe a trait. Example: Enset Ensete ventricosum and banana Musa acuminata are in the same family (Musaceae).

Exam tip

Define binomial nomenclature and write a name correctly with capital/small letters and italics or underline.

Must remember
  • Two parts: Genus + specific epithet
  • Capital + small letter
  • Italic print or underline by hand

notes.title: 2.5 Common Ethiopian animals and plants: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.5

Common Ethiopian animals and plants

Ethiopia's location, topography, and climates make it a biodiversity hotspot with high endemicity.

Competency: classify common Ethiopian animals and plants based on taxonomic categories

Why Ethiopia is special

  • High wild plant and animal diversity with many endemic species
  • Primary centre of diversity for field crops such as noug (Guizotia abyssinica), tef (Eragrostis tef), and Ethiopian mustard (Brassica carinata)
  • Wide diversity also in barley, sorghum, durum wheat, finger millet, faba bean, chickpea, lentil, and cowpea
  • Gateway for domestic animals from Asia to Africa; diverse ecology favoured diversification

Selected Ethiopian examples (from the textbook table)

  • Elephant: Loxodonta africana (Animalia → Chordata → Mammalia)
  • Ethiopian wolf: Canis simensis
  • Gelada: Theropithecus gelada
  • Lion: Panthera leo
  • Walia ibex: Capra walie
  • Ostrich: Struthio camelus (bird / Aves)
  • Wattled ibis: Bostrychia carunculata
  • Enset: Ensete ventricosum (Plantae)
  • Maize: Zea mays
  • Noug: Guizotia abyssinica
  • Tef: Eragrostis tef
  • Wheat: Triticum aestivum

Dichotomous keys

Key term Dichotomous key. Identification tool made of pairs of contrasting features (dichotomous = two branches). Start with general traits, then more specific ones.
  • At each step choose one of two options, then move to the next item.
  • Example idea: cold-blooded (poikilothermic) vs warm-blooded (homoiothermic) leads to different next choices.
  • Can place an organism into class, genus, or species when features are clear.
Exam tip

Know Ethiopia as a primary centre for tef and noug. Write scientific names of common local species correctly.

Must remember
  • Ethiopia = biodiversity hotspot + crop diversity centre
  • Tef = Eragrostis tef; noug = Guizotia abyssinica
  • Dichotomous key = paired choices for identification

notes.title: 2.6 The five-kingdom system of classification: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.6

The five-kingdom system of classification

Two kingdoms (plants and animals) were not enough. Whittaker (1969) proposed five kingdoms.

Competency: list the characteristic features of the five kingdoms

Criteria used: cell structure, body organization, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships.

Five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

Attention · Viruses

Viruses are not placed in a kingdom. They are particles (nucleic acid DNA or RNA in a protein coat). They do not grow, develop, or respire on their own. They replicate only inside a host cell.

2.6.1 Kingdom Monera

Key termKingdom Monera. Simple prokaryotic unicellular organisms (eubacteria and archaebacteria). No well-defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Most have a rigid cell wall. Nutrition may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
  • Includes eubacteria (true bacteria) and archaebacteria (Archaea)
  • Simple prokaryotic unicellular organisms
  • No well-defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles
  • Most have a rigid cell wall
  • Nutrition: autotrophs or heterotrophs (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic forms exist)
  • Decomposers and mineralizers in the biosphere
  • Eubacteria: many habitats; some cause disease (strep throat, pneumonia, tuberculosis); most are harmless or helpful (digestion, cheese, yogurt)
  • Archaea: extreme environments (swamps, deep-ocean vents, evaporating ponds); often no oxygen; different cell walls from bacteria
Key term Chemosynthetic. Making food using chemical reactions (not only sunlight).

2.6.2 Kingdom Protista

Key termKingdom Protista. Most diverse kingdom. Shared feature: they are eukaryotes. May be unicellular or multicellular, microscopic or large, autotroph or heterotroph (protozoans, algae, and some fungus-like forms).
  • Most diverse kingdom. No single "typical" protist
  • Shared feature: they are eukaryotes
  • Unicellular or multicellular; microscopic or large; autotroph or heterotroph
  • Protozoans: animal-like, usually one cell
  • Algae: plant-like, photosynthetic, no roots/stems/leaves. Unicellular algae support aquatic food chains and make much atmospheric oxygen
  • Some fungus-like forms exist but with different cell walls from fungi

2.6.3 Kingdom Fungi

Key termKingdom Fungi. Eukaryotes such as yeasts, moulds, and mushrooms. Cell wall of chitin and polysaccharides. Heterotrophs that absorb food after extracellular digestion.
  • Eukaryotes: yeasts, moulds, mushrooms
  • Except yeasts, mostly filamentous multicellular bodies of hyphae
  • Cell wall of chitin and polysaccharides
  • Heterotrophs that absorb food after extracellular digestion (enzymes secreted outside the cells)
  • Many are saprophytes (decomposers) on dead material
  • May be parasites (example: athlete's foot, Candida) or mutualists (example: with termites, lichens with algae, mycorrhiza with plant roots)
  • Reproduce vegetatively (fragmentation, fission, budding), by spores, or sexually
  • Ethiopian link: yeast used for injera rising and drinks such as tej, tella, and beer
Key terms Parasitism. One benefits; the other is harmed.
Mutualism. Both species benefit.
Symbiosis. Close permanent association between different species.

2.6.4 Kingdom Plantae

Key termKingdom Plantae. Eukaryotic, multicellular autotrophs. Photosynthesis with chloroplasts and chlorophyll. Rigid cell wall of cellulose.
  • Eukaryotic, multicellular autotrophs
  • Photosynthesis with chloroplasts and chlorophyll; release oxygen
  • Mostly land-living and stationary; sexual reproduction common; also vegetative propagation
  • Rigid cell wall of cellulose
  • Over 250,000 species: flowering plants, mosses, ferns, conifers
Key termBryophytes. Mosses, liverworts, hornworts; no vascular tissue; seedless.
Key termGymnosperms. Vascular plants with naked seeds (example: conifers); no flowers or fruits.
Key termAngiosperms. Vascular plants with flowers and fruits. Monocots (one seed leaf, parallel veins) and dicots (two seed leaves, branching veins).

2.6.5 Kingdom Animalia

Key termKingdom Animalia. Multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes. Ingest food then digest inside the body. No cell walls; structural proteins such as collagen hold cells together.
  • Multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes
  • Ingest food, then digest with enzymes inside the body (unlike fungi absorption)
  • No cell walls; cells held by structural proteins such as collagen (animals only)
  • Many have muscle and nerve cells for movement and impulses
  • Most reproduce sexually
Key termInvertebrates. Animals with no backbone (sponges, flatworms, roundworms, annelids, molluscs, arthropods such as insects).
Key termVertebrates. Animals with a backbone (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals).
Exam tip

Compare kingdoms by cell type, nutrition, and cell wall material (peptidoglycan / chitin / cellulose / none).

Must remember
  • Five kingdoms + viruses outside
  • Monera = prokaryotes; others = eukaryotes (Protista onward)
  • Fungi absorb; animals ingest; plants photosynthesize
  • Invertebrate vs vertebrate

notes.title: 2.7 Renowned taxonomists in Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.7

Renowned taxonomists in Ethiopia

Ethiopia has rich biodiversity, but taxonomic work needs trained scientists. Several Ethiopian taxonomists have made major contributions.

Competency: appreciate the works of renowned taxonomists in Ethiopia

  • Ethiopia has high species diversity and endemicity, yet many groups are still poorly studied at gene, species, and ecosystem levels.
  • One reason: historically few taxonomists relative to the country's richness.
  • Over about six decades, Ethiopia has trained scientists who published Flora volumes and related work.

Plant taxonomists named in the textbook

  • Professor Sebsebe Demissew: research with universities in Europe and Africa; books and articles on Ethiopian and African vegetation and plants; leadership roles (Biological Society of Ethiopia; AETFAT; International Association for Plant Taxonomy); director of Flora of Ethiopia and Gullele Botanic Garden.
  • Dr. Mesfin Taddese
  • Professor Ensermu Kelbessa
  • Professor Silesh Nemomissa

Animal taxonomy

  • Professor Abebe Getahun: contributions to animal taxonomy
Exam tip

Name at least two Ethiopian taxonomists and state that their work supports Flora of Ethiopia and biodiversity knowledge.

Must remember
  • Ethiopia needs taxonomy because biodiversity is high and still under-documented
  • Remember Sebsebe Demissew and at least one other name from the list

notes.title: Cells: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 3

Cells

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. This unit covers what a cell is, cell theory, organelles, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells, plant vs animal cells, microscope observation, transport across membranes, and levels of organization.

Study lessons 3.1 to 3.8 in order. Use this page to check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 3
  • Define a cell (lesson 3.1)
  • Outline the contributions of Theodor Schwann and Matthias Schleiden to the development of the cell theory (lesson 3.2)
  • Compare and contrast the structures of plant and animal cells (lessons 3.3, 3.5)
  • Differentiate between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells (lesson 3.4)
  • Make temporary slides of plant and animal cells (lesson 3.6)
  • Observe and draw animal and plant cell parts under the microscope (lesson 3.6)
  • Conduct experiments about the movement of substances across animal and plant cells (osmosis, diffusion) (lesson 3.7)
  • Construct with examples the different levels of biological organization (lesson 3.8)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • A cell is the smallest and basic unit of living things. All living things are composed of cells.
  • Cell theory: organisms are made of one or more cells; cells are the smallest unit of life; cells arise only from pre-existing cells.
  • Hooke named cells (1665). Leeuwenhoek saw microbes. Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) stated cells as units of life. Virchow: cells from cells.
  • Common features: membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material, energy system.
  • Prokaryotic: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles (bacteria). Eukaryotic: nucleus + organelles (plants, animals, fungi, protists).
  • Plant only: cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts, large vacuole. Animal only: centrioles, lysosomes (as emphasized in the textbook).
  • Diffusion and osmosis are passive. Active transport needs energy and moves against the gradient.
  • Organization: atoms → molecules → organelles → cells → tissues → organs → systems → organism.

notes.title: 3.1 What is a cell?: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.1

What is a cell?

Everything you do depends on processes that happen inside cells.

Competency: define a cell

Key term Cell. The smallest and basic unit of living things. All living things are composed of cells.
  • Unicellular organisms: one cell (example: paramecium). Most are too small to see without a microscope. Exceptions can be seen (example: chicken egg cell).
  • Multicellular organisms: many specialized cells working together (plants, animals, humans).

In the human body, muscle cells help movement, nerve cells gather information, and brain cells help turn messages into action.

Most cells are microscopic. Extreme examples from the textbook:

  • Ostrich egg: one huge cell (about 6 inches across, about 1.36 kg)
  • Some nerve cells can stretch several feet; giant squid nerve cells can be more than 30 feet long
Exam tip

Define a cell and give one unicellular and one multicellular example.

Must remember
  • Cell = basic unit of life
  • Unicellular vs multicellular

notes.title: 3.2 Cell theory: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.2

Cell theory

Cell theory is the unifying idea of cell biology. Know the scientists and the three statements.

Competency: outline contributions of Schleiden and Schwann (also know Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Virchow)

Key scientists

  • Robert Hooke (1665): first to observe and name cells in cork slices. Saw pore-like boxes. Did not yet know cells are the fundamental unit of all life.
  • Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723): built strong microscopes (up to about 300×). Observed protozoa and bacteria ("animalcules"). Called the father of microbiology.
  • Matthias Schleiden (1838): all plants are made of cells.
  • Theodor Schwann (1839): all animals are made of cells. Together they established cells as the natural unit of structure and function in living things.
  • Rudolf Virchow (1856): cells arise only by division of existing cells.
Key term Cell theory.
  1. Living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  2. Cells are the smallest unit of life.
  3. Cells arise only by the division of a pre-existing cell.

Features shared by living cells

  • Surrounded by a membrane that separates inside from outside
  • Contain genetic material with instructions for cell activities
  • Have an energy release system that powers activities
  • Nothing smaller than a cell can survive as a living structure
Exam tip

State all three points of cell theory and match Schleiden → plants, Schwann → animals, Virchow → cells from cells.

Must remember
  • Three statements of cell theory
  • Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839)

notes.title: 3.3 Cell structure and function: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.3

Cell structure and function

Cells share major parts. Organelles do specialized jobs inside the cytoplasm.

Competency: identify main structures and describe their functions

Key termOrganelle. A distinct structure within a cell with a specific function. Some have membranes; some do not. Examples: nucleus, mitochondria, vesicles, endoplasmic reticulum.

Major structures common to plant and animal cells: nucleus, cytoplasm, and cell (plasma) membrane.

Key termCell wall. Rigid outer layer external to the membrane. Provides structural support and shape. Found in plants (cellulose), fungi, some algae, and bacteria. Not in animal cells.
Key termCell membrane (plasma membrane). Thin, selectively permeable outer covering that separates the cell interior from the surroundings. Controls entry and exit of organic molecules, ions, water, oxygen, and wastes such as CO₂.
Key termCytoplasm. Thick fluid-filled region containing organelles. About 70-80% water plus organic molecules (proteins, carbohydrates) and inorganic ions (sodium, potassium, calcium). Site of many reactions, including protein synthesis.
Key termNucleus. Largest organelle; surrounded by a double membrane. Contains chromosomes with DNA. Determines cell type (blood, liver, muscle, nerve) and controls cell division. The darker nucleolus is where new ribosomes are made. Exceptions: mature mammalian red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements lose their nucleus.
Key termRibosomes. Small structures found in large numbers in all cells. Synthesize proteins. Free in the cytoplasm or attached to rough ER.
Key termEndoplasmic reticulum (ER). Complex system of interconnected double membranes with fluid-filled spaces that transport materials through the cell.
Key termRough ER. ER with ribosomes on its surface (dotted look). Proteins are made and stored here and moved in vesicles.
Key termSmooth ER. ER without ribosomes. Makes lipids.
Key termVesicles. Small membrane sacs that store, transport, and ship materials in the cell (example: ER products to the Golgi).
Key termGolgi apparatus (Golgi body / complex). Smooth, concave membranous structure. Collects, packages, and distributes molecules inside or outside the cell. Named after Camillo Golgi (1898).
Key termMitochondria. Double-membrane organelles; sites of respiration that produce energy ("powerhouse"). Metabolically active cells such as muscle cells contain thousands of mitochondria.
Key termLysosomes. Membrane-bound packages of digestive enzymes. Digest bacteria or other cells taken in; break down unwanted or damaged organelles. Can fuse with food vacuoles.
Key termVacuoles. Single membrane with fluid inside. Large in many plant cells (often more than half the cell volume); small in animal cells. Food vacuoles digest food (phagocytosis). Contractile vacuoles in some freshwater unicells pump out excess water.
Key termChloroplasts. Double-membrane organelles in green plant cells (mainly leaves). Sites of photosynthesis. Contain chlorophyll that traps sunlight to make carbohydrates.
Key termMicrotubules. Small cylindrical fibres in the cytoplasm. Roles include moving chromosomes during cell division.
Key termCentrioles. Structures in animal cells that help anchor microtubules during cell division.
Key termCilia. Short, many, hair-like structures for locomotion or to move fluid next to the cell (example: lining of bronchi).
Key termFlagella. Long, few, thread-like structures that enable a whole cell to move.
Key termPhagocytosis. From Greek phagein (to eat) + kytos (cell). Taking in smaller organisms or food particles into a food vacuole.
Common confusions
  • Cell wall ≠ cell membrane. Wall = rigid support (plants). Membrane = selective control (all cells).
  • Rough ER has ribosomes; smooth ER does not.

notes.title: 3.4 Types of cells: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.4

Types of cells

Two main types by structure: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.

Competency: differentiate eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells

Key terms Prokaryotic (pro = before, karyon = nucleus): cells without a true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Usually smaller (about 1-10 μm). Unicellular. Example: bacteria.
Eukaryotic (eu = true): cells with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Larger (about 10-100 μm). Usually multicellular organisms (plants, animals). Also protists and fungi.

Comparison (from the textbook)

  • Organelles: eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles (nucleus, ER). Prokaryotes do not.
  • Ribosomes: relatively large in eukaryotes; relatively small in prokaryotes.
  • DNA: eukaryotes: long strands with proteins. Prokaryotes: DNA not with those proteins; circular plasmids may be present.
  • Cell wall: always in plant cells (cellulose); never in animal cells. Always in prokaryotes (mainly peptidoglycan).
  • Cilia/flagella: sometimes in eukaryotes. Some prokaryotes have flagella of different structure.

Prokaryotes are thought to have evolved first. Their cell wall adds protection, shape, and helps prevent dehydration.

Exam tip

Best short difference: nucleus and membrane-bound organelles present in eukaryotes, absent in prokaryotes.

Must remember
  • Prokaryote = no nucleus (bacteria)
  • Eukaryote = true nucleus + organelles

notes.title: 3.5 Animal and plant cells: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.5

Animal and plant cells

Same basic plan, with important differences you must compare in exams.

Competency: compare and contrast plant and animal cells

Shared features (both cell types)

Key termCell membrane. Selectively permeable covering that controls what enters and leaves.
Key termNucleus. Contains DNA and controls cell activities.
Key termCytoplasm. Fluid region with organelles; site of many reactions.
Key termMitochondria. Sites of respiration that release energy.
Key termGolgi apparatus. Packages and distributes cell products.

Also typically shared: ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth).

Plant cells only (or mainly)

Key termCell wall. Rigid cellulose wall outside the membrane; support and shape.
Key termChloroplast. Photosynthesis organelle with chlorophyll; mainly in green parts, especially leaves.
Key termLarge permanent vacuole. Membrane-bound fluid space that may fill more than half the cell. Fluid holds pigments, enzymes, sugars, organic compounds, salts, O₂, and CO₂. Helps regulate osmotic water flow in and out.

Animal cells (textbook emphasis)

Key termCentrioles. Help organise microtubules during cell division.
Key termLysosomes. Digestive enzyme packages for breaking down materials and damaged organelles.

Plant cells are often larger and easier to see under a light microscope than animal cells.

Exam tip

Use a present/absent table: cell wall, chloroplast, large vacuole, centriole, lysosome.

notes.title: 3.6 Observing cells under a microscope: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.6

Observing cells under a microscope

Practise temporary slides, staining, and drawing what you see.

Competency: make temporary slides; observe and draw cell parts

A microscope magnifies small objects using lenses that bend light toward the eye.

Plant cells (onion epidermis)

  1. Peel epidermal tissue from the inner side of an onion bulb.
  2. Place a small square on a slide.
  3. Add iodine stain (makes structures clearer).
  4. Lower a coverslip at about 45° to avoid air bubbles.
  5. Wait a few minutes for the stain.
  6. Focus on low power first, then higher power.
  7. Draw and label: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus.

Animal cells (cheek epithelium)

  1. Rinse mouth. Collect cheek cells gently with a clean cotton bud.
  2. Smear saliva sample on a slide. Dispose of bud in alcohol.
  3. Stain with methylene blue.
  4. Add coverslip carefully. Focus low power first.
  5. Draw and label: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus.
  6. Disinfect or autoclave used slides before washing.
Safety

Cheek-cell work needs hygiene precautions (including infection risk). Follow school safety rules.

Must remember
  • Stain improves visibility of nucleus and other parts
  • Start on low power; avoid air bubbles under the coverslip
  • Onion: wall visible. Cheek: no cell wall

notes.title: 3.7 The cell and its environment: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.7

The cell and its environment

The membrane is selectively permeable. Substances move by diffusion, osmosis, or active transport.

Competency: define diffusion and osmosis; describe importance of active transport

Cells need food, salts, and water. They must remove wastes such as CO₂. Movement is passive (diffusion, osmosis) or active (needs energy).

Key term Passive transport. Movement down a concentration gradient (high → low) without energy input.

3.7.1 Diffusion

Key term Diffusion. Movement of molecules from high concentration to low concentration down the concentration gradient.

Example: oxygen enters cells for respiration by diffusion.

Factors that speed diffusion:

  • Steeper concentration gradient
  • Higher temperature (more kinetic energy)
  • Lighter molecules
  • Shorter distance
  • Greater surface area (example: microvilli in intestine and kidney)

Osmosis

Key term Osmosis. Special case of diffusion: water moves from high water concentration (low solute) to lower water concentration (high solute) across a partially permeable membrane.
  • Hypotonic surroundings: water in → plant cell becomes turgid; animal cell may swell and burst (hemolysis in red blood cells).
  • Isotonic: water in and out at equal rates; size stable.
  • Hypertonic: water out → plant cell plasmolyses (membrane pulls from wall; wilting); animal cell shrinks.

Plant cells: strong wall resists bursting; turgor keeps plants upright. Animal cells: no wall, so balance is critical. Vertebrates adjust water via brain and kidneys.

Amoeba: contractile vacuole expels excess water in fresh water.

Rural example: salting meat uses osmosis-related water loss for preservation without a fridge.

3.7.2 Active transport

Key term Active transport. Movement of particles through a membrane from lower to higher concentration (against the gradient) using energy from respiration.
  • Lets cells concentrate useful substances
  • Examples: ion uptake by root hairs; glucose uptake by epithelial cells of villi; nerve cells pump Na⁺/K⁺ to keep unequal ion levels
Common confusions
  • Diffusion/osmosis = down gradient, no energy. Active transport = against gradient, needs energy.
  • Osmosis is about water, not all solutes.
Must remember
  • Diffusion: high → low
  • Osmosis: water across a partially permeable membrane
  • Active transport: low → high + energy

notes.title: 3.8 Levels of biological organization: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.8

Levels of biological organization

Life is hierarchical: each level builds on the one below it.

Competency: construct with examples the different levels of biological organization; define tissue, organ, and organ system

Life forms a hierarchy from atoms to complex multicellular organisms, then beyond the individual to populations, communities, ecosystems, and the biosphere.

Key termAtom. The fundamental element of matter.
Key termMolecule. Cluster of atoms joined by chemical bonds. Complex biological molecules are assembled into organelles.
Key termOrganelle. Tiny structure inside a membrane-bounded cell (example: nucleus, mitochondrion).
Key termCell. Membrane-bounded unit that is the smallest level able to show the characteristics of life. Many cells become specialized in shape and chemistry for one job.
Key termTissue. Group of similar cells that act as a functional unit (example: nerve tissue; muscle contracts to cause movement; xylem carries water in plants). Leaf tissues include epidermis, palisade, spongy, xylem, and phloem.
Key termOrgan. Body structure of several different tissues acting as a structural and functional unit (example: stomach with epithelial, gland, and muscle tissues; heart, lungs, intestines, brain, eyes; in flowering plants: root, stem, leaves).
Key termOrgan system (system). Different organs working together (example: digestive system = stomach, intestine, and related organs).
Key termOrganism. Independent plant or animal formed when organs and systems work together.

Beyond the individual: population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.

Exam tip

Place examples correctly: muscle cells = cell level; muscle tissue = tissue; stomach = organ; digestive system = system.

Must remember
  • Tissue = similar cells, one function
  • Organ = several tissues, one special function
  • System = organs working together

notes.title: Reproduction: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 4

Reproduction

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. This unit covers asexual and sexual reproduction, human puberty, reproductive structures, the menstrual cycle, fertilization and pregnancy, birth control, and STI transmission and prevention.

Study lessons 4.1 to 4.11 in order. Use this page to check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 4
  • Appreciate that life perpetuates from generation to generation through reproduction (lesson 4.1)
  • Define asexual and sexual reproductions (lessons 4.1, 4.2, 4.4)
  • Describe asexual reproductions in bacteria, fungi, animals, and plants (lessons 4.2, 4.3)
  • Compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction (lessons 4.2, 4.4)
  • Describe the biological, psychological, and social changes during the puberty stage (lesson 4.5)
  • Differentiate between the primary and secondary sexual characteristics of males and females in humans (lesson 4.5)
  • Identify the structure and functions of the male reproductive organs (lesson 4.6)
  • Identify female reproductive structures and their functions (lesson 4.7)
  • Outline the phases of the menstrual cycle (lesson 4.8)
  • Define fertilization and pregnancy (lesson 4.9)
  • Discuss the methods of prevention of pregnancy (lesson 4.10)
  • Describe the types, modes of transmission and preventive mechanisms of sexually transmitted diseases (lesson 4.11)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Reproduction continues life across generations. Modes: asexual (one parent, no gametes) and sexual (gametes fuse).
  • Asexual forms: fission, fragmentation, budding, vegetative propagation, parthenogenesis. Absent in vertebrates.
  • Sexual reproduction: gametes by meiosis → fertilization → zygote.
  • Primary vs secondary sexual characteristics; puberty changes are biological, psychological, and social.
  • Male: testes (sperm + testosterone) in scrotum; epididymis → vas deferens → urethra; semen includes gland secretions.
  • Female: ovaries (eggs + hormones); oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina. Ovulation about day 14 of a ~28-day cycle.
  • Menstrual cycle: flow, follicular, luteal phases. FSH and LH from pituitary; estrogens and progesterone from ovary/corpus luteum.
  • Fertilization usually in oviduct. Implantation in uterus. Embryo → fetus after about 8 weeks. Placenta and umbilical cord exchange materials.
  • Family planning: natural, barrier, hormonal, IUD, surgical. Some methods also reduce STI risk (example: condoms).
  • Common STIs in Ethiopia include trichomoniasis, syphilis, gonorrhea, chancroid, and HIV/AIDS. Prevention: abstinence, fidelity, condoms, early treatment.

notes.title: 4.1 Introduction to reproduction: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.1

Introduction to reproduction

Individuals die, but species continue because organisms reproduce their own kind.

Competency: appreciate that life perpetuates through reproduction; define asexual and sexual reproduction

Key term Reproduction. The ability of organisms to form their own kind. One of the clearest distinctions between living and non-living matter.
Key term Asexual reproduction. Reproduction that involves one parent and does not require special reproductive organs or gametes in the basic sense. Offspring are identical copies of the parent (clones), so there is little genetic variation among them.
Key term Sexual reproduction. Reproduction that usually involves two parents. Each parent contributes germ cells (gametes: egg or sperm). Fertilization joins them and produces a new individual that differs from the parents (variation).
Key term Gamete. A sex cell (egg or sperm) produced by reproductive organs, usually by meiosis.
Key term Fertilization. Union of male and female gametes to form a zygote.
Must remember
  • Reproduction = own kind continues
  • Asexual = one parent, identical copies; sexual = gametes + fertilization + variation

notes.title: 4.2 Asexual reproduction: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.2

Asexual reproduction

New individuals without eggs or sperm, and without a second parent.

Competency: define asexual reproduction; advantages and disadvantages

Key term Asexual reproduction. Production of individuals without gametes (eggs or sperm). No sex and no second parent.
  • Found in bacteria, unicellular eukaryotes, many invertebrates, fungi, and plants
  • Absent among vertebrates
  • Basic forms: fission (binary and multiple), budding, fragmentation (and related plant methods)
  • Example: a stem piece planted in soil may root and become a full plant

Advantages

  • No mate needed
  • No gametes needed
  • Useful parent traits all pass to offspring
  • Offspring grow in the same favourable place as the parent
  • Many asexual plants store food that supports survival

Disadvantages

  • Little variation, so adaptation to change is unlikely
  • If the parent has no disease resistance, offspring lack it too
  • Little dispersal can cause competition for nutrients, water, and light
Exam tip

Know that asexual offspring are genetically identical to the parent, and that vertebrates do not reproduce asexually.

notes.title: 4.3 Types of asexual reproduction: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.3

Types of asexual reproduction

Know each mechanism and a clear example.

Competency: describe asexual reproduction in bacteria, fungi, animals, and plants

4.3.1 Fission

  • Binary fission: parent divides into two roughly equal parts (bacteria, algae, protozoa). In bacteria, DNA is copied first so each daughter gets a copy.
  • Multiple fission: nucleus divides many times; many daughter cells form with bits of cytoplasm (example: some parasitic protozoa such as malaria parasites).

4.3.2 Fragmentation

  • Parent breaks into parts; each part can become a whole organism
  • Examples: Spirogyra filaments; worms and many invertebrates that regenerate missing parts

4.3.3 Budding

  • Division into unequal parts
  • A bulge forms; nucleus divides; bud detaches
  • Examples: yeast; hydra

Sporulation (fungi): many fungi form spores. Spores disperse (often by air) and grow into new hyphae/mycelium if conditions are good. Examples: Penicillium, Mucor.

4.3.4 Vegetative propagation (plants)

Natural:

  • Stolons / runners: grow along soil surface; new plant at nodes (example: strawberry)
  • Rhizomes: underground horizontal stems with buds (example: couch grass)
  • Corms: rounded fleshy storage stems (example: gladiolus)
  • Tubers: swollen stem ends storing starch with buds (example: potato)
  • Bulbs: underground storage with fleshy leaves (example: onion)

Artificial: grafting (scion + stock), cutting, layering, marcotting, micro-propagation.

4.3.5 Parthenogenesis

Key term Parthenogenesis. An unfertilized egg develops into an adult ("virgin birth"). Example: honeybee drones develop from unfertilized eggs; workers are females from fertilized eggs.
Must remember
  • Binary = two equal; budding = unequal
  • Potato tuber and strawberry runner are classic plant examples
  • Parthenogenesis = development without fertilization

notes.title: 4.4 Sexual reproduction in humans: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.4

Sexual reproduction in humans

Two parents, gametes, fertilization, then a zygote that grows into a new individual.

Competency: define sexual reproduction; compare with asexual

Key term Sexual reproduction. Involves sex cells (gametes) made in reproductive organs by meiosis. Usually two parents. Fertilization joins sperm and egg to form a zygote.
Key term Zygote. The first cell of a new individual formed when sperm and egg unite.
Key term Internal fertilization. Sperm and egg join inside the female body.
Key term External fertilization. Sperm and egg join outside the bodies (common in many aquatic animals).
  • Female gametes are larger and not mobile; male gametes are smaller and mobile
  • Offspring differ from each other (variation), unlike identical asexual offspring
  • Later lessons cover male and female systems, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and birth control
Must remember
  • Gametes → fertilization → zygote
  • Sexual = variation; asexual = identical copies

notes.title: 4.5 Primary and secondary sexual characteristics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.5

Primary and secondary sexual characteristics

Puberty is when the body becomes capable of sexual reproduction, with biological, psychological, and social changes.

Competency: differentiate primary vs secondary traits; describe puberty changes

Key terms Primary sexual characteristics. Present at birth. Male: penis, scrotum, testes. Female: vagina, uterus, ovaries.
Secondary sexual characteristics. Develop at puberty as sexual maturity approaches.

Secondary characteristics in males

  • Growth and maintenance of male sex organs
  • More body hair; more muscle mass
  • Growth of long bones of arms and legs
  • Deepening of the voice

Secondary characteristics in females

  • More hair under arms and in the pubic area
  • Hips broaden; more fat in breasts, buttocks, and thighs
  • Menstrual cycle begins

Hormones from the endocrine system control puberty. In males, the hypothalamus and pituitary interact; testes produce testosterone. In females, LH helps eggs to be released; ovaries produce estrogens and progesterone.

Psychological and social changes

  • Body image changes quickly; worry about being "normal" can lower self-esteem
  • Timing of puberty varies; early or late development can cause stress
  • Adolescents work toward economic and moral adulthood and more independence from family
Exam tip

Primary = born with. Secondary = appear at puberty. List male and female examples separately.

notes.title: 4.6 Male reproductive structures: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.6

Male reproductive structures

Testes make sperm and testosterone. Accessory glands help form semen.

Competency: identify male structures and functions

  • Testes: sperm production in seminiferous tubules; testosterone from cells between tubules
  • Scrotum: holds testes outside the abdomen (slightly cooler; needed for viable sperm)
  • Epididymis: sperm mature here
  • Vas deferens: carries mature sperm toward the urethra
  • Urethra: carries sperm and urine through the penis
  • Seminal vesicles: fructose-rich fluid that feeds sperm
  • Prostate gland: alkaline secretions raise pH in the female tract (better for sperm)
  • Bulbourethral glands: lubricating mucus; helps clear residual urine from urethra
  • Semen: sperm mixed with seminal vesicle and prostate secretions
  • Penis: organ of intercourse

Sperm structure and function

  • Head: genetic material + enzymes to help penetrate the egg
  • Midpiece: many mitochondria for energy
  • Flagellum (tail): swimming toward the egg
Must remember
  • Path: seminiferous tubules → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra
  • Scrotum = cooler temperature for sperm

notes.title: 4.7 Female reproductive structures: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.7

Female reproductive structures

Ovaries make eggs and hormones. The uterus is where pregnancy develops.

Competency: identify female structures and functions

  • Ovaries: produce and release eggs; secrete estrogens and progesterone
  • Estrogens: female secondary characteristics; help maintain the tract lining
  • Progesterone: thickens the lining for pregnancy
  • Oviduct (Fallopian tube): carries egg toward uterus; usual site of fertilization
  • Uterus: hollow, pear-shaped; lining rich in glands, connective tissue, blood vessels
  • Cervix: narrow opening from uterus into vagina
  • Vagina: organ of intercourse and birth canal
  • Labia majora / labia minora: outer and inner folds
  • Clitoris: sensitive erectile tissue
Key term Ovulation. About two weeks into a ~28-day cycle, a mature follicle ruptures and releases an egg into the oviduct. Remaining follicle cells form the hormone-secreting corpus luteum. If no pregnancy, the corpus luteum breaks down.

A girl is born with about 2 million eggs. From puberty, eggs usually mature one at a time in the ovarian cycle.

Must remember
  • Ovary → oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina
  • Ovulation ≈ mid-cycle; fertilization usually in oviduct

notes.title: 4.8 The menstrual cycle: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.8

The menstrual cycle

Monthly changes in ovary and uterus prepare for possible pregnancy.

Competency: outline the phases of the menstrual cycle

Day 1 = start of menstruation (flow of uterine lining and some blood through cervix and vagina).

  • Follicular phase: FSH stimulates follicle maturation. Follicle cells secrete estrogens → endometrium thickens. Rising estrogens lead to more LH from the pituitary. LH surge triggers ovulation.
  • Luteal phase: after ovulation, LH forms the corpus luteum. Corpus luteum secretes estrogens and much progesterone → lining thickens and becomes ready for pregnancy.
  • If no pregnancy, corpus luteum breaks down → hormone drop → menstruation begins again.
Key terms FSH / LH. Pituitary hormones controlling the ovarian cycle.
Menopause. No follicles left to mature; estrogen and progesterone fall; cycles stop (known in humans and two whale species).

Menstrual hygiene (textbook tips)

  • Breathable clothing; change pads regularly
  • Keep the outer genital area clean; wipe front to back; rinse vulva with water
  • Prefer unscented products; drink enough fluids
  • Track periods; seek annual reproductive health check-ups when available
Exam tip

Link hormones: FSH matures follicle; LH triggers ovulation; progesterone from corpus luteum prepares uterus.

notes.title: 4.9 Fertilization and pregnancy: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.9

Fertilization and pregnancy

Sperm meets egg; the zygote implants and grows with help from the placenta.

Competency: define fertilization and pregnancy

Key terms Fertilization. Sperm enters the egg and male and female nuclei fuse.
Implantation. Early embryo sinks into the uterine lining.
Pregnancy. Development of the embryo/fetus in the uterus.
  • Sperm swim through cervix and uterus into the oviduct
  • Egg survives about 24 hours; sperm may fertilize for about 2-3 days → short fertile window (~4 days per month)
  • Zygote divides → ball of cells → travels to uterus → implants
  • After about 8 weeks, when organs are formed, the embryo is called a fetus
  • Amnion (water sac) with amniotic fluid protects the embryo
  • Placenta exchanges materials with mother; linked by umbilical cord. O₂ and nutrients (glucose, amino acids) to embryo; CO₂ to mother. Maternal and embryo blood do not mix

Twins

  • Identical (monozygotic): one zygote; same sex; look very alike
  • Fraternal (dizygotic): two zygotes; may differ like ordinary siblings
Must remember
  • Fertilization = fusion of nuclei (usually in oviduct)
  • Implantation in uterus; placenta feeds the embryo

notes.title: 4.10 Methods of birth control: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.10

Methods of birth control

Family planning spaces births and limits family size. Methods are natural or artificial.

Competency: discuss methods of preventing pregnancy

Textbook benefits include fewer pregnancy risks, lower infant mortality, more education and empowerment, fewer adolescent pregnancies, and slower population growth. Some methods (condoms) also reduce STI/HIV transmission.

Natural methods

  • Abstinence: no intercourse; also prevents STIs
  • Fertility awareness: calendar/standard days, symptothermal, ovulation/mucus methods (need partner cooperation; less reliable than many artificial methods)
  • Withdrawal: pull out before ejaculation; no STI protection; needs self-control
  • Temperature rise of about 0.5 °C around ovulation; mucus becomes more fluid near ovulation

Barrier and related

  • Male / female condoms: barrier to sperm and many pathogens
  • Diaphragm: rubber disc covers cervix; better with spermicide; little STI protection
  • Spermicides: kill/immobilize sperm; weak alone; stronger with condom/diaphragm

IUD and hormonal

  • IUD (coil): T-shaped device in uterus; helps prevent implantation; highly effective
  • Combined pill: estrogen + progesterone-like hormones suppress ovulation; take for 21 days between periods; does not protect against STIs
  • Implant: small tube under skin releases progesterone (~3 years)
  • Injection: progesterone effect for weeks; thickens cervical mucus; thins uterus lining

Surgical (sterilization)

  • Vasectomy: cut/seal sperm ducts; semen without sperm; desire and hormones unchanged
  • Tubal ligation: seal/tie oviducts so eggs cannot reach uterus
  • Considered permanent (sometimes reversible with microsurgery)
Exam tip

Classify methods as natural, barrier, hormonal, IUD, or surgical. Note which also reduce STI risk.

notes.title: 4.11 Sexually transmitted infections: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.11

Sexually transmitted infections

STIs spread mainly by sexual contact. Know common types in Ethiopia, transmission, and prevention.

Competency: describe types, transmission, and prevention of STIs

Common STIs named in the textbook for Ethiopia: trichomoniasis, syphilis, gonorrhea, chancroid, and HIV/AIDS.

  • Trichomoniasis: protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. May cause discharge and itching; untreated can affect fertility. Treat both partners with antiprotozoal medicine.
  • Chlamydia: bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. Often silent in women; can scar tracts and cause infertility; can pass to newborn. Antibiotics.
  • Gonorrhea: bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Painful urination and discharge often in men; many women have no early symptoms; can cause sterility. Antibiotics (resistance is rising).
  • HIV/AIDS: HIV attacks immune cells and can lead to AIDS. Spread by blood/body fluids: sex, shared needles, contaminated transfusion, mother to child (pregnancy, birth, breast milk). Early AIDS symptoms may include swollen nodes, weight loss, fever, night sweats, fatigue. Antibiotics do not cure HIV (it is viral).

Prevention and response

  • Abstinence from intimate sexual contact
  • Faithfulness to one uninfected partner
  • Male or female condoms as barriers
  • Do not share needles; test blood before transfusion
  • Seek confidential treatment early; partners need treatment too
  • Bacterial STIs (example: syphilis, gonorrhea) may respond to antibiotics if treated early; HIV needs antiviral care, not antibiotics
Must remember
  • STI = infection spread mainly by sexual contact
  • Prevention: abstinence, fidelity, condoms, no shared needles
  • HIV is viral; many other common STIs are bacterial or protozoan

notes.title: Human Health, Nutrition, and Disease: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 5

Human Health, Nutrition, and Disease

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. This unit covers food and nutrients, balanced diets, deficiency diseases, malnutrition, substance abuse, infectious and non-infectious diseases, and Ethiopian nutritionists.

Study lessons 5.1 to 5.9 in order. Use this page to check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 5
  • Define nutrition (lesson 5.2)
  • List the types of nutrients (lesson 5.3)
  • Describe the role of a balanced diet especially for children, nursing mothers, athletes, and people with HIV/AIDS (lesson 5.4)
  • Describe with examples the sources and deficiency diseases of vitamins and minerals (lessons 5.3, 5.5)
  • Define malnutrition (lesson 5.6)
  • Discuss the feeding habits that may lead to obesity (lesson 5.6)
  • Examine the effects of smoking, alcohol use, chewing khat, cannabis, and other drug use on wellbeing (lesson 5.7)
  • Explain the modes of transmission and prevention of infectious and noninfectious diseases (lesson 5.8)
  • List and appreciate renowned nutritionists in Ethiopia (lesson 5.9)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Food sustains life: growth, energy, repair, and protection from deficiency disease.
  • Nutrition = taking in food and converting it to energy and vital nutrients.
  • Nutrient classes: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, water (+ fibre/roughage).
  • Energy approx.: carb 16 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g, lipid 37 kJ/g.
  • Balanced diet = all nutrients in correct amounts. Needs vary by age, sex, activity, pregnancy, breastfeeding.
  • Deficiency examples: kwashiorkor (protein), marasmus (energy), anaemia (iron), rickets (vitamin D), scurvy (vitamin C).
  • Malnutrition = insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced nutrients. Includes under-nutrition and obesity.
  • Substance abuse harms health and society (tobacco, alcohol, khat, cannabis, doping).
  • Infectious diseases spread by pathogens; non-infectious do not. Know HIV, TB, malaria, COVID-19 basics.

notes.title: 5.1 What is food?: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.1

What is food?

Food keeps living things alive, growing, and active.

Key term Food. Any beneficial substance eaten, drunk, or taken into the body to sustain life, provide energy, and promote growth. Usually from plants, animals, or fungi. Contains essential nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, and minerals).
Key term Nutrient. An important chemical substance found in foods and used for growth, energy, and health (see lesson 5.3 for each class).

Importance of food

  • Growth: materials for new cells, tissues, and organs
  • Energy: fuels running, moving, growing, reproducing, and other activities
  • Replacement: repair and replace damaged cells
  • Protection: enough of the right food groups helps prevent deficiency diseases and supports health
Must remember
  • Food = energy + materials for growth and repair

notes.title: 5.2 Nutrition: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.2

Nutrition

Nutrition is how food becomes usable energy and nutrients for life.

Competency: define nutrition

Key term Nutrition. The process of taking in food and converting it into energy and other vital nutrients required for life.
  • Energy from food supports body activities (movement, growth, repair, and other work)
  • Food keeps us alive and nourishes growth, cell repair, and good health
  • Without enough nutrition, deficiency diseases and poor growth can follow (see lessons 5.5 and 5.6)
Exam tip

Write the definition in one clear sentence: take in food → convert to energy and nutrients.

Must remember
  • Nutrition ≠ food alone. Nutrition is the process of taking in and using food.

notes.title: 5.3 Nutrients: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.3

Nutrients

Nutrients are the chemical substances in food that we need to grow, get energy, and stay healthy.

Competency: list types of nutrients; explain importance and deficiency links

Key termNutrients. Important chemical substances found in foods. The body needs them for growth, energy, and health. Classes: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids (fats and oils), vitamins, minerals, and water.
Key termMacronutrients. Nutrients needed in large amounts: carbohydrate, protein, and fats.
Key termMicronutrients. Nutrients needed in very small amounts: vitamins and minerals. They do not supply much energy, but they regulate metabolism and help the body use proteins, fats, and carbohydrates. Minerals also help build body structures.
Key termCarbohydrates. Main energy nutrient (C, H, O). About 16 kJ per gram. Made by green plants (photosynthesis → starch). Starch foods: potatoes, bread, maize, rice, cereals. Sugars: sucrose, fruits, some vegetables. Animals store carbohydrate as glycogen. Fibre (roughage) is mainly indigestible plant cell wall (cellulose). It adds bulk, softens faeces, and supports colon health.
Key termFats and oils (lipids). High-energy nutrients (about 37 kJ per gram). Fats are usually animal and solid at room temperature (meat, milk, cheese, butter, egg yolk). Oils are usually plant and liquid (example: sunflower). Lipids form adipose tissue under the skin (reduces heat loss) and help absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Key termProteins. Nutrients for growth and new cells, made of amino acids (C, H, O, N). About 17 kJ per gram. Animal sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese. Plant sources: beans, chickpea, soybeans, nuts.
Key termVitamins. Organic substances needed in small amounts for cell chemical reactions. Missing a vitamin can cause a deficiency disease. Examples: A, E, B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), C.
Key termMinerals. Inorganic nutrients needed in small amounts. Calcium: bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve impulses (milk, cheese). Iron: haemoglobin for O₂ transport (red meat, liver, kidney, eggs, groundnuts, tikur teff). Iodine: thyroid function (iodized salt, seafood). Phosphorus: builds bones.
Key termWater. Main part of blood, lymph, and tissue fluid. Helps transport digested food and remove excess salts and urea.
Must remember
  • Energy per gram: lipid > protein ≈ carbohydrate
  • Iron → haemoglobin; calcium → bones/teeth; iodine → thyroid

notes.title: 5.4 Balanced diets: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.4

Balanced diets

Ethiopia has many cultural foods. A good diet is about the right nutrients in the right amounts.

Competency: role of balanced diet for children, nursing mothers, athletes, people with HIV/AIDS

Key term Balanced diet. A diet that contains all nutrients in the correct amounts and proportions: enough carbohydrate and fat for energy, enough of the right proteins for growth and repair, plus vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water.

Needs depend on age, sex, activity, and lifestyle

  • Children: higher energy than adults because they are growing; more protein for new cells
  • Pregnant woman: more food for the baby; more minerals such as calcium for bones and teeth
  • Breastfeeding mother: higher energy need (textbook table shows higher kcal than a non-pregnant adult woman office worker)
  • Elderly: generally lower energy and protein needs, but still need balance
  • Men vs women: women often have more fat tissue and lower metabolic rate, so often lower energy need than men of similar activity
  • Manual workers and athletes: high energy; athletes also need more protein for muscle
  • People with HIV/AIDS: need careful, adequate balanced nutrition to support health (linked to higher energy/protein needs and recovery in clinical guidance discussed with balanced-diet groups)

Example daily energy values from the textbook table (kcal): 8-year-old ~2031; teenage boy 14 ~2987; teenage girl 14 ~2318; adult office man ~2629 / woman ~2342; adult manual man ~3585 / woman ~2987; pregnant ~2390; breastfeeding ~2748.

Exam tip

Define balanced diet, then explain why children, pregnant/breastfeeding women, and athletes need different amounts.

notes.title: 5.5 Deficiency diseases: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.5

Deficiency diseases

Too little of one nutrient can cause a specific health problem.

Competency: sources and deficiency diseases of vitamins and minerals

Key term Deficiency disease. Health problems from not having enough of a particular nutrient.
  • Marasmus: severe energy shortage (Greek for "decay"). Child becomes very thin; skin may hang in folds. Treat with energy-rich balanced diet.
  • Kwashiorkor: inadequate protein, especially in children. Dry/flaky skin, swollen legs and abdomen, hair colour change, weakness, irritability. Prevent/treat with enough protein.
  • Anaemia: lack of iron → less haemoglobin → less O₂ → less energy. Weak, tired, irritable. Iron-rich food or iron capsules.
  • Rickets: lack of vitamin D → soft/deformed bones (legs bow). Vitamin D helps absorb Ca and P. Body can make vitamin D from morning/evening sunlight; also oily fish, butter, milk, cheese, egg yolk.
  • Scurvy: lack of vitamin C. Bleeding under skin/joints, bleeding gums, poor wound healing. Vitamin C is not stored well, so need it daily. Sources: citrus fruits, tomatoes, fresh green vegetables.

Textbook summary links: protein → kwashiorkor; carbohydrate energy shortage → marasmus; vitamin C → scurvy; vitamin D → rickets; iron → anaemia (low haemoglobin).

Must remember
  • Match nutrient → disease → key symptom
  • Tikur teff and liver are iron-rich Ethiopian-relevant sources

notes.title: 5.6 Malnutrition: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.6

Malnutrition

Malnutrition is not only "too little food." It can also mean too much or the wrong balance.

Competency: define malnutrition; discuss habits that lead to obesity

Key term Malnutrition. Insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced consumption of nutrients that leads to health problems.
  • Causes can include poverty, famine (drought/flood), soil erosion, war, too little land, ignorance of needs
  • Dual burden: under-nutrition and overweight/obesity, plus diet-related non-communicable disease
  • Under-nutrition harms growth, brain development, school performance, and disease resistance
