  • Stunting / wasting / underweight / micronutrient deficiency are forms linked to poor growth and missing vitamins/minerals
  • Too much fat can contribute to coronary heart disease (fatty build-up in arteries)

Obesity

  • Eating more energy than you use → store as fat
  • Often linked to high-fat and sugary foods and low activity
  • Risks: heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, arthritis
  • Control: eat less high-energy food, exercise more, keep a balanced lower-energy diet
Key term BMI. Body mass (kg) / height² (m²). Underweight <18.5; normal 18.5-24.9; overweight 25.0-29.9; obese ≥30. Also: about 20% above recommended weight for height.

Prevention ideas: diverse nutrient-dense foods, avoid junk/sugary foods, regular exercise.

Must remember
  • Malnutrition = too little, too much, or unbalanced
  • Obesity = energy in > energy out

notes.title: 5.7 Substance abuse: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.7

Substance abuse

Legal or illegal substances used wrongly or in excess can damage health, family, and society.

Competency: effects of smoking, alcohol, khat, cannabis, and other drug use

Key terms Drug. Any substance taken into the body that changes chemical reactions (medicinal or recreational).
Substance abuse. Using legal or illegal drugs in the wrong way or in excess.

Tobacco / cigarettes

  • Main chemicals: tar, carbon monoxide, nicotine
  • Tar → cough, chronic bronchitis, carcinogens → lung tumours/cancer; damaged alveoli → emphysema
  • CO binds haemoglobin → carboxyhaemoglobin → less O₂ carried
  • Nicotine → dopamine/pleasure pathway → addiction; raises heart rate and blood pressure; sticky platelets → clotting risk

Alcohol

  • Ethiopian examples: tella, arekie/katikala, beer, wine
  • Short-term: loss of coordination, self-control, judgment; slower reaction time
  • Addiction (alcoholism): tolerance, family and social harm, crime risk
  • Long-term: ulcers, heart disease, brain damage, liver cirrhosis

Other substances

  • Heroin: powerful depressant; related to brain endorphin pathways
  • Cannabis (marijuana): THC; altered mind/time sense, poor concentration/memory; high doses may cause panic, hallucinations, psychosis
  • Khat (Catha edulis): chewed leaves; cathinone stimulates CNS (fresh leaves)
  • Doping: banned performance drugs in sport (unfair + health risks: heart, hormones, mental health, bans, money loss). WADA prohibited list and TUE process

Recovery steps from the textbook: admit the problem, find support, change routine, celebrate small wins, avoid relapse.

Must remember
  • Tobacco trio: tar, CO, nicotine
  • Alcohol depresses judgment and can destroy the liver
  • Khat stimulant = cathinone; cannabis psychoactive = THC

notes.title: 5.8 Infectious and noninfectious diseases: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.8

Infectious and noninfectious diseases

Some diseases spread between people. Others come from diet, genes, chemicals, or lifestyle.

Competency: transmission and prevention of infectious and noninfectious diseases

Key terms Disease. Body not functioning normally (symptoms such as headache, fever, pain, weakness).
Infectious disease. Caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi) and can spread person to person.
Non-infectious disease. Not caused by pathogens (malnutrition, chemicals, inheritance, lifestyle).

How infectious diseases spread

  • Direct contact
  • Contaminated water or food
  • Insect bite
  • Sexual intercourse

Control breaks the transmission cycle (hygiene, safe water, waste disposal, sewage systems far from drinking water, treating cases).

HIV/AIDS

  • HIV attacks T-lymphocytes → weaker immunity → AIDS with opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia, cancers)
  • Spread: blood/body fluids, sex, shared needles, contaminated transfusion, mother to child
  • Prevention: avoid risky sex, condoms, sterile needles, test blood, antiretroviral treatment

Tuberculosis (TB)

  • Bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (rarely M. bovis)
  • Airborne droplets from cough/sneeze; worse in crowded places
  • BCG vaccine (often in infancy); cover coughs; ventilation; avoid undercooked meat and unpasteurized milk for animal-related risk

Malaria

  • Protozoan Plasmodium; vector = female Anopheles mosquito
  • Sexual stage in mosquito; asexual stage in human
  • Control: reduce breeding water, nets/repellents, anti-malarial drugs (resistance is a problem)

COVID-19

  • Caused by SARS-CoV-2; spreads mainly by respiratory droplets; also surfaces
  • Symptoms: fever, cough, tiredness, breathlessness, loss of taste/smell, and others (2-14 days after exposure)
  • Prevention: distance, avoid crowds/poor ventilation, handwashing/sanitizer, masks, vaccines, isolate if ill

Non-infectious examples

  • Deficiency diseases (kwashiorkor, scurvy, marasmus, night blindness)
  • Smoking-related disease (lung cancer, chronic bronchitis)
  • Sickle cell anaemia, cancer, allergies, diabetes, podoconiosis
  • Risk raised by tobacco, inactivity, harmful alcohol, unhealthy diets → high BP, high blood sugar/lipids, obesity → cardiovascular disease
Must remember
  • Infectious = pathogen + transmission route
  • Malaria = Plasmodium + Anopheles; TB = airborne bacterium; HIV = immune attack

notes.title: 5.9 Renowned nutritionists in Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.9

Renowned nutritionists in Ethiopia

Nutrition science helps Ethiopia fight under-nutrition and diet-related disease.

Competency: list and appreciate renowned nutritionists in Ethiopia

Key term Nutritionist. A researcher or scientist who studies nutrition.
  • Nutritionists study how food affects health and help communities improve diets
  • Ethiopia needs this work for child and maternal nutrition, school feeding, food security, and support for people living with illness
  • The textbook asks you to research named Ethiopian nutritionists from books and trusted sources and write a short paragraph about their contribution
Exam tip

Define nutritionist and explain why Ethiopia needs strong nutrition research and practice.

Must remember
  • Nutritionist = scientist of food and health
  • Appreciate local experts who improve community diets

notes.title: Ecology: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Biology · Unit 6

Ecology

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Biology student textbook. This unit covers ecological terms, biotic and abiotic factors, ecological levels, ecosystems, biomes, succession, and species interactions.

Study lessons 6.1.1 to 6.2 in order. Use this page to check every learning competency before a quiz.

Learning competencies · Unit 6
  • Define ecological terms (lesson 6.1.1)
  • Explain the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem (lesson 6.1.2)
  • Describe the ecological levels (lesson 6.1.3)
  • Explain terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems (lesson 6.1.4)
  • Define biome; describe major terrestrial and aquatic biomes; mention fauna and flora of each (lesson 6.1.5)
  • Describe ecological succession (lesson 6.1.6)
  • Discuss ecological relationships in ecosystems (lesson 6.2)
  • Express love and respect for fauna, flora, and their biomes; investigate how elders care for plants and wildlife (local study)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Ecology: study of interactions among organisms and with their environment.
  • Abiotic = non-living (light, temperature, water, nutrients, salinity). Biotic = living (predators, herbivores, parasites, competitors).
  • Levels: organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.
  • Ecosystem = community + abiotic environment. Types: terrestrial and aquatic.
  • Biome = major life zone (vegetation type on land; physical factors in water).
  • Succession: primary (lifeless start) vs secondary (soil/organisms remain). Climax = stable end community.
  • Interactions: competition (-/-), predation (+/-), herbivory (+/-), parasitism (+/-), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0).

notes.title: 6.1.1 Definitions of ecological terms: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.1

Definitions of ecological terms

Your environment affects you and every organism that shares it.

Competency: define ecological terms

Key termEcology. Branch of biology that studies interactions among organisms and with their environment. Scientists who study it are ecologists.
Key termEcosystem. A study area made of the physical environment (abiotic factors) and all living things (biotic factors) within it.
Key termHabitat. The place where an organism lives.
Key termNiche. The combination of the job an organism does and the place where it lives.
Key termProducers. Plants and algae that trap sunlight and make their own food.
Key termConsumers. Animals that cannot make food; they eat producers or other consumers.
Key termDecomposers. Bacteria and fungi that break down dead remains into substances that can be reused.
Key termQualitative data. Information from observing organisms and their environment.
Key termQuantitative data. Information from measurements and experiments (lab and field).
Must remember
  • Ecology = organisms ↔ each other ↔ environment
  • Habitat = where; niche = where + role

notes.title: 6.1.2 Biotic and abiotic components: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.2

Biotic and abiotic components

Living and non-living factors together shape where species can live.

Competency: explain biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem

Key term Abiotic factors. Non-living components that influence where organisms live. Examples: energy, light, temperature, water, nutrients, salinity.

Important abiotic ideas

  • Solar energy powers most ecosystems via photosynthesis. In water, light fades with depth, so most photosynthesis is near the surface.
  • Some dark ecosystems run on bacteria that oxidize inorganic chemicals (example: hydrogen sulfide).
  • Temperature affects metabolism. Near 0°C few stay active; above about 45°C enzymes of most organisms are destroyed.
  • Water: aquatic species face water-balance problems if solute levels differ; land species risk drying out (scales, waxy leaves help).
  • Nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus limit plant/algae growth. Soil structure, pH, and nutrient content matter on land.
  • Aquatic-only: dissolved oxygen (cold fast water holds more O₂), salinity, currents, tides.
  • Land-only examples: wind (increases water loss), storms, fire.
Key term Biotic factors. Living components that influence distribution. Examples: predators, herbivores, pollinators, food resources, parasites, pathogens, competitors.
Exam tip

List 5 abiotic and 5 biotic factors, then say how each can limit where a species lives.

notes.title: 6.1.3 Ecological levels: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.3

Ecological levels

Ecologists organise life into nested levels so interactions are easier to study.

Competency: describe the ecological levels

Key termOrganism (individual). One living being studied on its own.
Key termPopulation. A group of interbreeding organisms that are members of the same species living in the same area at the same time. Members may compete for food, water, mates, or other resources.
Key termBiological community. The different species in an area and the interactions among them (predation, parasitism, herbivory, competition, pollination). A change in one population can change another (more hawks → fewer mice).
Key termEcosystem. The community of organisms plus the abiotic (non-living) surroundings with which they interact.
Key termBiosphere. All parts of Earth's surface that contain living organisms; can be seen as one vast ecosystem.

Some species reduce competition within a population. Example: tadpoles eat algae; adult frogs eat insects, so young and adults do not compete for the same food.

Must remember
  • Order: organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere
  • Same species → population; many species → community; + abiotic → ecosystem

notes.title: 6.1.4 Ecosystems: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.4

Ecosystems

An ecosystem is a self-supporting unit of life plus its physical setting.

Competency: explain terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems

Key termHabitat. The place where an organism lives.
Key termEcosystem. The community of organisms in a habitat plus the non-living environment (air, water, soil, light, and so on).
Key termSelf-supporting ecosystem. Plants use light and water; animals feed on plants and each other; decomposers return nutrients to the soil so materials recycle.
Key termTerrestrial ecosystem. Ecosystem on land (forests, fields, even a rotting log).
Key termAquatic ecosystem. Ecosystem in water: freshwater (ponds, lakes, streams) or salt water / marine (oceans).
Key termQuadrat. A marked square area used to sample population size and density for plants or slow/small organisms.
  • Example: a lake = plant and animal communities + water, minerals, dissolved O₂, soil, sunlight
  • The biosphere can be seen as one vast ecosystem powered by the Sun, with chemicals recycled and little net material gain or loss from space
Must remember
  • Ecosystem = biotic community + abiotic environment
  • Terrestrial = land; aquatic = water (fresh or marine)

notes.title: 6.1.5 Biomes: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.5

Biomes

Biomes are Earth's major life zones, shaped by climate on land and by physical factors in water.

Competency: define biome; describe major biomes; mention fauna and flora

Key term Biome. A major terrestrial or aquatic life zone. Characterised by vegetation type on land and by the physical environment in water.

Terrestrial biomes

  • Tropical rain forest: near equator; 130-200 cm rain/year; ~25°C; evergreen broad-leaf trees; highest animal diversity (amphibians, birds, reptiles, mammals, arthropods). Threat: deforestation.
  • Desert: <10 cm rain/year; hot or cold extremes; succulents (cacti/euphorbs), deep-rooted shrubs; snakes, lizards, scorpions, beetles, rodents (many nocturnal).
  • Savanna: equatorial/sub-equatorial; 30-50 cm rain; long dry season; scattered trees + grasses; fire-adapted. Fauna: giraffe, zebra, elephant, antelope, wildebeest; lions, hyenas. Human impact: ranching, over-hunting, fire.
  • Temperate grassland (prairie): warm summers, cold winters; 25-100 cm rain; deep grass roots hold soil. Once elk, bison, wolves; much converted to cropland.
  • Boreal forest (taiga): cold dry winters; snow; evergreen conifers (pine, spruce); acidic, low-N soils; lower plant diversity than temperate/tropical forests.
  • Temperate broad-leaf forest: mid-latitudes; deciduous trees drop leaves in winter; mammals may hibernate; birds migrate. Heavily logged historically; can recover.
  • Tundra: arctic (~20% of land) or alpine; mosses, grasses, forbs, lichens; permafrost limits roots. Musk ox, migratory caribou/reindeer; bears, wolves, foxes. Impact: mining and oil.

Aquatic biomes (~75% of Earth)

  • Freshwater: salt usually <1%. Marine: salt usually ~3%.
  • Lakes: plants near shore; phytoplankton/zooplankton in open water; fish where O₂ is enough. Zones: photic, aphotic, pelagic; ocean abyssal 2000-6000 m. Nutrient pollution → algal bloom → O₂ drop → fish kills.
  • Wetlands: soil saturated (marshes, swamps, bogs). Highly productive; filter pollutants; reduce floods. Swamps: woody plants; bogs: sphagnum moss.
  • Streams and rivers: headwaters cold, clear, O₂-rich; downstream warmer, muddier, more nutrients. Pollution and dams harm species.
  • Estuaries: river-sea transition; high productivity; saltmarsh grasses and algae; breeding grounds for fish and invertebrates; waterfowl feeding areas.
Exam tip

Match climate → biome → typical plants and animals. Remember Ethiopia links: savanna wildlife; invasive water hyacinth on lakes such as Tana.

notes.title: 6.1.6 Ecological succession: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1.6

Ecological succession

Communities change in an orderly way after disturbance or on new land.

Competency: describe ecological succession

Key term Succession. The orderly, natural changes that take place in the communities of an ecosystem.
Key term Primary succession. Colonisation of virtually lifeless ground (new volcanic island, glacial rubble). Starts with prokaryotes and protists; lichens and mosses often first macroscopic photosynthesizers (pioneer species). Soil builds slowly; then grasses, shrubs, trees. May take hundreds or thousands of years.
Key term Secondary succession. Re-colonisation after a major disturbance removes most but not all organisms (example: abandoned farmland). Soil already present. Herbaceous plants → shrubs → trees if not burned or heavily grazed.
  • Climax community: stable community with little further change; dominant vegetation of the area
  • Limiting factor: any biotic or abiotic factor that restricts existence, numbers, reproduction, or distribution
  • Tolerance: ability to withstand changes in biotic and abiotic conditions
  • Early species may facilitate, inhibit, or tolerate later arrivals
Exam tip

Flood that strips vegetation but leaves soil → usually secondary. Bare cooled lava → primary.

notes.title: 6.2 Ecological relationships: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.2

Ecological relationships

Species help, harm, or leave each other alone when they interact.

Competency: discuss ecological relationships in ecosystems

Interspecific interactions include competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism. Signs show effect on each partner: + benefit, - harm, 0 no effect.

Key term Competition (-/-). Individuals of the same or different species use a limited resource so both do worse. Example: weeds vs garden plants for water and nutrients; predators competing for hares. Oxygen on land is rarely competed for.
Key term Predation (+/-). Predator kills and eats prey. Adaptations of both are shaped by natural selection.
Key term Herbivory (+/-). Herbivore eats parts of a plant or alga (usually does not kill it). Examples: cattle, sheep, giraffe, goat; many insects (grasshoppers, caterpillars). Adaptations: sensing toxicity, specialised teeth/digestion.
Key term Parasitism (+/-). Parasite gains nourishment from a host that is harmed. Endoparasites live inside (roundworms); ectoparasites live on the surface (ticks). Some have complex cycles (blood fluke: human + freshwater snail).
Key term Mutualism (+/+). Both species benefit. Examples: gut microbes digesting cellulose in termites/ruminants; pollination and seed dispersal; mycorrhizae (fungus ↔ plant roots); algae in corals; acacia-ant.
Key term Commensalism (+/0). One species benefits; the other is neither helped nor harmed. Example: cattle egrets eat insects flushed by grazing mammals.
Must remember
  • Learn the +/- table cold for matching questions
  • Intra-specific = within one species; interspecific = between species

notes.title: Geological History and Topography of Ethiopia: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 1

Geological History and Topography of Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. Start with what geography is, then Ethiopia's location, size, and shape, then the geology and landforms that built the country.

Study lessons 1.1 to 1.3 in order. Use this page to check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 1
  • Recognize the concept, scope, and branches of geography (lesson 1.1)
  • Express the basic land features of the physical environment (lessons 1.1, 1.3.2)
  • Describe the absolute and relative location of Ethiopia (lesson 1.2)
  • Analyze the effects of shape and size of Ethiopia on its sociocultural, political, and economic condition (lesson 1.2)
  • Explain geologic processes that shaped the land surface of Ethiopia (lesson 1.3.1)
  • Describe the different landforms of Ethiopia (lesson 1.3.2)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Geography: scientific study of Earth; spatial and temporal variation of physical, biological, and human phenomena and their links.
  • Two main branches: physical and human geography.
  • Absolute location: about 3°N-15°N and 33°E-48°E. Relative: landlocked Horn of Africa; 6 neighbours; 5,260 km border.
  • Size: about 1,106,000 km² (10th in Africa). Shape: more or less compact.
  • Eras: Precambrian → Paleozoic → Mesozoic → Cenozoic. Landforms mainly from Cenozoic tectonics and volcanoes.
  • Altitude: Dallol / Kobar Sink (~116 m below sea level) to Ras Dashen (4620 m). Three divisions: Western highlands/lowlands, Southeastern highlands/lowlands, Rift Valley.

notes.title: 1.1 Geography: Meaning, scope and branches: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.1

Geography: Meaning, scope and branches

Geography is more than place names. It explains where things are and how people and nature interact.

Outcomes: define geography; describe its scope; identify branches

Key term Geography. From Greek Geo (earth) + Graphos (writing). There is no single definition everyone accepts at all times, because the discipline keeps changing. Still, every good definition ties geography to the Earth (usually its surface).

Five textbook definitions

Key termEratosthenes (276-196 BC). Coined the term geography. Geography is the description of the earth.
Key termAlexander von Humboldt (1769-1859). Geography is a synthesizing discipline that connects the general with the particular through measurement, mapping, and a regional emphasis.
Key termConcise Oxford Dictionary (1964). Geography is the science of the earth's surfaces.
Key termHartshorne, R. (1899-1992). Geography is a branch of knowledge that provides an accurate, orderly, and rational description of distributions on the surface of the earth.
Key termYeates, M. (1968). Geography is a science concerned with developing and testing theories that explain and predict the spatial distribution and locations of things and phenomena on the surface of the earth.
Key term Widely accepted modern definition. Geography is the scientific study of the Earth that describes and analyses spatial and temporal variations of physical, biological, and human phenomena, and their interrelationships and dynamism over the surface of the Earth.
Key term Scope. How broad or narrow a discipline's content is. Geography's scope is wide and dynamic (new ideas and tools change it), but not limitless.

Geography studies physical and human features, their causes, effects, and interactions. That includes the five Earth "spheres" below, plus everyday economic, social, political, and ecological problems. It also uses tools such as computers, GPS, and GIS.

Key term Hydrosphere. All bodies of water: oceans, rivers, lakes, and others.
Key term Biosphere. All living organisms in and on Earth's surface.
Key term Atmosphere. All aspects of the air that surrounds our planet.
Key term Lithosphere. The solid layer of rocks that covers the entire surface of the planet.
Key term Anthroposphere. The part of the environment made or modified by humans.

Major focus areas

  • Earth's position and movements
  • Physical surface features, forces that form them, place-to-place and time change
  • Human-environment relationships (two-way impacts)
  • Lower atmosphere, weather, and climate patterns
  • Earth materials and landforms
  • Major economic activities and their environmental impact

Branches

Key termPhysical geography. Studies natural features (climate, landforms, soil, vegetation, drainage, water, animals) and their causes and effects. Subfields include geomorphology, climatology, biogeography, oceanography, soil geography, phytogeography, and zoogeography.
Key termHuman geography. Studies human aspects (culture, population, settlement, economy, politics). Subfields include cultural, population, economic, political, urban, and historical geography.
Exam tip

Be ready to name all five definitions (or at least Eratosthenes + the modern one). Disagree with "geography is only place names." Stress spatial distribution plus human-environment interaction.

notes.title: 1.2 Location, size, and shape of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.2

Location, size, and shape of Ethiopia

Where Ethiopia sits, how big it is, and how round its outline is all shape politics, defence, and development.

Outcomes: absolute and relative location; effects of size and shape

Key terms Relative location. Position compared with other features.
Vicinal location. Position next to neighbouring countries.
Strategic (natural/global) location. Position relative to major landmasses and water bodies.
Absolute (astronomical) location. Exact position using latitude and longitude.

Vicinal location

Landlocked; six neighbours; total boundary about 5,260 km.

  • Somalia 1,600 km (longest)
  • South Sudan 1,006 km
  • Eritrea 840 km
  • Kenya 760 km
  • Sudan 744 km
  • Djibouti 310 km (shortest)

Strategic location

  • Northeastern (Horn) Africa
  • Southwest of Asia; south of Europe
  • In the Nile Basin
  • Northwest of the Indian Ocean; southwest of the Red Sea; south of the Mediterranean

Absolute location

About 3°N to 15°N and 33°E to 48°E. Extreme tips: northern Tigray (N), Moyale/Borena (S), Akobo/Gambella (W), tip of Ogaden (E).

Size

  • About 1,106,000 km²; 10th largest in Africa; ~3.6% of Africa's land; largest country in the Horn
  • Advantages: diverse agro-ecology and biota; much arable land; varied minerals; diverse ethnic groups
  • Disadvantages: costly administration and infrastructure; large defence need; harder socio-economic integration

Shape

Ethiopia is more or less compact (circular): north-south and east-west spans are similar. Compactness aids administration, defence, and economic links compared with elongated or truncated shapes.

Compactness indicators (circle ideal near 1 for most ratios): boundary/circumference (B/C), area/boundary (A/B), actual area / area of inscribing circle (A/A'). Values near 0.5-1.5 often mean roughly compact; near 0 means elongated/truncated.

Must remember
  • 3°N-15°N, 33°E-48°E · 1,106,000 km² · longest border = Somalia
  • Relative ≠ absolute; vicinal ≠ strategic

notes.title: 1.3.1 Geological processes in Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3.1

Geological processes in Ethiopia

Millions of years of sinking, rising, volcanoes, and erosion built today's rocks and structures.

Outcomes: explain geological history; distinguish processes that shaped landforms

Key terms Geological time scale. Eras → periods → epochs.
Orogenic. Mountain building (often with volcanism).
Epeirogenic. Slow broad uplift or sinking of a landmass.
Transgression / regression. Sea advances onto / retreats from the land.

Eras differ by continent positions, climate, and dominant life forms.

Precambrian (about 4.5 billion to 600 million years ago)

  • Oldest and longest era (~5/6 of Earth's geological time)
  • Orogeny, intensive volcanism, later denudation, folded mountains
  • Oldest rocks: crystalline basement complex (beneath all other rocks)
  • Surface outcrops today: central/northern Tigray; Metekel, Assosa, Illubabor, Abbay Gorge; central Sidama, southern Omo, southern Bale, Borena (also parts of Eritrea)
  • Early one-celled life

Paleozoic (600 to 250 million years ago)

  • Mainly denudation and peneplanation; little new structure
  • Only era with a major gap in rock formation in Ethiopia; some inselbergs left
  • Age of invertebrates

Mesozoic (250 to 70 million years ago): sedimentary rocks

  • Epeirogenesis: alternate sinking and uplift
  • Triassic: sinking + sea transgression → Adigrat sandstone (oldest in SE, younger toward NW)
  • Jurassic: continued NW sea advance → Hintalo limestone
  • Cretaceous: uplift + SE regression → Upper Sandstone (youngest; overlies the others)
  • Later buried by Cenozoic igneous rocks; exposed in SE lowlands, central Tigray, Abbay and Wabishebele gorges
  • Age of reptiles (dinosaurs); end: dinosaurs gone; mammals, birds, flowering plants appear

Cenozoic (70 million years to now): builds modern landforms

  • Tertiary: strong uplift → domes; Trappean basaltic lava → NW and SE highlands and Somali plateaus; cracking forms the Great East African Rift (Ethiopian Rift is part; ~1,700 km in Eritrea/Ethiopia)
  • Quaternary: Afar Horst; Erta Ale (active); Fentale (dormant); Metahara lava; rift thermal springs/fumaroles; pluvial deposits in lowlands. Modern humans evolve in this period.
Exam tip

Match era → event: Precambrian basement; Paleozoic gap/denudation; Mesozoic sediments (Adigrat, Hintalo, Upper Sandstone); Cenozoic Trappean lava + Rift.

notes.title: 1.3.2 Landforms of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3.2

Landforms of Ethiopia

Ethiopia is the "Roof of Eastern Africa": high plateaus cut by a diagonal rift and bordered by lowlands.

Outcome: describe the different landforms of Ethiopia

Key terms Landform. An individual Earth-surface feature.
Endogenic forces. From inside Earth (volcanoes, tectonics).
Exogenic forces. At the surface (denudation, peneplanation).
Both together made Ethiopia's relief.
  • Altitude: Kobar Sink / Dallol ~116 m below sea level → Ras Dashen 4620 m (Simien)
  • Using 1000 m as the highland/lowland line: about 56% highland
  • Three physiographic divisions: Western highlands and lowlands; Southeastern highlands and lowlands; Rift Valley

I. Western Highlands and Associated Lowlands (~44% of Ethiopia)

Tigray to Gamo-Gofa; source of Abbay, Baro, Tekezze. Four highland groups:

  • Plateau of Tigray: Mereb (N) to Tekezze (S); sandstones/limestones after basalt eroded; peaks Tsibet 3988 m, Ambalage, Assimba
  • North Central Massif: between Tekezze and Abbay gorges (Gondar, Gojjam, Wollo); most rugged; ambas; Ras Dashen 4620 m and other high peaks; Yeju-Wadla Delanta ridge links groups
  • Plateau of Shewa: smallest western highland unit; dome watershed for Awash, Omo-Gibe, Abbay; peaks Abbuye Meda, Guraghe
  • Southwestern Highlands: wettest (>1500 mm); Wollega, Illubabor, Jimma, Kafa, Gamo-Gofa; coffee, enset, spices, forest; Mount Gughe 4200 m

Western lowlands (500-1000 m): Tekezze-Angereb, Abbay-Dinder, Baro-Akobo (wettest lowland), Omo-Gibe. Often arid/semi-arid; pastoral/semi-pastoral; border towns such as Humera, Metema, Kurmuk.

II. Southeastern Highlands and Associated Lowlands

  • Highlands: Hararghe, Arsi, Bale, Sidama; basalt-capped; sources of Wabe Shebelle and Genale
  • Peaks: Chillalo/Bada/Kaka (Arsi); Tulu Dimtu 4377 m, Batu (Bale); Gara Muletta (Hararghe)
  • Lowlands: Ogaden, Elkeri, Borena, Genale plains; often <500 mm rain; pastoral

III. Rift Valley (~18% of area; ~1700 km in Ethiopia/Eritrea)

NE-SW strip from Afar through lakes region to Chew Bahir / Lake Turkana. Formed late Tertiary. Three parts:

  • Afar Triangle (N): widest; much below sea level; Dallol; salt plains; Assale, Afrera; fossils/archaeology
  • Main Ethiopian Rift / Lakes Region (central): highest, wettest, most populated; lower Awash to Chamo; farming and lakes
  • Chew Bahir Rift (S): Omo-Gibe trough; marshy; pastoral; Amaro range splits valleys near Arba Minch
Must remember
  • Three divisions · Ras Dashen highest · Dallol lowest · Shewa = smallest western highland unit
  • Rift formed in Tertiary; still shows volcanoes, hot springs, faulting

notes.title: Climate of Ethiopia: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 2

Climate of Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. Climate shapes plants, animals, farming, shelter, and clothing. This unit covers weather vs climate, elements, controls, regions/seasons, and how we measure them.

Study lessons 2.1 to 2.5 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 2
  • Recognize the meaning and concepts of weather and climate (lesson 2.1)
  • Identify elements of climate (lesson 2.2)
  • Distinguish elements of climate from its controls (lessons 2.2, 2.3)
  • Compare and contrast the spatial and temporal variations of climate (lesson 2.4)
  • Identify factors affecting climate of Ethiopia (lesson 2.3)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Weather = short-term atmosphere. Climate = long-term pattern.
  • Elements: precipitation, temperature, humidity, air pressure, wind, sunshine, cloud.
  • Controls: latitude, altitude, mountain barriers, Earth revolution/tilt, distance from sea, ocean currents. In Ethiopia, altitude and latitude dominate.
  • Five agro-zones by altitude: Wurch → Dega → Woina Dega → Kolla → Bereha.
  • Seasons: Kiremt (Jun-Aug), Belg (Mar-May), Meher (Sep-Nov), Bega (Dec-Feb). Kiremt + Belg give >90% of rain.
  • Five rainfall regions: year-round, summer, autumn-spring, winter, merged spring-summer-autumn.

notes.title: 2.1 Meaning of weather and climate: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.1

Meaning of weather and climate

People mix up these two words. Exams love the difference.

Outcomes: define weather and climate; describe the difference

Key term Weather. Condition of the atmosphere (temperature, rainfall, pressure, wind, moisture, cloud cover, humidity, and so on) at a place over a short time. Changes from hour to hour and day to day.
Key term Climate. Pattern of weather conditions experienced in an area over a long period of time. It includes averages plus trends and departures from average conditions in time and space. A large area can experience only one type of climate.

Main differences

  • Time scale: weather = short (hours/days); climate = long (years to decades of records)
  • Variability: weather changes quickly; climate is the usual pattern
  • What each describes: weather = today's state; climate = typical long-term behaviour
Exam tip

"Weather and climate mean the same" is false. Write at least three contrasts: time length, variability, and what each describes.

notes.title: 2.2 Elements of weather and climate: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.2

Elements of weather and climate

Elements are what we measure. Controls are what cause their uneven pattern.

Outcomes: identify and define elements; differentiate from controls

Key termPrecipitation. Any liquid or frozen water that forms in the atmosphere and falls to Earth (rain, sleet, hail, snow).
Key termTemperature. Degree of hotness or coldness of an object or place.
Key termHumidity. Concentration of water vapour present in the air.
Key termAir pressure. Force exerted on a surface by the air above it as gravity pulls it to Earth.
Key termWind. Movement of air caused by uneven heating of Earth by the Sun and by Earth's rotation.
Key termSunshine. Direct sunlight to which a given area is exposed.
Key termCloud. Any visible mass of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere.
Key term Climate controls. Physical factors that govern the spatial and temporal distribution of climatic elements (studied in lesson 2.3). Elements ≠ controls.
Must remember
  • Elements = what the atmosphere is like
  • Controls = factors that decide those values (altitude, latitude, and so on)

notes.title: 2.3 Controls of weather and climate: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.3

Controls of weather and climate in Ethiopia

Ethiopia has many climates because physical controls rearrange heat and rain.

Outcomes: distinguish elements from controls; identify factors affecting Ethiopia's climate

Main controls: latitude, altitude, mountain barriers, Earth revolution and axial tilt, distance from the sea, ocean currents.

a) Latitude

  • Angle of sun rays: vertical near equator, slanting toward poles
  • Ethiopia in the tropics → high temperatures much of the year; high diurnal range; small annual range; little summer/winter daylight difference
  • Overhead sun twice a year (tropical location)

b) Altitude (strongest control of temperature pattern)

Same latitude can have different temps if height differs. Example on 9°N:

  • Addis Ababa 2,200 m → ~16°C
  • Bako 1,800 m → ~17°C
  • Awash 916 m → ~25°C

Temperature generally falls as you climb from lowlands to highlands.

c) Mountain barriers

  • Windward: moist wind side → more rain
  • Leeward / rain shadow: dry side → little rain

d) Revolution and 23½° axial tilt

Changes day length and sun angle → seasons and year-round temperature variation.

e) Distance from the sea

Land heats/cools faster than water. Matters mainly for coastal Horn areas near the Red Sea and NW Indian Ocean. Inland, effect is weak.

f) Ocean currents

Warm/cold currents affect coasts when sea winds blow inland. In Ethiopia this control is largely inconsequential.

Exam tip

Textbook note: Ethiopia's climate is dominated by altitude and latitude. Temperature MCQs usually answer altitude.

notes.title: 2.4 Climatic regions and seasonal variations: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.4

Climatic regions and seasonal variations

Altitude stacks agro-zones. Winds and the ITCZ decide when and where rain falls.

Outcomes: identify agro-climatic zones; compare spatial and temporal climate variation

2.4.1 Agro-climatic zones (by altitude)

  • Wurch/Kur (≥3,300 m): Alpine/Afro-Alpine; <10°C. High mountains (Ras Dashen, Guna, Batu, and so on)
  • Dega (2,300-3,300 m): Temperate; 10-15°C. Historic dense settlement (defence, reliable rain, less malaria); intensive farming → erosion risk. Some humid spots: two growing seasons
  • Woina Dega (1,500-2,300 m): Subtropical; 15-20°C. Most of Ethiopia's agricultural land; surplus grain, enset
  • Kolla (500-1,500 m): Tropical; 20-30°C. Semi-arid lowlands; rain often 410-820 mm (up to ~1600 mm in wet Gambella west); highly variable
  • Bereha (<500 m): Desert; >30°C; rain usually <400 mm. Hot, windy, dry; example Danakil

2.4.2 Seasonal variation

Season: part of the year with typical weather from axial tilt and revolution.

  • Temperature: often highest Mar-Jun; lowest Nov-Feb. Danakil can exceed 45°C. Coolest: Simien and Arsi-Bale mountains
  • Bega (northern winter): clear skies → hot days, cold nights → high diurnal range

ITCZ: low-pressure belt where NE and SE trades meet; follows the overhead sun.

  • June (ITCZ near Cancer): Equatorial Westerlies/Easterlies bring moisture; rain stronger in highlands, weaker northwards → Kiremt
  • December (ITCZ near Capricorn): dry NE trades (continental); little rain except some Afar near Red Sea → Bega dry for most areas
  • March/September (ITCZ near equator): Equatorial Easterlies rain on SE lowlands and central highlands → Belg / transitional rains

Rain seasons: Kiremt Jun-Aug and Belg Mar-May give >90% of national rain. Meher Sep-Nov weaker. Bega Dec-Feb mainly dry (small Afar rains).

2.4.3 Five rainfall regions

  • Year-round (B): SW plateau (Wollega, Kafa, Illubabor, Gamo-Gofa); Equatorial Westerlies from Atlantic; ~1400-2200 mm; most rainy days (Gore, Mizan, Metu, Bonga, Gambella)
  • Summer (A): largest; NW highlands and western lowlands; Equatorial Westerlies/Easterlies (Debre Markos, Fitche, Gondar, Bahir Dar)
  • Autumn and spring (E): SE highlands/lowlands; Equatorial Easterlies from Indian Ocean; <500-1000 mm (Gode, Moyale, Jigjiga, Yabello)
  • Winter (D): eastern escarpment of western highlands, middle Rift, Afar; mostly NE trades; short, low totals (example Assaita)
  • Merged spring-summer-autumn (C): smallest; western foothills of SE highlands, Sidama to Hararghe corridor; ~1000-1500 mm

Highland rain is more dependable than lowland; dependability falls away from the rainy southwest.

Exam tip

Woina Dega = most farmland (not Dega). Year-round rain / least drought-prone ≈ southwestern highlands. Kiremt winds = Equatorial Westerlies/Easterlies; Bega = dry NE trades.

notes.title: 2.5 Measurements of weather and climate: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.5

Measurements of weather and climate

Know the instrument, the unit, and the simple averages exams ask for.

Outcomes: use thermometer, rain gauge, barometer, wind vane (and anemometer for speed)

  • Thermometer: temperature (mercury or alcohol expands/contracts). °C: freeze 0, boil 100. °F: freeze 32, boil 212. Convert: $C = \dfrac{5}{9}(F - 32)$, $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$
  • Rain gauge: rainfall depth in mm; top ~30 cm above ground; often read daily ~9:00
  • Barometer: air pressure in millibars or mm of mercury. Sea level ≈ 1013.25 mb or 760 mm
  • Anemometer: wind speed (cups free to spin)
  • Wind vane: wind direction named by where it comes from (westerly = from the west)

Useful formulas

  • Mean daily temperature = (max + min) / 2
  • Daily (diurnal) range = daily max − daily min
  • Mean monthly temperature = average of daily means in the month
  • Mean annual temperature = sum of 12 monthly means / 12
  • Annual range = hottest month − coldest month
  • Mean monthly rainfall = sum of daily rain / days in month
  • Total annual rainfall = sum of 12 monthly totals
  • Mean annual rainfall = average of annual totals over ~30-35 years
Must remember
  • Instrument map: thermometer, rain gauge, barometer, anemometer, wind vane
  • Pressure at sea level ≈ 1013 mb

notes.title: Natural Resource Base of Ethiopia: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 3

Natural Resource Base of Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. Soils, water, vegetation, wildlife, and minerals underpin food security and development.

Study lessons 3.1 to 3.6 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 3
  • Recognize the concept of natural resources (lesson 3.1)
  • Elaborate on the major drainage systems of Ethiopia (lesson 3.2)
  • Explain the distribution of the major water resources in Ethiopia (lesson 3.3)
  • State soil types and distribution in Ethiopia (lesson 3.4)
  • Explain factors responsible for difference in types of natural vegetation (lesson 3.6)
  • Describe types of wildlife and factors that affect their distribution (lesson 3.6)
  • Describe spatial distribution and variation of minerals (lesson 3.5)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Renewable vs non-renewable resources. Population pressure and misuse drive degradation.
  • Three drainages: Western/Mediterranean (~60%), Southeastern/Indian Ocean (~32%), Inland/Rift (smallest).
  • "Water Tower" of NE Africa: many highland-fed rivers and lakes. Longest river: Wabe Shebelle. Deepest lake: Shalla. Largest: Tana.
  • Nithosols (red basalt): most widely farmed. Vertisols: clay-rich, hard to plough.
  • Vegetation follows altitude and rainfall: Afroalpine → forest → savanna → desert xerophytes.
  • Endemics include Walia ibex, mountain nyala, gelada, Semien fox (key kebero).

notes.title: 3.1 Meaning of natural resources: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.1

Meaning of natural resources

Natural assets from nature that people use for production or consumption.

Outcomes: recognize the concept; describe classification

Key term Natural resources. Natural assets occurring in nature that can be used for economic production or consumption.
Key term Renewable resources. Resources that can be replenished by nature. Examples: plants, animals, soil, water, geothermal energy, wind energy, solar radiation.
Key term Non-renewable resources. Resources that cannot be regenerated by nature on a human time scale and exist in limited amounts. Examples: minerals, coal, crude oil, natural gas.
Key term Sustainable utilization. Using resources so present needs are met without destroying the chance for future generations to use them too.

In Ethiopia these resources face pressure from population growth, farm expansion, migration, rapid urbanization, resettlement, climate change, and pollution. Result: linked degradation of land, water, forest, rangeland, and wildlife.

Exam tip

Coal = non-renewable; wind/water/plants = renewable.

notes.title: 3.2 Drainage systems of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.2

Drainage systems of Ethiopia

Where rivers flow and where they end. Patterns were set mainly by Cenozoic structures.

Outcome: elaborate major drainage systems

Key term Drainage system. Flow direction and destination of rivers.

Three major systems

  • Western (Mediterranean): largest (~60% of annual water discharge). Tekezze, Abbay, Baro-Akobo → Nile in Sudan → Mediterranean. Abbay rises near Lake Tana / Gojjam; Baro-Akobo drains wet SW highlands.
  • Southeastern (Indian Ocean): second (~32%). Genale and Wabe Shebelle from Hararghe, Sidama, Bale, Arsi. Genale joins Dawa → Juba and reaches the ocean. Wabe Shebelle (longest) ends at Somalia's Benadir coast (does not reach the ocean).
  • Inland (Rift Valley): smallest. Awash (to Lake Abbe on Djibouti border), Omo-Gibe, plus streams into Abaya, Chew Bahir, Ziway, and so on. Awash basin ~110,000 km²; most utilized rift basin.
Must remember
  • Western = Nile/Mediterranean · SE = Genale/Wabe · Inland = Awash/Omo

notes.title: 3.3 Water resources of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.3

Water resources of Ethiopia

Second richest African country in water potential (after DR Congo). Often called the Water Tower of northeastern Africa.

Outcome: explain distribution of major water resources

Major rivers (catchment / total length)

  • Wabe Shebelle: largest catchment (~205,407 km²); longest total (~2,000 km)
  • Abbay (~198,508 km²; ~1,360 km)
  • Genale, Awash (~1,200 km inside), Tekezze, Gibe/Omo, Baro

Names after the border: Abbay → Blue Nile; Tekezze → Atbara; Genale → Juba; Baro → Sobat.

River characteristics

  • Seasonal volume fluctuation
  • Steep profiles (highlands → peripheral lowlands)
  • Rapids and waterfalls; steep valleys and gorges
  • Often form international or domestic boundaries
  • Most are poor for navigation (steep, rocky, fluctuating)

Lakes

  • Mostly Quaternary structural lakes (many in dry areas), not climate lakes
  • Highland: crater (Haik, Hashenge, Bishoftu group, Wonchi, Dendi, Ziquala) or watershed/lava-dam (Lake Tana)
  • Rift: linear cluster (Ziway, Langano, Abijatta, Shalla, Hawassa, Abaya, Chamo, and so on)
  • Largest area: Tana (~3,600 km²). Deepest: Shalla (~266 m). Shallowest among listed: Ziway (~4 m)

Significance

  • HEP: Gibe/Gilgel Gibe, Awash, Fincha, Tekezze, Melka Wakena; GERD and Koysha under construction
  • Fishery (Chamo, Abaya, Tana, Baro)
  • Irrigation (Awash most used)
  • Navigation: Baro is the main navigable river; lakes Tana, Ziway, Abaya as inland ways
  • Tourism and recreation (gorges, falls, wildlife, scenery)
Exam tip

Deepest = Shalla; largest = Tana; longest river = Wabe Shebelle; inland rivers = Awash and Omo-Gibe.

notes.title: 3.4 Major soil types of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.4

Major soil types of Ethiopia

Soil is loose crust material (water, air, organic and inorganic parts) that supports life.

Outcomes: distinguish major soil types; explain characteristics

Formation factors

  • Parent rock (weathering)
  • Climate (heat/moisture speed processes)
  • Vegetation (adds humus)
  • Topography (hill slopes → shallow soils from erosion)

Volcanic plateaus → red and black basaltic soils. Crystalline rock areas (Hararghe, Borena) → thin, rocky, acidic. Afar recent volcanics/lake beds → shallow saline soils. SE sedimentary lowlands → low humus, rich P and potash, low N. River lower courses → fertile alluvial soils.

Main FAO types (cover most of the country)

  • Nithosols (red basalt, ~12%): high-rain former forest areas (Wollega, Kafa, Illubabor, Sidama, Shewa, Gojjam, Hararghe). Deep, leached of Na/Ca but rich in Fe/Al; friable. Most widely cultivated; best for coffee, enset, cereals.
  • Vertisols (black basalt, ~10%): high clay, sticky, poor drainage; rich nutrients but hard to farm (often grazing). Arsi, Bale, central Hararghe.
  • Cambisols: young, shallow; recent Quaternary lava; Shewa eastern escarpment, Chercher
  • Regosols: young, coarse, low farm value; Danakil and Ogaden
  • Xerosols: arid/semi-arid; salty, low humus; little farming unless irrigated
  • Luvisols: good nutrients; wet-dry seasons, less leaching; Tana area, parts of N-central highlands and southern lowlands
  • Lithosols: immature on steep dry escarpments
  • Fluvisols (~10%): river/lake deposits; high farm potential; lower Omo, Awash, Abbay, Baro-Akobo
Must remember
  • Nithosols = farming champion · Vertisols = clay trouble · Fluvisols = fertile transported soils

notes.title: 3.5 Major mineral resources: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.5

Major mineral resources and their distribution

Surveys show many deposits, but large-scale commercial extraction is still limited.

Outcomes: elaborate major minerals; describe spatial distribution

Non-metallic minerals are produced more than metallic ones each year. Except common salt, most output is small-scale; some is exported.

Key termMetallic minerals. Minerals valued for metal content (example: gold, platinum, tantalum).
Key termGold. Found in Precambrian veins and alluvial deposits. Areas include Adola, Bule Hora, Arero, Moyale, Akobo, Lega Dembi, Sakaro, and Tigray.
Key termPlatinum. Used in electronics. Found NE of Yubdo, north of Gimbi, and Akobo (Gambella).
Key termTantalum. Used in electronics. Kenticha deposit (~50 km SE of Shakiso, Adola).
Key termNon-metallic minerals. Minerals not mined mainly for metal (example: potash, salt, soda ash, limestone, clay, silica sand, coal, oil and gas).
Key termPotash and salt. Danakil / Dallol (northern Rift).
Key termSoda ash. Abijatta, Shalla, and other rift lakes (~460 million metric tons sodium carbonate potential).
Key termLimestone. Used for cement and chalk. Tigray, Shewa, Hararghe.
Key termClay. Used for pottery and bricks in many areas.
Key termSilica sand. Used for glass. Harer, Shewa, Gondar, Gojjam, Sidama, Arsi, Tigray, Wollega.
Key termOil and natural gas. Believed present in the Ogaden basin.
Key termCoal (lignite). Shewa (Debre Birhan-Dessie road, Sululta, near Mojo), Sidama, Wollega.
Exam tip

Match: platinum/gold = metallic; potash = non-metallic (Danakil).

notes.title: 3.6 Biotic resources of Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.6

Biotic resources of Ethiopia

Living parts of ecosystems: producers, consumers, and decomposers (bacteria and fungi).

Outcomes: vegetation types and factors; wildlife types and distribution

Key term Natural vegetation. Original plants covering an area. Main controls: altitude, climate, soil, drainage. In Ethiopia strongly tied to altitude and rainfall.

Four vegetation types

  • Afroalpine / sub-Afroalpine: high mountains (Simien, Bale). Sub-Afroalpine ~3,000-3,300 m; Afroalpine above. Tussock grass, mosses, lichens; gibra (Lobelia), asta (Erica)
  • Forests (~450-3,300 m; rain ~200-2,200 mm):
    • Highland: kerkha bamboo; tid (juniper); zigba (Podocarpus); woira and kosso
    • Lowland gallery/riverine along Awash, Wabe Shebelle, Genale: sholla, warka; Baphia where rain >500 mm
  • Woodland savanna (~250-2,300 m): grass with scattered trees/shrubs (juniper, acacia/ghirar, mixed deciduous). Park-like where rain >1,000 mm; e.g. south of Ziway-Langano-Abijatta-Hawassa
  • Semi-desert and desert: xerophytes (short acacia, thorn, succulents, rough grass); Afar, NW and SE/Ogaden lowlands; rain often <600 mm

Wildlife

~277 mammal, 862 bird, 201 reptile, 63 amphibian species; about 7 mammal and 25 bird endemics. Concentrated especially in south and west.

  • Common: hyena, jackal
  • Game: giraffe, wild ass, zebra; lion, leopard, cheetah
  • Arboreal (rainforest): colobus, apes, baboons
  • Aquatic: hippo, fish, crocodile
  • Birds: endemic and migratory (rift sanctuaries and forests)
  • Endemics (rare): Walia ibex (Simien); mountain nyala (Bale); gelada (Simien); Menelik's bushbuck (Shewa/Bale); Swayne's hartebeest (Nechsar, Sankalle); Semien fox/key kebero (Bale and Simien); wild ass (Afar and SE lowlands)
Must remember
  • Vegetation ladder follows height and rain
  • Decomposer example in reviews: fungi
  • Walia and Semien fox are near extinction risk

notes.title: Population and Demographic Characteristics: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 4

Population and Demographic Characteristics of Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. Growth, composition, distribution, settlements, health, pressure on development, and language/religion diversity.

Study lessons 4.1 to 4.8 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 4
  • Define the concept of human population (lesson 4.1)
  • Recognize the pattern of population growth in Ethiopia (lesson 4.2)
  • Examine population structure and trends in Ethiopia (lesson 4.3)
  • Explain the population characteristics of Ethiopia (lessons 4.2, 4.3)
  • Demonstrate population distribution and settlement patterns (lessons 4.4, 4.5)
  • Identify factors influencing spatial distribution of health and diseases in lowlands and highlands (lesson 4.6)
  • Analyze the influence of population pressure on resources (lesson 4.7)
  • Describe the diversity of language and religion (lesson 4.8)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Second most populous in Africa (~114.9 million in 2020; growth ~2.6%). Pyramid: broad base (high fertility).
  • ~77.5% live above 1,800 m. Altitude is the key physical control of distribution.
  • ~80% rural. Urban criteria include ≥2,000 people and mostly non-farm work.
  • Lowlands: malaria/yellow fever; sparse settlement. Highlands: denser settlement.
  • Rapid growth pressures land, food, fuel wood, services, and pollution.
  • ~80+ languages (Afro-Asiatic + Nilo-Saharan). Religions (2007): Orthodox 43.5%, Islam 33.9%, Protestant 18.6%.

notes.title: 4.1 Concept of human population: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.1

Concept of human population

People are not just a count. They shape and are shaped by place.

Outcomes: define human population; discuss why we study it

Key termPopulation (in population studies). The total number of human inhabitants of a specified area (city, country, or continent) at a given time.
Key termHuman population. The number of people living in a definite area. Studying it matters for development and socio-economic activities.
Key termPopulation geography. Branch of geography concerned mainly with spatial analysis of the human population. It focuses on population-space relationships and on interaction between people and the physical environment.

Why study human population?

  • It is dynamic: size, composition, structure, and location change over time and space, with large socio-economic effects.
  • Those changes can have policy implications.
  • Knowledge helps governments plan health, education, housing, social security, employment, and environment, and to form population policies.
  • People are the main labour force and creators of material wealth.
Exam tip

Define population, then say population geography studies spatial patterns and people-environment links.

notes.title: 4.2 Trends of population growth: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.2

Trends of population growth in Ethiopia

Ethiopia's people count has grown fast since 1900, and doubling time has shortened.

Outcomes: explain growth trends; compare regional size context

Key termPopulation size. How many people live in the country (or area) at a stated time.
Key termGrowth rate. How fast population size increases each year, usually as a percent. Ethiopia's recent rate is about 2.6%.
Key termPopulation doubling time. Years needed for a population to become twice as large. Faster growth shortens doubling time.
  • Ethiopia is the second most populous country in Africa (~114.9 million in 2020, UN; about 12th in the world).
  • 2007 census: 73.8 million. 1984: 42.6 million. 1900: only ~11.8 million.
  • 1960 (~23.5 m) roughly doubled by 1990 (~51 m): doubling time about 30 years (earlier it took much longer).
  • Growth <1% until ~1920 (high mortality). Rose after disease control (example: malaria). ~2.8% by 1980; ~3% in the 1980s; ~2.6% in 2010-2020.
Must remember
  • Slight fall in rate can still mean a huge absolute increase
  • Link: high growth rate → short doubling time

notes.title: 4.3 Population composition: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.3

Population composition

Composition tells who the people are, not only how many.

Outcomes: explain structure change over time; describe Ethiopian composition

Key termPopulation composition. Aspects of population that can be measured by age, sex, marital status, family size, economic activities, nationality, language, and religion.
Key termAge structure. Pattern from grouping people into age categories (example: five-year groups 0-4, 5-9, … or broad groups 0-14, 15-64, 65+).
Key termYoung / working / old age. Broad groups: 0-14 young dependent; 15-64 working (economically active); 65+ elderly dependent.
Key termAge dependency ratio. Measure of how many young and/or old depend on the working-age group.
Key termSex structure / sex ratio. How males and females are distributed. Sex ratio is usually males per 100 females (or a stated base).
Key termPopulation pyramid. Diagram of age-sex structure. Developing countries like Ethiopia often have a broad base (many young people from high birth rate) and a narrow top (fewer elderly; lower life expectancy historically).
Must remember
  • Ethiopia: high share of young age group because of high birth rate
  • Broad-base pyramid = youthful population

notes.title: 4.4 Population distribution: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.4

Population distribution

People are not spread evenly across Ethiopia.

Outcomes: discuss spatial distribution; identify factors that shape it

Key termPopulation distribution. How population spreads over an area (from a small place to the whole Earth).
Key termPopulation density. Average number of people per square kilometre (or other unit area). Crude density is the most widely used measure.
Key termDense population. High number of people per unit area (often highland and plateau zones with favourable conditions).
Key termSparse population. Low number of people per unit area (often lowlands with harder conditions or disease risk).
  • Ethiopia's distribution is uneven for physical and human reasons.
  • People prefer moderate climate, water, vegetation, fertile soil, and fewer disease-carrying insects.
  • About 77.5% live above 1800 m; about 22.5% live below 1800 m.
  • Highlands and plateaus attract denser settlement and crop farming; lowlands are generally more sparse.
Exam tip

Define distribution, then density, then give the highland vs lowland contrast with the 77.5% / 22.5% figures.

notes.title: 4.5 Urban and rural settlement patterns: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.5

Urban and rural settlement patterns

Settlement is where people live and make a living, with houses, paths, and shared facilities.

Outcomes: describe settlement patterns; differentiate urban and rural

Key termSettlement. Characteristic grouping of people into occupancy units, with houses, streets, and facilities. Also: a place where people live and carry out activities such as trade, agriculture, and manufacturing. Includes hamlets, villages, towns, cities, and larger urban forms.
Key termRural settlement. Settlement where people are mainly engaged in agriculture; usually lower density than urban places.
Key termUrban settlement. Settlement branded by non-agricultural economic activities and usually higher population density.
Key termDispersed settlement. Homes spread out across the landscape rather than tightly clustered.
Key termNucleated settlement. Homes and buildings clustered together (a compact village or town core).
Key termVillagization. Organizing or regrouping rural people into village settlements (policy and planning context in Ethiopia).
  • Ethiopia: broadly rural vs urban, based mainly on dominant economic activity and density.
  • Majority of Ethiopians (about 80%) live in rural areas.
  • Rural settlements may be permanent (location does not change often) or temporary (location shifts with livelihood, example: pastoral movement).
Must remember
  • Rural ≈ agriculture; urban ≈ non-agriculture + denser
  • ~80% rural

notes.title: 4.6 Health and disease: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.6

Health and disease in the highlands and lowlands

Health has improved, but preventable disease and nutrition problems remain heavy.

Outcomes: link health patterns to highland and lowland conditions

Key termLife expectancy. Average years a newborn is expected to live. Ethiopia rose from about 56.8 years (2005) to about 65.5 years (2016).
Key termHealth Extension Program (HEP). Community-level program that widened access to high-impact public health interventions (malaria control, safe water, toilets, childhood vaccination, and related work).
  • EDHS surveys (2005, 2011, 2016) show falling neonatal, infant, under-five, and maternal mortality, yet disease burden stays high.
  • Much ill health links to preventable communicable diseases and nutritional disorders.
  • Root causes include unsafe water, inadequate nutrition, and harmful traditional practices.
  • Lowlands tend to face more tropical vector diseases (example: malaria, yellow fever). Highlands historically had fewer vector-borne diseases and denser settlement.
Exam tip

Contrast highland vs lowland disease risk, then name HEP and life-expectancy improvement.

notes.title: 4.7 Impacts of population growth: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.7

Impacts of population growth on sustainable development

When people grow faster than the economy and resources can support, pressure builds on land, forests, food, and services.

Outcomes: explain socio-economic and environmental impacts

Key termEnvironmental degradation. Process that harms the natural environment, reducing biodiversity and environmental health (often sped by deforestation, over-grazing, and poor farming under population pressure).
Key termDeforestation. Clearing forests faster than they regrow, often for farmland, fuel wood, settlement, and grazing.
Key termFood scarcity / famine risk. When domestic food production and access fail to meet needs; rapid growth plus traditional rain-fed farming deepen the risk.
Key termPollution. Undesirable change in natural conditions of water, air, or other environmental components.
Key termDrought and land degradation. Linked pressures that reduce soil fertility and productivity, especially where vegetation cover is lost.
  • Growth (~2.6%) can outpace economic growth and the carrying capacity of land, water, soil, and forest.
  • Direct deforestation effects: more soil erosion, lost biodiversity, changed rainfall via less evapotranspiration, damaged natural beauty.
  • Socio-economic pressure: jobs, health care, education, housing, and food systems face rising demand.
Must remember
  • Rapid growth → resource pressure → degradation + development strain

notes.title: 4.8 Language and religious diversity: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.8

Language and religious diversity

Ethiopia's people differ strongly by language family and by religion.

Outcomes: describe language diversity; identify major religions

Key termLinguistic diversity. Ethiopia has about 80 languages. Major differences among ethnic groups are often described by language category.
Key termAfro-Asiatic super family. Largest group of Ethiopian languages. Divided into Cushitic, Semitic, and Omotic families.
Key termCushitic. Spoken widely in central, southern, eastern, and northeastern areas (example regions: Afar, Oromia, Sidama, Somali). Examples: Afaan Oromoo, Af-Somali, Sidaamu Afo, Qafaraf, Kambatissa, Hadiyissa, Gedeoffa.
Key termSemitic. Spoken in northern, central, and eastern areas (example: Tigray, Amhara, Harari, and parts of the south). Examples: Amarigna, Tigrigna, Guragigna, Aderigna, Argobigna.
Key termOmotic. Spoken mainly in south-central and south-western zones between southern Rift Valley lakes and the Omo River. Examples: Wolaitatto, Dawurootsuwa, Kafi noono, Kontaatsuwa.
Key termNilo-Saharan super family. Second super family of Ethiopian languages (smaller share than Afro-Asiatic).

Religion: Ethiopia has long-standing Christian and Muslim communities and other faiths. Treat religion as part of cultural diversity alongside language.

Must remember
  • ~80 languages; two super families: Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan
  • Afro-Asiatic = Cushitic + Semitic + Omotic

notes.title: Major Economic and Cultural Activities: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 5

Major Economic and Cultural Activities in Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. How Ethiopians produce, trade, move, stay safe on roads, and use cultural landscapes for tourism.

Study lessons 5.1 to 5.5 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 5
  • Recognize the importance of the major economic activities of Ethiopia (lessons 5.1, 5.2)
  • Examine the trade and transport systems of Ethiopia (lesson 5.3)
  • Appreciate cultural landscapes and their contribution to tourism (lesson 5.5)

Also covered for exams: agriculture problems (5.2.3) and road safety (5.4).

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Five sectors: primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary → quinary.
  • Agriculture employs ~80%; supplies most exports; GDP share fell as services rose.
  • Coffee still top export; Ethiopia runs a trade deficit (imports > exports).
  • Road is the main modern mode; Baro is the main navigable river; new Addis-Djibouti railway; Ethiopian Airlines is a major African carrier.
  • Road deaths are high; victims often passengers and pedestrians.
  • Konso Cultural Landscape (UNESCO 2011); tourism = "smokeless industry."

notes.title: 5.1 Major economic activities: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.1

Major economic activities in Ethiopia

Economic activity = production, distribution, and exchange of goods and services.

Outcomes: list five types; explain characteristics; how activities transform resources

Five sectors

  • Primary: extract from nature (agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining). Depend on environment; make food and raw materials.
  • Secondary: manufacturing, construction, power. Turn raw materials into products (factories).
  • Tertiary: services (trade, transport, tourism, legal, medical).
  • Quaternary: knowledge services (research, finance, government, education, media). Need higher education; often urban.
  • Quinary: top decision-making and high science (executives, senior officials, research leaders). Often in big cities and research hubs.

Primary focus in Ethiopia

  • Agriculture (since ~4000 BC; early crop centre): mainly Dega and Woina Dega. Crop farming + livestock. Cattle: 1st in Africa, 10th in world.
  • Crops: seed/grain (cereals, pulses, oilseeds); permanent (enset, coffee, cotton) in south/SW; shifting cultivation (cut-and-burn) in W/SW fringes (Benishangul, Gambella, south) where density is low; plantations (sugarcane, cotton, coffee, tea, rubber) with rain or irrigation.
  • Forestry ~6.1% GDP locally (fuel wood, timber, construction); little foreign exchange.
  • Fishery: mostly freshwater lakes and rivers; still underdeveloped.
  • Mining ~1.5% GDP.

Secondary in Ethiopia

  • Cottage/traditional: weaving, carving, pottery, metal, basketry (often low social status historically).
  • Modern: mainly light consumer-goods industries; still limited.
Exam tip

Fishing/forestry = primary. Tourism/trade/transport = tertiary. Construction = secondary (not tertiary). Shifting cultivation = cut-and-burn, periodic abandoning of plots.

notes.title: 5.2 Farming, cash crops, and agriculture problems: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.2

Farming, cash crops, and problems of agriculture

Farming feeds people and earns most export dollars, but it faces hard limits.

Outcomes: describe practices; importance of subsistence and cash crops

  • ~80% of people employed in agriculture
  • >90% of export commodities from agriculture
  • ~32.7% of GDP (2019/20); share falling while industry rises; services became largest sector after ~2015/16
Key terms Subsistence farming. Almost all output for the household; little surplus for market. Traditional tools; rain-fed smallholders. Cuts rural food insecurity when it works.
Cash crop / commercial farming. Grown mainly for sale (coffee, oilseeds, pulses, chat, sugarcane, cotton, fruit, flowers).

Cash crop roles

  • Food and raw materials for people and agro-industry
  • Capital: tax and export earnings. Coffee ~28.6% of export value (2019/20); oilseeds ~11.5%; chat ~10.9%; pulses ~7.9%; flowers rose strongly
  • Rural wages and jobs

Problems of agriculture (5.2.3)

  • Land degradation / erosion: ~50% of cultivable land exposed; fertility and water-holding fall
  • Variable rainfall: late/early, too little or too much
  • Tiny fragmented farms: many households <0.5 ha; hard to feed a family
  • Backward technology: ox plough, hand broadcast, sickle harvest
  • Poor rural infrastructure: bad roads raise transport costs and cut farm income
Must remember
  • Agriculture = pillar, but stagnating production + rising people → food stress
  • Match: cereal = wheat; perennial = enset; oilseed = sunflower; pulse = haricot beans

notes.title: 5.3 Trade and transport: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.3

Trade and transport in Ethiopia

Trade moves goods; transport makes that move possible.

Outcomes: expand trade; types of trade; importance of transport

Key terms Domestic (internal) trade. Exchange inside the country (base for foreign trade).
Foreign (external) trade. Exchange between countries.
Trade balance. Exports minus imports. Ethiopia: trade deficit (imports > exports).

Exports vs imports

  • Exports: mainly farm products (coffee still #1; flowers, oilseeds, chat, pulses, gold, textiles, and so on)
  • Imports: finished/capital goods, fuel, machinery, transport equipment, consumer goods
Key term Transport. Moving people or goods for a purpose. Links surplus to deficit areas; speeds ideas and trade. Tertiary activity.

Modes

  • Traditional: pack animals, human porterage
  • Modern: road, rail, inland water, air
  • Road: most important and flexible; network grew to ~138,127 km (2018/19); asphalt still a small share (~11.5%)
  • Rail: old Addis-Djibouti metre gauge closed; new standard-gauge Addis-Djibouti (~753 km) opened 2018 (sea access; >95% of trade via Djibouti). AA Light Rail ~31.6 km, ~60,000 riders/day
  • Water: limited by rugged land and seasonal rivers. Navigable river: Baro. Small lake traffic on Tana, Abaya, Ziway
  • Air: Ethiopian Airlines (est. 1945); leading African carrier; many African and world destinations; large cargo role (including COVID vaccine logistics)
Exam tip

Limited river navigation = topography + seasonal flow + rapids/falls (all of the above).

notes.title: 5.4 Road safety: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.4

Road safety in Ethiopia

Roads move the country, but crashes kill and injure far too many people.

Outcomes: causes and consequences; road safety performance

Key term Road safety. Making roads safe for vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians (rules, speed limits, drink-driving laws, lights, crossings).
  • Fatal accident: death within 30 days of the crash
  • Serious injury: hospital inpatient damage; slight = outpatient; property damage only = no injury
  • Deaths rose sharply (example: 2,161 in 2007 → 4,597 in 2018); ~43 deaths per 10,000 vehicles (2018); about 13 people/day
  • Victims mostly passengers and pedestrians
  • ~85% of fatalities concentrated in Oromia, Amhara, SNNPR, and Addis Ababa
  • National Road Safety Council led with Transport and other ministries/police/roads agencies

Factor groups and causes

  • Vehicle, road, road-user, and environment factors
  • Common causes: distraction, impairment (alcohol, drugs, sleep, illness), mechanical failure, bad road surface, unsafe speed

Consequences

  • Lost productivity, legal costs, pain/suffering, lower quality of life for victims and families

Rules (sample): pedestrians use sidewalks, face traffic if none, cross at designated places, bright/reflective clothing. Drivers: no drink-driving, seat belts, safe distance, no red-light running, speed limits, avoid drowsiness and distraction.

Must remember
  • Road = main mode → road safety is a national development issue

notes.title: 5.5 Cultural landscapes and tourism: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.5

Cultural landscapes and tourism

Culture plus nature can draw visitors and jobs without smokestacks.

Outcomes: identify cultural landscapes; importance of tourism; attraction sites

Key term Cultural landscape. Geographic area (cultural + natural resources) tied to historic events, activities, people, or aesthetic value. "Combined works of nature and man."
  • Konso Cultural Landscape (south Ethiopia, dry Rift-edge hills): dry-stone terraces and walled towns (~400 years). Terraces hold soil and create farm saddles on rocky slopes (some walls up to ~5 m). UNESCO listed in 2011.
Key term Tourism. Travel experience industries (transport, lodging, food, retail, entertainment, hospitality). Jobs + income; called a smokeless industry.

Attraction sites

  • Natural: Simien, Bale, Awash, Nech Sar, Omo, Mago, Gambella, Abijatta-Shalla parks; Blue Nile/Tis Issat Falls; Lake Tana; Sof Omar Cave; Rift Valley
  • Human-made: Lalibela, Harar, Axum, Gondar castles, Tiya
Exam tip

Tourism is tertiary (not primary). Konso = terraces + walled towns = cultural landscape.

notes.title: Human-Natural Environment Interactions: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 6

Human-Natural Environment Interactions in Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. How people and nature shape each other, and what rapid growth does to resources.

Study lessons 6.1 to 6.5 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 6
  • Describe the relationship between human activities and the environment with local examples (lesson 6.1)
  • Describe the link between optimal population and sustainable development (lesson 6.2)
  • Explain why protecting the environment serves humans and other living beings (lessons 6.1, 6.5)
  • Examine human-environment flows in Ethiopia's highlands and lowlands (lessons 6.1, 6.5)
  • Recognize what population growth trends mean for sustainable resources (lessons 6.3 to 6.5)
  • Assess over-exploitation in over-populated areas of Ethiopia (lesson 6.3)
  • Explain advantages and disadvantages of underpopulation (lesson 6.4)
  • Assess impacts of rapid population growth on environment and socio-economic development (lesson 6.5)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Three interaction modes: dependence, modification, adaptation.
  • Two activity types: use natural resources; produce wastes and pollutants.
  • Optimum = population needs match available resources (highest quality of life / income per capita).
  • Overpopulation = too many people for resources / living standards (relative is more common than absolute).
  • Underpopulation = too few people to use resources efficiently.
  • Ethiopia: rapid growth (~2.6%) drives deforestation, pollution, land degradation, and pressure beyond carrying capacity.

notes.title: 6.1 Human-environment relationship: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1

Human-environment relationship

People and the environment shape each other every day: clothes for weather, farms for food, floods that force people to move.

Outcomes: describe the relationship; identify three modes of interaction; explain two-way effects

Key termEnvironment. Physical surroundings and characteristics of the place where we live, and the wider natural world of land, sea, and atmosphere.
Key termDependence. Living things (including humans) need the environment for air, water, food, shelter, and other resources. Survival requires interaction with nature.
Key termModification. Human activities change the environment (positive or negative). Examples: farming, renewable energy projects, building homes, shopping centres, and schools. Even "green" projects still use natural resources.
Key termAdaptation. People adjust to environmental conditions so they can live in places such as the Arctic, deserts, or dense forests. Better knowledge of the environment supports more successful adaptation.
Key termResource use. Taking natural resources for daily life: land, food, water, soils, minerals, plants, and animals. Clothes, transport, buildings, and tools all need many resources to make.
Key termPollution. Introduction into the environment of substances that can harm humans and other living organisms (example: tanning wastes with toxic chemicals; greenhouse gases such as CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide).

How the environment helps or harms people

  • Enabling: good climate, clean water, fertile soil help people live and thrive.
  • Harsh: very hot or cold climate, limited water, infertile land make survival harder.
  • Hazards: earthquakes, floods, and drought damage homes, farms, and water systems; can displace people, cause injury or death, and spread waterborne disease.

Two main human-environment activity types

  • Use of natural resources (land, food, water, soils, minerals, plants, animals; energy for cooking and industry).
  • Production of wastes and pollutants from agriculture, industry, mining, and human bodies. Open defecation and poor sanitation spread waterborne disease.
Ethiopia example · forests

Clearing forests for crops, fuel, and construction reduces forest cover, cuts biodiversity, speeds soil erosion, and weakens groundwater recharge (roots open soil pores so rain can soak in).

Exam tip

Name the three modes (dependence, modification, adaptation) and give one local example for each.

notes.title: 6.2 Optimum population and resource use: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.2

Optimum population and resource use

Optimum is the "sweet spot": enough people and enough resources for the best living standard.

Outcomes: define optimum population; show balance between population size and resources

Key termOptimum population. Population size where available resources match the country's population needs, so resources can maintain the population. It is the best and most desirable size. It yields the highest quality of life (adequate food, water, energy, air quality, medical care, recreation, culture) and, with given resources and technology, the highest income per capita.
  • Possible signs (not exact rules): high average living standards, full employment, rational resource development, balanced age structure.
  • The optimum changes with time and place: state size, geography, social structure, technology, communications.
  • Varied open economies have a wider "safe" range than specialized or isolated communities (where war, drought, or crisis can break the balance fast).
Must remember
  • Optimum ≠ biggest population. Optimum = best balance with resources and technology.
  • Exam matching: balanced population and resource use → optimum population.

notes.title: 6.3 Overpopulation and resource use: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.3

Overpopulation and resource use

Too many people for the resources (or for a decent living standard) is overpopulation.

Outcomes: define overpopulation; explain how growth and resources affect each other

Key termOverpopulation. Excess of population over utilized or potential resources. Too many people to support to a good standard of living with the region's resources. Can follow a rise in population, a fall in resources, falling labour demand, or a mix. Also: resource development does not keep up with population growth.
Key termAbsolute overpopulation. Absolute production limit already reached, yet living standards stay low.
Key termRelative overpopulation. Present production is not enough for the population, but greater production is still possible. More common than absolute overpopulation.
Key termCarrying capacity. How many people (or organisms) an area's resources can support without lasting damage. Overpopulation means numbers exceed this capacity.

Where it shows up

  • Levels: rural, industrial, regional, national. Rural overpopulation is common in populous underdeveloped areas.
  • Rural causes: uneven land ownership; more machines and less need for farm labour; shift from crops to livestock (less labour); rapid rural population growth.
  • Symptoms: famine, hunger, long unemployment, more landless labourers. It hits the poorest first (landless, smallholders; unskilled workers in industry).
Exam tip

Relative overpopulation is more common than absolute. Matching: population size greater than resource support → overpopulation.

notes.title: 6.4 Underpopulation and resource use: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.4
