Underpopulation and resource use

Too few people to use resources well is underpopulation.

Outcomes: define underpopulation; identify causes and effects on resource use

Key termUnderpopulation. Population too small to use resources fully, or resources could support more people without lowering living standards or raising unemployment. More resources (food, energy, minerals) than people can use. Too few workers to exploit resources efficiently, support retirees, and drive growth.
Key termAbsolute underpopulation. Rare. Numbers cannot replace themselves demographically or produce enough economically (often isolated groups).
Key termRelative underpopulation. Resources are not developed enough relative to what is possible. Common on the southern continents.

Typical features and effects

  • Often large areas rich in resources that can export surplus food, energy, and minerals; may have high incomes, technology, and immigration.
  • Positive for resources: lower demand can mean less depletion and less environmental pressure.
  • Negative: fewer workers → less production; aging workforce; fewer taxpayers; weaker demand for services.
Exam tip

High birth rate is not a cause of underpopulation (true/false traps). Matching: resources greater than population size → underpopulation.

notes.title: 6.5 Impacts of rapid population growth: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.5

Impacts of rapid population growth

Fast growth strains land, forests, water, and services. Ethiopia feels this in the highlands especially.

Outcomes: link growth and resources both ways; assess environmental and socio-economic impacts

Key termRapid population growth. Fast rise in numbers that raises demand for food, land, housing, transport, and energy, and can push use beyond the carrying capacity of land, water, soil, and forest.
Key termPhysical environment. Non-living environment: land, air, water, soil, and minerals.
Key termDeforestation. Removal of forest cover without adequate replacement; indiscriminate destruction of natural vegetation. In Ethiopia it rises with needs for wood, farmland, settlement, and grazing. Density and deforestation are linked: more people → more trees cut.
Key termDegradation. Fall in the quality or condition of land, forest, or other resources (example: soil erosion after trees and undergrowth are removed).
Key termPollution. Harmful substances enter air, land, or water. More people → more houses, goods, fossil fuels, fertilizers, and pesticides → more pollution that also harms the biological environment.
Key termBiodiversity. Variety of living organisms. Converting forest to farmland cuts biodiversity. Humans depend on other species for food, medicines, and ecological services (oxygen, clean air and water, waste breakdown, erosion control).

Ethiopia snapshot

  • Very large population; growth rate about 2.6%. Many livelihoods sit on moderately to severely degraded highland land.
  • Growth often outruns economic growth and resource carrying capacity.
  • Historical forest loss: high forests once maybe ~35-40% of land (with woodlands ~66%); ~16% early 1950s; ~3.6% early 1980s; ~2.7% by 1989/1994. Annual high-forest loss estimated ~150,000-200,000 ha.

Direct costs of deforestation

  • More soil erosion; less biodiversity; less rainfall recycling via evapotranspiration; wood shortages; damaged natural beauty.
  • More atmospheric CO₂ risk (plants absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis); disrupted food webs.
  • Weaker groundwater recharge when root channels are lost.
Must remember
  • Rapid growth → deforestation, pollution, land degradation, resource depletion.
  • True/false style: deforestation in Ethiopia is a direct impact of rapid population growth (true).

notes.title: Contemporary Geographic Issues: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 7

Contemporary Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Ethiopia

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. Resource degradation (soil, vegetation, water) and Ethiopia's Green Legacy response.

Study lessons 7.1.1 to 7.2 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 7
  • State causes of natural resource degradation (lessons 7.1.1 to 7.1.3)
  • Explain the effects of natural resource degradation (lessons 7.1.1 to 7.1.3)
  • Elaborate Ethiopia's vision to develop without undermining the natural environment (lesson 7.2)

Section outcomes also ask you to identify conservation measures (soil, forests, water) and describe Green Legacy effects.

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Ethiopia has rich resources, but pressure from population, farming expansion, urbanization, climate change, and pollution drives degradation.
  • Main soil problem: erosion by running water (natural + human factors). Highlands lose huge topsoil each year.
  • Fight erosion with reforestation, afforestation, terracing, strip cultivation, intercropping, contour ploughing, check dams, and related measures.
  • Vegetation: deforestation from fuelwood, construction, farms, slash-and-burn, overgrazing, fire, and settlement. Mitigate with conservation, capacity building, and institutions.
  • Water: "Water Tower of East Africa," yet drought, shrinking lakes, pollution, and rising potable-water demand. National conservation and management strategy applies.
  • Green Legacy (from 2019): tree planting and related greening to curb climate change and deforestation; forest cover reported raised toward about 15.7% (2018 NFI context in the textbook summary).

notes.title: 7.1.1 Soil degradation and conservation: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.1.1

Soil degradation and conservation

Running water is Ethiopia's most serious soil threat. People often make natural erosion worse.

Outcomes: describe causes; recognize effects; identify conservation measures

Key termSoil degradation. Change in the state of soil from increased erosion, leaching, or both.
Key termErosion. Wearing away of soil by natural agents (running water, wind, ice, waves, corrosion) and transport of particles to be deposited as sediment elsewhere.
Key termSoil erosion. Natural removal of soil from land. Human activities frequently aggravate it. In Ethiopia, erosion by running water is the most serious soil problem.
Key termLeaching. Loss of soluble nutrients washed down through the soil (linked with degradation when it increases).
Key termSoil conservation. Wise use of soil so society gains the greatest long-term benefit. Soil is renewable if conservation measures are applied (some are costly).

Natural factors that speed erosion

  • Steep slopes (topography)
  • Rainfall intensity, duration, and seasonality
  • Soil type (example: texture)
  • Torrent rivers in summer
  • Vegetation cover (less cover → more erosion)

Human-made factors

Key termDeforestation. Clearing highland forests that once protected watersheds and held soil. Rapid deforestation is a main cause of faster erosion.
Key termOvergrazing. Too many livestock on a small area. Animals destroy vegetation faster than it regrows; bare land erodes easily. Goats are especially damaging (including roots).
Key termOver cropping. Planting too densely so nutrients are used faster than nature can replace them.
Key termOver cultivation. Tilling every year (or too often) so nutrients leave faster than they return.
Key termSlash and burn. Cutting and burning vegetation to clear land or prepare fallow. Bare soil is left open to erosion. Also used to clear forest for farming.

Scale in Ethiopia: about 1.9 billion tons of highland topsoil washed away each year. River Abbay alone carries about 3000-4000 million cubic metric tons of soil yearly. Lost topsoil is essentially irreplaceable on human time scales.

Conservation measures

Key termReforestation. Planting trees on land that was forested before but lost its trees.
Key termAfforestation. Planting trees on land that was not formerly forested (bare or unproductive land) to create forest.
Key termTerracing. Building level surfaces at right angles to the slope to hold water and cut erosion (example: Konso).
Key termStrip cultivation. Planting different crops in alternating strips to retain water and soil.
Key termIntercropping. Growing two or more crops on the same field so land is not left bare to erode.
Key termContour ploughing. Ploughing across slopes (not up and down) to create barriers to runoff.
  • Control livestock numbers; develop improved grasses that feed more animals
  • Build tracks and routes so drainage does not wash them away easily
  • Construct check dams; plug gullies
  • Install shelter-belts and windbreaks in arid and semi-arid areas
Exam tip

Reforestation = replant former forest. Afforestation = plant where there was no forest. Know at least four soil measures (terrace, contour plough, strip, check dam).

notes.title: 7.1.2 Vegetation degradation and mitigation: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.1.2

Vegetation degradation and mitigation

Growing deforestation is the clearest sign of vegetation degradation in Ethiopia.

Outcomes: causes of degradation; effects; conservation and mitigation measures

Key termDeforestation (vegetation focus). Clearing forests and woodlands faster than they recover. Major causes: fuelwood demand; construction material; farm expansion; slash-and-burn; overgrazing; forest fires (natural and artificial); settlement expansion.
Key termOvergrazing. Too many livestock on a piece of land, stripping it bare. People also convert forest to pasture, expanding grazing at the expense of forest.
Key termSlash and burn (forest clearing). Cutting and burning forest to make farmland. Common in southwestern Ethiopia; destroys large forest areas yearly. Also used on farms left fallow to regain nutrients.
Key termBuilt-up area expansion. Factories, housing, and recreation take land. Some of that land was formerly forest.

Mitigation approaches (textbook)

  • Conservation
  • Capacity building
  • Institutional development

These help, but need more ideas and sustained effort.

Key termReforestation. Plant trees after every tree harvest.
Key termAfforestation. Plant trees on bare and unproductive lands.
Key termAgroforestry. Combining trees with farming systems to protect land and support livelihoods.
  • Control burning (slash-and-burn); control overgrazing; slow population growth
  • Use alternative household energy and alternative construction materials
  • Environmental education and public awareness
  • Forest curricula in schools and forestry institutions
  • Protect community forests with strict legal measures
  • Community participation; change lifestyles that drive deforestation
Must remember
  • List at least five deforestation causes for exams.
  • Textbook summary: forest cover once ~40% of the country fell below ~3%; Green Legacy context later cites about 15.7% (2018 NFI).

notes.title: 7.1.3 Water resources: problems and management: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.1.3

Water resources: problems and management

Ethiopia is called the Water Tower of East Africa, yet drought, pollution, and demand still threaten water.

Outcomes: causes and effects of water degradation; conservation and management responses

Key termWater Tower of East Africa. Name for Ethiopia's rich water potential over recent decades. Second richest African country in water-resource potential after the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Key termWater pollution. Contamination of rivers and other waters by sewage, organic wastes, fertilizers, and related pollutants. Volume and purity of many rivers are falling.
Key termWater management. Planning and practices that conserve water quantity and quality, protect ecosystems that regulate water, and guide dams, irrigation, and use.

Problems highlighted in the textbook

  • Drought recurs about every 3 to 5 years
  • Some Rift Valley lakes (example: Abijata, Cheleklektu) are disappearing or nearly so
  • River volume and purity are decreasing under pollution pressure
  • Rapid population growth raises demand for potable water

National strategy themes (remember the ideas)

  • Count costs and benefits of protecting watershed forests, wetlands, and key ecosystems in major projects
  • Treat wetlands and upstream forests as essential for water quality and quantity; rehabilitate and protect them
  • Control environmental health hazards in dam and irrigation design and use
  • Study and assess exotic species before introducing them to water ecosystems
  • Protect lake shores, river banks, and wetlands (land-water interface)
  • Involve users (including women and herders) in local water planning
  • Recycle wastewater when safe; recharge ground and surface water where viable
  • Improve farm-level water management for irrigation; support private water development with tech and credit
Exam tip

Link "Water Tower" reputation with the contrast: drought cycle, shrinking lakes, pollution, and rising potable demand.

notes.title: 7.2 The Ethiopian Green Legacy movement: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.2

The Ethiopian Green Legacy movement

A national tree-planting and greening drive launched to fight climate change and deforestation.

Outcomes: describe the Green Legacy concept; recognize its effects and goals

Key termGreen Legacy Initiative / movement. Government plan launched in 2019 by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. A tree-planting campaign to curb climate change and deforestation. It also covers agroforestry, forest sector development, urban greening and renewal, and integrated water and soil management.
Key termClimate change. Long-term shift in climate patterns. Green Legacy aims to curb its effects (distinct from short-term climate variability).
  • Plan: plant about 20 billion seedlings across the country over four years (2020-2023).
  • After planting: watering, weeding, and replacement planting to raise survival rates.
  • Supports national development goals and international commitments (Paris Agreement, UN 2030 Agenda, African Agenda 2063).
  • Guided by strategies such as Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE), Ten-Year National Forest Sector Development Program, and Bamboo Development Strategy and Action Plan.

Overall goals

  • Curb climate change and deforestation
  • Intensify climate-smart agriculture and raise productivity
  • Improve food security
  • Prevent environment-related conflicts
  • Battle desertification and soil erosion
  • Build a climate-resilient green economy
  • Ensure gender equality
Must remember
  • Start year 2019; ~20 billion seedlings (2020-2023); post-planting care matters.
  • Primary aim often tested as building a climate-resilient green economy / curbing climate change and deforestation.

notes.title: Geographic Inquiry Skills and Techniques: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Geography · Unit 8

Geographic Inquiry Skills and Techniques

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Geography student textbook. How to read maps, use scale, find position, sketch, and interpret graphs.

Study lessons 8.1 to 8.5 in order. Practise calculations before the quiz.

Unit outcomes · Unit 8
  • Recognize the concept of a map and its basic components (lesson 8.1)
  • Categorize scales and interpret maps at different scales (lesson 8.2)
  • Make measurements of area and distances using maps (lesson 8.2)
  • Demonstrate position on maps and make sketch maps (lessons 8.3, 8.4)
  • Investigate, gather geographic information, and analyze data with appropriate techniques (lesson 8.5)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Map = simplified, diminished, plane (2D) bird's-eye view of all or part of Earth's surface, drawn to scale.
  • Scale types: statement, representative fraction (RF), graphic (linear) scale.
  • Large scale ≥ 1:50,000 (small area, more detail). Medium 1:50,000 to 1:250,000. Small scale ≤ 1:250,000 (large area, less detail).
  • Position: geographic grid (lat/long) or national grid (eastings/northings; 4-digit or 6-digit).
  • Direction clockwise from north (compass points or bearings in degrees). Three norths: true, magnetic, grid.
  • Read legends; use line graphs, bar graphs, and pie charts for data.

notes.title: 8.1 Map and its basic components: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.1

Map and its basic components

A map shrinks the world onto a flat page so you can see place, pattern, and distance at a glance.

Outcomes: explain what a map is; outline map history; list basic map components

Key termMap. A simplified, diminished, plain representation of all or part of Earth's surface as viewed vertically from above (bird's-eye view).
Key termCartography / map making. The skill and practice of making maps.
Key termTraditional map making. Early maps on sticks, shells, clay, parchment, paper, or metal. Often locational (water holes, hunting grounds, paths). Distances and directions measured by hand in the field; accuracy often imperfect. Might show 3D pictographic drawings.
Key termModern map making. Later stage of map development with more accurate survey and standardized components (title, scale, grid, legend, and so on).

Main features of maps

  • Represent all or part of Earth's surface (city, world, or even a garden)
  • Two-dimensional (plane) representation (example: printed on paper)
  • Bird's-eye view from directly above
  • Always smaller than the real area; drawn to scale
  • Simplified; use agreed symbols plus notes for title, date, and scale

Basic components a map should include

Key termTitle. Tells what, where, and possibly when. Lets you know the purpose before reading detail.
Key termScale. Relationship between a length on the map and the matching length on the ground (how much the area was reduced).
Key termDirection / north arrow. Shows north. By convention, north is usually at the top.
Key termGrid reference. Coordinate system (parallels and meridians, or national grid) so the area sits in its correct place on Earth.
Key termLegend / key. Explains signs and symbols used on the map.
Key termDate / year of publication. Shows how old the map is and whether content may be outdated.
Key termPlace of publication and publisher. Where it was published and which organization published it.

Also: magnetic declination (variation) and compass information when given.

Exam tip

Meaning of symbols → key/legend. Map vs ground distance relationship → scale.

notes.title: 8.2 Scale, conversion and measurements: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.2

Scale, scale conversion and measurements on maps

Scale tells how many times reality was shrunk. Use it to turn map centimetres into ground kilometres.

Outcomes: distinguish large/medium/small scale; calculate scale; measure distance and area

Key termScale / map scale. Ratio or proportion of distance (and area) on the map to the corresponding distance (and area) on Earth's surface. The exact degree to which the map was reduced.

Large, medium, small scale

Key termLarge-scale map. Scale ≥ 1:50,000. Covers a small area with high detail. (1 cm on map = 50,000 cm on ground at 1:50,000.)
Key termMedium-scale map. Scale between 1:50,000 and 1:250,000. Medium area and medium detail.
Key termSmall-scale map. Scale ≤ 1:250,000. Covers a large area with less detail.

Memory hook: large scale = large fraction (1/50,000 is larger than 1/250,000) = zoomed in.

Three ways to express scale

Key termScale statement. Scale in words. Example: 1 cm to 1 km (one centimetre on the map represents one kilometre on the ground).
Key termRepresentative fraction (RF). Scale as a ratio or fraction. Example: 1:400,000 or $1/400000$.
Key termGraphic / linear / bar scale. A line drawn on the map and divided into ground-distance units (often in the lower margin). Primary divisions right of zero; secondary divisions left of zero for smaller readings.

Useful conversion

$1\ \mathrm{km} = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{cm}$

  • RF → statement: 1:500,000 means 1 cm to 500,000 cm = 1 cm to 5 km.
  • Statement → RF: 1 cm to 10 km = 1 cm to 1,000,000 cm → RF 1:1,000,000.

Measuring distance

Key termMap distance (MD). Distance measured on the map (usually in cm). Straight-line map distance is air distance (ignores ups and downs).
Key termField / ground distance. Real distance on Earth (km or m), found from map distance × scale.
  • Straight line: measure with a ruler; multiply by scale. Example: 4 cm on a 1:800,000 map → ground = 32 km.
  • Curved line (roads, rivers, coasts): use thread, string, or dividers; split into near-straight parts; add lengths. Example: 8.4 cm on 1:50,000 → 4.2 km.

Measuring area

  • Regular shapes: use geometry on map lengths, then convert with scale. Square $A=s^2$; rectangle $A=l\times w$; right triangle $A=\frac12 bh$; circle $A=\pi r^2$ ($\pi\approx 3.14$).
  • Example: grazing land 3 cm × 2 cm on scale 1 cm to 2.5 km → 7.5 km × 5 km = $37.5\ \mathrm{km}^2$.
  • Irregular shapes: planimeter (instrument) or grid-square method (manual counting of squares).
Exam tip

Which is small-scale? Pick the largest denominator (example: 1:250,000 over 1:40,000). Field distances are not usually in centimetres.

notes.title: 8.3 Position on maps: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.3

Position on maps

Say exactly where a place is: geographic grid, national grid, compass direction, or which "north" you mean.

Outcomes: use geographic and national grids; express direction; distinguish true, magnetic, and grid north

Geographic grid

Key termLatitude. Angular measurement from Earth's centre north or south of the equator (°, ′, ″). Lines of equal latitude are parallels.
Key termLongitude. Angular measurement east or west of the Prime Meridian (°, ′, ″). Lines of equal longitude are meridians.
Key termGeographic grid reference. Most accurate international way to locate a place: latitude then longitude (example: $10^\circ\mathrm{N}\ 75^\circ\mathrm{W}$). Read N/S of equator, then E/W of Prime Meridian.

National grid reference

Key termGrid. Criss-cross numbered lines that frame positions on a map. Vertical lines = eastings. Horizontal lines = northings. They meet at coordinates.
Key termNational grid origin (Ethiopia). Southwestern corner of the national grid: where $34^\circ 30'\mathrm{E}$ crosses the equator ($0^\circ$) in SW Kenya. Eastings number eastward from the origin; northings number northward. Eastings do not show true north (unlike meridians).
Key termFour-digit grid reference. Common on smaller-scale maps. Read easting (left of point) then northing (below point), each with tenths of the square. Example procedure ends as 5525 for point F in the textbook figure.
Key termSix-digit grid reference. Used on larger-scale maps for greater accuracy (finer division of each square).

Always give easting first, then northing.

Compass direction

Key termCompass. Instrument that shows direction (mariners, aviators, travellers). Thirty-two compass points. Four cardinals: N, E, S, W ($90^\circ$ apart). Midpoints: NE, SE, SW, NW ($45^\circ$). Finer points at $22.5^\circ$ (NNE, ENE, and so on).

Bearings in degrees start at north ($0^\circ$) and increase clockwise (example: $180^\circ$ = south; $135^\circ$ = southeast).

Three north points

Key termTrue / geographic north. Direction along a meridian toward the North Pole (Earth's spin axis).
Key termMagnetic north. Direction a compass needle points. Magnetic pole drifts yearly.
Key termMagnetic declination. Angle difference between true north and magnetic north at a place. Magnetic bearing (azimuth) is measured from magnetic north.
Key termGrid north. Direction of the north-south grid lines (eastings). Only coincides with true north along one central meridian; convenient for measuring bearings on the map.
Exam tip

Bearing $135^\circ$ → southeast. Direction is always measured clockwise from north.

notes.title: 8.4 Map sketching: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.4

Map sketching

A sketch map is a quick freehand outline that keeps the big geographic story and drops the clutter.

Outcomes: draw a local sketch map; mark selected feature positions

Key termSketch map. Outline map drawn from observation (not exact survey), showing only main features. Freehand on a board or pad to present geographic ideas. Minimizes irrelevant detail and maximizes major points. Ultimate geographic simplification.

How to draw one (textbook steps)

  • Decide the region and set boundaries so you do not sketch more than needed
  • Choose space so equal real sizes stay equal on the sketch
  • Note orientation (usually north "up")
  • Pick clear reference points (major street or river)
  • Choose detail level: larger area → less detail
  • Sketch general shapes first (circles, rectangles, triangles if unsure)
  • Add names and major land features
  • Do not overwork it: keep it clear, not perfect
Exam tip

Sketch map ≠ surveyed topographic sheet. Stress observation, main features, and north orientation.

notes.title: 8.5 Interpreting maps and graphs: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.5

Interpreting maps and graphs

Read the legend first. Then use graphs to see trends and parts of a whole.

Outcomes: interpret physical and human landscapes on maps; construct statistical diagrams from data

Key termConventional signs and symbols. Agreed worldwide map signs that represent the same detail in every country. Always check the legend/key first.
  • Symbols should be uniform, easy to read, and constant in size and orientation on one map
  • Common examples: towns as dots or shaded patches; water often blue; political boundaries as dotted or solid lines
Key termStatistical diagrams. Pictorial forms of numbers (charts, graphs, diagrams). Make comparisons, trends, and conclusions easier, especially for large data sets.
Key termSimple line graph. Uses a line to show change over time or the link between two variables. X-axis often time (independent); y-axis dependent value; start y at zero; mark points with dots or crosses. Example: Ethiopia population 1950-2020.
Key termSimple bar graph. Uses horizontal or vertical bars; bar length is proportional to the value. Good for amounts by place or by time (example: monthly rainfall at Kokosa, West Arsi).
Key termPie chart. Circle graph. Whole circle = 100%. Segments (slices) show parts of the whole and relative to each other. $1\% = 3.6^\circ$ of the circle. Example: Ethiopia's export destinations by continent.
Must remember
  • Line = change over time. Bar = compare amounts. Pie = parts of one total.
  • Always start map reading at the key.

notes.title: Discipline of History and Human Evolution: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 1

The Discipline of History and Human Evolution

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. How we study the past, where humans came from, the Stone Age, and how early states began.

Study lessons 1.1 to 1.5 in order. Check every unit outcome before a quiz.

Unit learning outcomes · Unit 1
  • Discuss the main objectives of studying history (lessons 1.1, 1.2)
  • Evaluate the place of Africa and Ethiopia in human evolution (lesson 1.3)
  • Summarise the theories on the origin of the state and its major features (lesson 1.5)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Prehistory = before writing. History = after writing begins (~5,500 years ago).
  • Sources: primary (original/contemporary) vs secondary (derived). No sources → no history.
  • Dating uses decade, century, millennium; calendars include Gregorian (BC/AD) and Islamic (BH/AH). Ethiopian calendar is 7-8 years behind Gregorian.
  • Human origin theories: creationist vs evolutionist (Darwin). Ethiopia/Horn rich in fossils (Lucy/Dinkinesh).
  • Stone Age: Paleolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic (agricultural revolution).
  • State features: population, territory, government, sovereignty, recognition.

notes.title: 1.1 Meaning of prehistory and history: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.1

Meaning of prehistory and history

History is an inquiry into what people did in the past. Prehistory is the long stretch before writing.

Outcomes: define history; explain the difference between prehistory and history

Key termHistory (word origin). From Greek Istoria: "inquiry" or "an account of one's inquiries."
Key termHistory (discipline). Study of humans in the past: what they did and what happened to them. As a body of knowledge, an account of the past based on historical facts and evidence. A branch of social science dealing with political, economic, social, and cultural change in past societies.
Key termHistorian. A person who studies and writes about the human past.
Key termPrehistory. Study of the distant past before people developed writing. Archaeologists and anthropologists find clues about early human life.
  • Historians often say "history" as a written record begins about 5,500 years ago when writing started. The human past as a whole still begins in prehistory.
  • History studies human interaction, civilizations, technology, and people's relationship with the environment (in the past; other fields may study the present).
  • People interact with nature to get food, shelter, and clothing, and improve tools and production over time.
Exam tip

Prehistory ends with the invention of writing (not stone tools). True: prehistory = before writing.

notes.title: 1.2 The discipline of history: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.2

The discipline of history

History is a social science about the past. Learn why it matters, how it is written, where evidence comes from, and how we date events.

Outcomes: importance of history; sources; historiography; dating

1.2.1 Importance of history

  • Know the past, understand the present, and foresee future developments
  • Understand national and international issues (including democracy and nationalism)
  • Build skills to collect and analyse information and reach conclusions
  • Live as conscious citizens who help shape the future
  • Develop research skills, a clearer present, and a sense of identity

1.2.2 Historiography and interpretation

Key termHistoriography. Study of how knowledge of the past is attained and transmitted.
  • Oldest written history traditions include China (records before 1000 BC).
  • Herodotus (c. 484-425 BC): often called the "father of history"; organized study and narration of the past. Thucydides wrote more critically and accurately.
  • History as an academic discipline grew in the second half of the 19th century. Leopold von Ranke (1795-1886): "father of modern historiography"; pushed scientific study of the past.
  • Ethiopia: indigenous chronicle tradition; academic History grew strongly from the 1960s.
Key termHistorical interpretation. Describing, analysing, evaluating, and explaining past events using primary and/or secondary sources. History should be systematic (follow rules and methods) and aim at objective truth; bias is hard to avoid in practice.

1.2.3 Sources of history

Where there are no sources, there is no history.

Key termPrimary sources. Contemporary with the events; original materials with a direct link. Examples: monuments, tools, ornaments, artifacts (coins, fossils, inscriptions, weapons, utensils, ruins), manuscripts, chronicles, diaries, letters, minutes, laws, court and admin files, travel documents, photos, maps, video/AV materials.
Key termSecondary sources. Information derived from primary sources; second-hand. Examples: articles, books, textbooks, biographies, published stories or movies about events, and oral traditions.
Key termOral tradition. Historical information passed by word of mouth from generation to generation. Cross-check with other sources; it can be distorted over time.

Evaluate critically: primary for originality/authenticity (avoid forgery); secondary for reliability of reconstruction.

1.2.4 Dating in history

Key termDating. Numerical statements that express when historical events or processes happened (short or long spans).
Key termDecade / century / millennium. 10 years / 100 years / 1,000 years. Example: 1900-1909 = first decade of the 20th century; 1900-1999 = 20th century; 1000-1999 = second millennium.
Key termChronology. Organising past events in sequence using calendars.
Key termGregorian calendar. Counts from the birth of Jesus Christ: BC (Before Christ) and AD (anno Domini, "Year of the Lord").
Key termEthiopian calendar. Ethiopia's own calendar and periodization; about 7 to 8 years behind the Gregorian calendar.
Key termIslamic calendar. Counts from the Hijra (Prophet Mohammed's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD): BH before Hijra, AH after Hijra.
Exam tip

Oral tradition is secondary (not "written materials"). Ranke = modern historiography; Herodotus = father of history.

notes.title: 1.3 The evolution of human beings: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3

The evolution of human beings

Two big origin stories compete: creation and evolution. Fossils put Africa, and Ethiopia, at the centre of the scientific story.

Outcomes: appraise theories; chart major stages; map African/Ethiopian sites

Key termCreationist theory. All living things, including humans, were created by God or a supernatural being. Still widely believed worldwide.
Key termEvolutionist (scientific) theory. Living things result from gradual change from earlier forms (evolution). Formulated by Charles Darwin (1809-1882); dominant in science today.
Key termHominids. Family of bipedal ancestors (walk upright on two feet). Living humans are Homo sapiens, from genus Homo.

Homo stages (succession in the Horn)

Key termHomo habilis. "Handy" human; oldest of the three Homo stages. Fossils in the Omo valley (Ethiopia); also Olduvai (Tanzania) and Lake Turkana (Kenya).
Key termHomo erectus. "Upright" human; ~2 million years ago. Larger, varied tools; first to leave Africa for Europe and Asia; used fire. Ethiopian sites: Omo Basin, Melka-Kunture, Konso-Gardula, Middle Awash.
Key termHomo sapiens. "Wise" humans, very like us. Fossils in Awash and Omo valleys and near Dire Dawa.
Key termHomo sapiens sapiens (modern humans). Appear ~100,000 years ago: large brains, bipedal, language, culture, tools, and knowledge passed across generations.

Key African / Ethiopian fossils

  • Sahelanthropus tchadensis (northern Chad, 2001): ~7-6 million years (oldest Australopithecine noted in the text).
  • Australopithecus ramidus (Afar, 1994): ~4.4 million years (Aramis / Middle Awash; Tim White's team).
  • Australopithecus afarensis / Lucy (Dinkinesh) (Hadar, Afar, 1974): ~3.18 million years; Donald Johanson; most complete skeleton then; bipedal; likely ancestor among Australopithecines.
  • Australopithecus africanus (Taung, South Africa, 1924): ~2.5 million years.

East African Rift Valley is central because of rich archaeological evidence. Ethiopia and the Horn illustrate all three Homo sub-species in succession.

Must remember
  • Creationist ≠ evolutionist (evolution is not "created by God").
  • Lucy = Dinkinesh = A. afarensis at Hadar, ~3.18 mya.

notes.title: 1.4 The Stone Age: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.4

The Stone Age

Making stone tools marks early humans. Three ages lead from crude hand-axes to farming.

Outcomes: analyse Stone Age stages; discuss achievements

Key termStone Age. Long period when tools were mainly stone, on the path from hunting-gathering toward civilization. Divided into Paleolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic.
Key termPaleolithic (Old Stone Age). Greek for "old stone." Longest stage, until about 11,000 years ago (~9,000 BC). Crude hand-axes; cave life; discovery of fire; beginnings of language.
Key termMesolithic (Middle Stone Age). Transition between Old and New Stone Ages (~9,000-8,000 BC). Slightly improved, more adaptable stone tools.
Key termNeolithic (New Stone Age). ~8,000-4,000 BC. Neolithic / Agricultural Revolution: shift from hunting and gathering to keeping animals and growing crops regularly (systematic agriculture). Laid prerequisites for civilization.
  • In parts of Ethiopia the Neolithic is placed about 7,000 years ago.
  • Domesticated plants noted: teff, dagussa, nug, enset; pottery begins.
  • Neolithic archaeological sites: Aksum, Lalibela, near Chercher (Hararghe), Metehara.
Exam tip

Domestication of plants and animals = Neolithic. Paleolithic = fire and crude hand-axes.

notes.title: 1.5 The emergence of states: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.5

The emergence of states

Settled farming communities grew. Over time some became states with territory, government, and sovereignty.

Outcomes: features of the state; factors and theories of origin

Key termState. A politically organised body of people on a defined territory, with an organised legitimate government, free from external control so it can exercise sovereignty in its area. Differs from a kingdom or an empire.

Features of a state

  • Population
  • Territory
  • Government
  • Sovereignty
  • Recognition

Theories on the origin of the state

Key termTheocratic state theory. Religion and priests took central administrative roles; early states ruled by priests.
Key termAgricultural / class theory. Farming created surplus; elites (wealthy higher status) gained control over others → state.
Key termTrade-route theory. Control of trade and routes empowered village chiefs (tribute, security); markets helped replace priestly dominance → state.
Key termWar / conquest theory. Conflict and force combined villages under powerful chiefs into states.

Sedentary life after the Neolithic made larger communities possible; simple organisation existed before complex states.

Must remember
  • List all five state features in exams.
  • Name at least three origin theories with one line each.

notes.title: Peoples and States in Ethiopia and the Horn: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 3

Peoples and States in Ethiopia and the Horn to the end of 13th C.

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Language families, religions, and early states through Zagwe and early Muslim sultanates.

Study lessons 3.1 to 3.5 in order.

Unit learning outcomes · Unit 3
  • Differentiate main language super-families of Ethiopia (lesson 3.1)
  • List major religions of Ethiopia (lesson 3.1)
  • Examine interaction among peoples to the end of the 13th century (lessons 3.1 to 3.5)
  • Analyse achievements of Pre-Aksumite and Aksumite kingdoms (lessons 3.2, 3.3)
  • Evaluate political-economic, social and cultural features to the 13th century (lessons 3.3 to 3.5)
  • Evaluate success and failure of the Zagwe Dynasty (lesson 3.4)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Super-families: Afro-Asiatic (Cushitic, Semitic, Omotic) and Nilo-Saharan (Chari-Nile, Koman).
  • Religions: indigenous, Judaism (Bete-Israel), Christianity (~330 AD via Frumentius/Ezana), Islam via trade routes.
  • Pre-Aksumite: Punt, Yeha, Damat, and other centres.
  • Aksum: 1st century AD; Adulis trade; Christianity state religion under Ezana.
  • Zagwe (~1150): Agaw of Lasta; power shift, not a brand-new kingdom; rock churches of Lalibela.
  • Sultanate of Shewa (896 AD): early Muslim state on Zeila trade routes (Makhzunmite dynasty).

notes.title: 3.1 Languages, religions and peoples: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.1

Languages, religions and peoples of Ethiopia and the Horn

Over 80 languages and several faiths, held together by long shared history.

Key termAfro-Asiatic super-family. Covers the largest share of Ethiopia's population. Divided into Cushitic, Semitic, and Omotic families. Cushitic has the widest areal coverage and most speakers (North, Central, Eastern subdivisions; North Cushitic includes Beja).
Key termNilo-Saharan super-family. Second super-family in Ethiopia and the Horn. Divided into Chari-Nile and Koman families. Many speakers live along Ethiopia's western border.

Some languages are endangered or extinct (example: Gafat disappeared).

Key termIndigenous religion. Beliefs native to a culture. Supreme creator deity; sacred natural powers; ancestor reverence; priests for rain, thanksgiving, and safety; farmers paid tributes.
Key termJudaism in Ethiopia. Practised from ancient times by Bete-Israel ("house of Israel"). Maintained Jewish tradition for generations; many lived in northwest Ethiopia before large flights to Israel in the 1980s-1990s. Shares Old Testament and Ge'ez liturgy links with Orthodox practice, but kept distinct Judaic rituals.
Key termChristianity in Ethiopia. Introduced ~330 AD by Frumentius (Freminatos), who converted King Ezana (r. 320-350). Became state religion. Nine Saints (late 5th century) spread it among the masses; Debre-Damo monastery; Bible into Ge'ez. First bishop Abuna Salama consecrated from Alexandria; Egyptian bishops until 1959 (Abune Basilios first Ethiopian Patriarch).
Key termIslam in the Horn. Entered mainly peacefully along trade routes via Red Sea (north), Gulf of Aden (east), and Indian Ocean (southeast). Clerics and merchants as missionaries. After Adulis's destruction (702 AD), Muslims occupied Dahlak; later Dahlak sultanate. Converted many Red Sea lowland pastoralists; harder to penetrate the northern Christian interior.
Exam tip

Western-border languages → often Chari-Nile and Koman. Afro-Asiatic = Cushitic + Semitic + Omotic.

notes.title: 3.2 Pre-Aksumite states: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.2

Pre-Aksumite states and their geographical setting

Before Aksum, several centres already traded and built monuments in the north.

Key termPunt. Ancient Horn state known from Egyptian sources. Exact borders unclear; likely Red Sea and Indian Ocean coasts of today's Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia. Trade with Egypt from the 3rd millennium BC (land and sea). Exports from the interior: gold (western Ethiopia), ivory, skins, myrrh, ostrich feathers, and related goods.
Key termYeha. About 30 km northeast of Aksum; oldest of the local centres (~1000 BC; peak ~750-500 BC). Famous temple, stone masonry, walls, and inscriptions.
Key termDamat. Pre-Aksumite state centred a few kilometres south of Aksum. Rulers used the South Arabian title Mukarib; links with South Arabia (inscriptions from 5th century BC). Used the Red Sea port of Adulis.
Key termOther early centres. Hawulti-Melazo (inscribed stone tablets SE of Aksum), Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase, Coloe, and related sites.
Exam tip

Which state formed first in the region? Options often include Punt, Damat, Yeha, Aksum. Know Punt/Yeha/Damat as pre-Aksumite.

notes.title: 3.3 Aksumite Kingdom: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.3

Aksumite Kingdom

Aksum rose in the first century AD into a Red Sea trading power and early Christian kingdom.

Outcomes: describe Aksumite features and achievements

Key termAksumite Kingdom. Emerged in the 1st century AD with nucleus at Aksum (political and religious centre: temples and monolithic steles). Between the 4th and 6th centuries it expanded east beyond the Red Sea (southern Arabia), west toward the Nile, and south into parts of the Ethiopian highlands.
  • Economy: agriculture plus Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade (ivory, gold, incense, slaves; imported luxuries).
  • Minted its own coins; used Ge'ez writing; famous for tall carved steles.
  • Ezana (4th century) adopted Christianity; Aksum became one of the earliest Christian states.
  • Decline after the 7th century as Red Sea trade routes shifted with the rise of Islam; political centre later moved inland.
Exam tip

Aksum = trade + steles + coins + early Christianity under Ezana.

notes.title: 3.4 Zagwe Dynasty: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.4

Zagwe Dynasty

Power shifted to Agaw rulers of Lasta, famous for Lalibela's rock churches.

Outcomes: explain Zagwe political and cultural achievements

Key termZagwe Dynasty. From the local Agaw ruling class in Lasta (within the former Aksumite world). Founded ~1150 AD by Mera Tekle Haymanot; new capital at Adefa (Roha) in Lasta. Not a brand-new kingdom: a political power shift from Semitic to Agaw elites while continuing Christian Aksumite traditions.
  • Best known for rock-hewn churches of Lalibela (King Lalibela), a lasting cultural and religious achievement.
  • Other noted Zagwe rulers include Yimrhane Kristos.
  • Ended when Yekuno-Amlak overthrew Zagwe rule in 1270 and founded the "Solomonic" dynasty (Unit 7).
Exam tip

Zagwe = Agaw of Lasta + Lalibela churches. Overthrown 1270.

notes.title: 3.5 The Sultanate of Shewa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.5

The Sultanate of Shewa

Islam and Zeila trade routes produced early Muslim states in the southeast.

Outcomes: describe early Muslim states linked to trade

Key termSultanate of Shewa. First major Muslim sultanate established in 896 AD after Islam spread along trade routes. Founders claimed Makhzumite clan descent from southern Arabia (Makhzumite dynasty). Located in hot lowlands east/southeast of the highland Christian core.
  • Grew with control of inland links to the Zeila trade corridor.
  • Later replaced/overshadowed when Ifat (Walasma) destroyed the Makhzumite line in 1285 (Unit 7).
  • Shows how Islam and long-distance trade created durable Muslim polities in the Horn alongside the Christian kingdom.
Exam tip

Shewa sultanate 896 = Makhzumite. Zeila trade is the economic key. Ifat/Walasma later take over.

notes.title: Ancient World Civilizations: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 2

Ancient World Civilizations up to c. 500 AD

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Major early civilizations across Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Europe, plus the rise of Christianity.

Study lessons 2.1 to 2.5. Match each civilization to its river/region and one signature achievement.

Focus for exams
  • Outline and analyse major achievements of African, Asian, American, and European civilizations
  • Evaluate their impact on modern society
  • Describe the origin and spread of Christianity

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Egypt: Nile, pharaoh, hieroglyphics, papyrus, pyramids, mummification.
  • Nubia/Kush: Nile Sudan; Meroe iron; Ezana destroys Meroe ~350 AD.
  • Mesopotamia: Tigris-Euphrates; cuneiform; ziggurats; bronze, plough, potter's wheel.
  • Persia: Cyrus ~550 BC; roads and first postal service; Zoroastrianism.
  • India: Indus Valley; Hinduism then Buddhism as reform.
  • China: Yellow River; Shang then Zhou; Confucianism; Great Wall; logographic writing.
  • Maya, Inca, Aztec: Americas; Spanish conquest in 16th century.
  • Greece: polis, Athens/Sparta; democracy, philosophy, drama. Rome: republic then empire; law, engineering, Coliseum.
  • Christianity: Palestine, 1st century AD; Constantine Edict of Milan 313; official under Theodosius 392.

notes.title: 2.1 Ancient civilizations of Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.1

Ancient civilizations of Africa

Two Nile civilizations shaped early Africa: Egypt and Nubia (Kush).

Outcomes: outline, analyse, and evaluate achievements of ancient African civilizations

Key termAncient Egypt. Civilization in the Nile Valley from about 3000 BC. Tradition: Upper and Lower Egypt unified by Menes ~3200 BC. Economy based on agriculture (Nile silt; wheat, barley), livestock, and trade.
Key termPharaoh. Absolute king of Egypt, also regarded as a god (incarnated; a god after death watching over Egypt). Ruled through viziers (mayors, tax collectors, judges).
Key termPolytheism. Worship of many gods (Egyptians were polytheists).
Key termMummification. Preserving the body for belief in life after death; skill later advanced Egyptian medicine.
Key termPyramid. Massive tomb for pharaohs, built by peasant labour with temples and palaces.
Key termHieroglyphics. Egyptian writing (~3000 BC): pictograms, ideograms, phonograms, and determinatives. Egyptians also used papyrus (paper-like writing material).
Key termNubia / Kush. Kingdom along the Nile in today's northeastern Sudan (~2000 BC to ~350 AD). Cereals, vegetables, dates; pastoralism; trade. Divine kings and queens like Egyptian pharaohs. Meroe: metal centre (gold, copper, silver, iron). Kushites conquered Egypt in the 8th century BC. Aksumite king Ezana invaded and destroyed Meroe ~350 AD.
Exam tip

Mesopotamia wrote on clay (cuneiform); Egyptians used papyrus. Nubia = advanced iron at Meroe.

notes.title: 2.2 Civilizations in Asia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.2

Civilizations in Asia

River valleys and empires from Mesopotamia to China left writing, law, roads, and philosophy.

Outcomes: outline and analyse major Asian civilization achievements

Key termMesopotamia. "Land between rivers" (Tigris and Euphrates): eastern Syria, southern Turkey, much of Iraq. Sumerians built early cities with sun-dried mud brick. Ziggurat: large stepped temple tower. Fertile irrigated agriculture. Divine kings representing city gods; polytheism. First plough and potter's wheel; early bronze. Writing ~3200 BC: cuneiform (complex ideographs, not an alphabet). Also maths, astronomy, medicine, metalwork.
Key termPersia. Parts of today's Iran and Afghanistan ("Land of Aryans" → Iran). First Persian Empire under Cyrus the Great ~550 BC: Balkans to Indus, plus parts of North Africa. Contributions: government, law, religion; new roads; world's first postal service. Religion: Zoroastrianism (prophet Zoroaster).
Key termIndia (Indus Valley). Began ~2500 BC (Pakistan and western India); peak ~1500 BC. Counting, measuring, weighing, writing; irrigation canals; trade with Mesopotamia. Copper/bronze tools and gold ornaments. Hierarchical society by work and birth. Hinduism from early Indo-Aryan beliefs; Buddhism emerged from Hinduism as reform and spread to SE Asia, China, and Japan.
Key termChina. Yellow River (Hwang Ho) north China; height ~3000 BC in that valley. Shang dynasty (c. 1700-1122 BC): bronze vessels, war chariots, writing. Zhou (Chou) from ~1122 BC to 256 BC: classics and philosophy. Confucius (551-479 BC): Confucianism (ordered society: parents over children, men lead women, educated judge ordinary people). Great Wall (~7,400 km) against Central Asian invaders. Writing: logographic (pictorial symbols for words).
Matching tip

Cuneiform → Sumerians. Postal service → Persians. Great Wall → China (not Shang alone as "during Shang" is often false in reviews).

notes.title: 2.3 Ancient civilizations of Latin America: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.3

Ancient civilizations of Latin America

Maya, Inca, and Aztec built rich American empires before Spanish conquest.

Outcomes: outline achievements of ancient American civilizations

Key termMaya. Native American civilization peaking ~250-900 AD. Architecture, painting, pottery, sculpture; strong astronomy and maths; accurate yearly calendar; advanced writing; many gods. Limestone pyramids with temples on top. Spanish took the south in the 16th century; full domination by late 17th century.
Key termInca. South American empire expanding from ~1438 across present Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina. Capital Cusco (southern Peru). Skilled engineering and crafts: road network; gold and silver artifacts; fine cotton and wool cloth. Conquered by Spanish after 1532.
Key termAztecs. Powerful empire in Mexico in the 15th-16th centuries; centre in the Valley of Mexico. Capital Tenochtitlan (site of today's Mexico City). Agriculture-based economy; hundreds of gods; pictographic writing. Destroyed by Spaniards in 1521.
Exam tip

Match capital to people: Cusco → Inca; Tenochtitlan → Aztec. Spanish destroyed Aztec empire in 1521.

notes.title: 2.4 Civilizations in Europe: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.4

Civilizations in Europe

Greece shaped Western culture; Rome shaped law, engineering, and empire.

Outcomes: outline and analyse Greek and Roman achievements

Key termAncient Greece / Hellas. Birthplace of Western civilization (~2,500 years ago). Culture in city-states (polis: city/town plus surrounding villages and farmland). Best known: Athens and Sparta. Shared language, religion, culture; people called themselves Hellenes. Never one united nation.
  • Architecture: Parthenon (temple of Athena) in Athens
  • Invented drama (theatre); marble/bronze sculpture of gods and heroes
  • History: Herodotus (Persian Wars; wider world); Thucydides (Peloponnesian War)
  • Medicine: Hippocrates (symptoms, classification, sensible remedies)
  • Words of Greek origin: democracy, psychology, Olympic, marathon
  • Philosophy: Plato and Aristotle (taught in Athens)
Key termAncient Rome. Began ~753 BC on hills above the Tiber (Italy). Influence: Roman law as base for many Western European and Latin American legal systems; roads, bridges, aqueducts as engineering models; public baths and amphitheatres (example: Coliseum).
Key termRoman Republic. From 509 BC after nobles overthrew the king. Two elected consuls (one year each); powerful Senate (life service). Lasted nearly 500 years until 27 BC.
Key termRoman Empire. After civil war destroyed the republic; lasted until Rome fell in 476 AD.
True/false trap

Republic began when nobles overthrew the king (not the reverse). Birthplace of Western civilization → Greece.

notes.title: 2.5 Rise and spread of Christianity: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.5

Rise and spread of Christianity

A faith born in Roman Palestine became the Empire's official religion within four centuries.

Outcomes: describe origin; explain spread

Key termChristianity. Religion based on the teaching of Jesus Christ. Began in Palestine in the 1st century AD. Jesus born in Bethlehem (Judea) under Roman rule.
  • Rome saw Christians as a threat to imperial unity and persecuted them (from Nero, AD 54-68).
  • Constantine became Christian (312) and favoured the faith. Edict of Milan (313) ordered religious toleration; persecution eased.
  • Under Theodosius the Great (378-395), Christianity became the official Roman religion in 392 AD.
  • In the Middle Ages, Christianity helped unify Western Europe after the Empire's political fall.
Key termMonotheism. Belief in one God (Christianity is monotheistic; contrast Egyptian/Greek polytheism).
Exam tip

Toleration / stop persecution → Constantine (Edict of Milan). Official state religion → Theodosius (392).

notes.title: Middle Ages and Early Modern World: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 4

The Middle Ages and Early Modern World, c. 500 to 1750s

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. From feudal Europe and Byzantium to Islam, Ottomans, early capitalism, exploration, Renaissance, Reformation, and the start of industrial change.

Study lessons 4.1 to 4.7. Link each big change (faith, trade, machines) to one date you can recall under exam pressure.

Focus for exams
  • Identify major characteristics of European feudal society in the medieval period
  • Examine main features of the Byzantine Empire
  • Discuss the rise and expansion of Islam during the period
  • Explain the relationship between Europe and the Ottoman Turkish Empire
  • Evaluate major changes in the medieval ages and early modern times

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Dark Age (c. 500-1000): Greco-Roman decline in the West; feudal order emerges.
  • Feudalism: fief/feud = land for service; manor; Church owns land and shapes culture.
  • Byzantine: East Rome; capital Constantinople; Greek; Orthodox split 1054; Justinian peak; Manzikert 1071.
  • Islam: Prophet Mohammed ~610; Hejira 622; caliphates expand west to Spain and east to Central Asia.
  • Ottomans: replace Seljuks; Constantinople 1453 → Istanbul; janissaries; block Far East route.
  • China: dynastic cycle and Mandate of Heaven (Qin to Qing, ended 1911/12).
  • Early capitalism: towns revive; merchants invest capital in production and long-distance trade.
  • Exploration: Portugal/Spain lead; da Gama 1498; Columbus 1492; Magellan 1519-22.
  • Renaissance: rebirth of learning from Italy; human ability emphasised.
  • Reformation: Luther 1517 → Protestant churches; Catholic Counter-Reformation.
  • Industrial Revolution: Britain from 1780s; steam (Watt); factories, then railways.

notes.title: 4.1 The Middle Ages in Europe: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.1

The Middle Ages in Europe

After West Rome fell, Western Europe went rural and feudal while the East Roman (Byzantine) Empire survived.

Outcomes: describe medieval features; analyse components; recognise merits and demerits

Key termDark Age. West European period from about 500 to 1000 AD. Called "dark" because civilization declined: cities shrank, societies became rural, Greco-Roman culture faded. West Rome fell from internal division/decay and 5th-century invasions (Anglo-Saxons, Franks; Huns, Magyars). By c. 1000, more stability returned and feudal society was in place.
Key termFeudalism. Socio-political system roughly 500-1500. Ruling class: kings, nobles, knights, higher clergy. Vassalage: higher lord gives a fief (feud: piece of land) to a lower lord, who becomes his vassal and owes service. Basic unit: the manor (village). Manorial lord held political, judicial, and military power over peasants. Mass of society (peasants, craftsmen, traders) had little power. Exploitative system.
Key termChurch in feudal Europe. Roman Catholic Church owned land and held authority over rulers and ordinary people. Responsible for religion, education, and culture. Knights practiced chivalry; bishops and monks kept records.
Key termByzantine Empire. East Roman Empire after the West fell. Capital: Constantinople (modern Istanbul). Official language became Greek. Orthodox Church separated from Roman Catholic Church in 1054 and supported the emperor. Economy: agriculture, trade, crafts. Architecture: domes and coloured glass. Hierarchy: emperor, higher clergy, landowning nobility, peasants. Peak under Justinian (r. 527-565).
  • Seljuk Turks occupied Asia Minor from 1040; Crusades from the 1090s (first 1096; eight major) aimed to free Christian holy lands. Failed to crush Muslim power but helped shield Western Europe from eastern invasion.
  • Byzantine disaster at Battle of Manzikert (1071): lost most of Asia Minor to Seljuks, later to Ottomans.
Exam tip

Dark Age = West Europe decline 500-1000. Fief = land for service. Orthodox split = 1054. Manzikert = 1071.

notes.title: 4.2 The Middle Ages in Asia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.2

The Middle Ages in Asia

Islam reshaped the Near and Middle East; Ottomans built a vast empire; China explained rule through the dynastic cycle.

Outcomes: describe medieval Asia; explain rise and expansion of Islam

Key termIslam. Means "submission to the will of Allah." Began in Arabia with Prophet Mohammed in Mecca around 610 AD. Worshippers are Muslims. Opposed by Quraysh Arabs; in 622 Mohammed and followers moved Mecca → Medina (Hejira): start of the Islamic calendar. After the Prophet's death, Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates led great conquests: North Africa and Spain in the west to Central Asia in the east.
Key termOttoman Empire. Named after chief Osman (Othman). Seljuks occupied Palestine, Asia Minor, Arabia from 1040; Ottomans replaced them by the late 13th century. Centre in today's Turkey. Seized Anatolia (1336); Adrianople 1356; Salonika 1387; defeated Serbs 1389 and Bulgarians 1393. By the 15th century the Balkans (including Greece) were largely conquered. Captured Constantinople in 1453, renamed Istanbul, made it capital. Syria 1516; Egypt 1517. Vienna held against Turks in 1529.
  • Janissaries: highly trained soldiers. Spread Islam; wealth from trade; controlled Europe-Asia route; banned European merchants from the Far East.
  • Society: Sultan, grand viziers (bureaucrats), janissaries, occupational groups. Culture of the Islamic world.
Key termDynastic cycle (China). New dynasty strong, rules well, has popular support. When corrupt and weak, it loses the Mandate of Heaven (authority/legitimacy) and is replaced (often by rebels). Cycle repeats. Long line of empires from Qin to Qing; Qing ended by revolution in 1911/1912. Chinese civilization strongly influenced Korea and Japan.
Date drill

Hejira 622. Constantinople → Istanbul 1453. Mandate of Heaven = right to rule China.

notes.title: 4.3 Development of early capitalism: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.3

Development of early capitalism

Capitalism grew when people used accumulated wealth to expand production, not only to fund monuments.

Outcomes: explain early capitalism; value its link to the modern world

Key termEarly capitalism. System that uses accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity (unlike investing mainly in unproductive projects such as pyramids or cathedrals). After Rome's fall, many cities were ruined; trade later revived and old Roman towns were restored as centres of production and exchange.
  • Merchants bought raw materials, paid workers to manufacture goods, and sold finished products for profit.
  • After the discoveries, long-distance international trade offered big profits.
  • Obstacles: transport difficulties, insecurity (war, robbery), and heavy tolls (transit taxes).
Exam tip

Key contrast: capital into productive capacity vs capital into prestige buildings. Towns = production and exchange hubs.

notes.title: 4.4 The Age of Explorations and Discoveries: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.4

The Age of Explorations and Discoveries

Fifteenth and sixteenth-century voyages sought new routes to Asia after Ottomans blocked the old path.

Outcomes: draw/recall early exploration routes

Key termAge of Explorations. European voyages in the 15th-16th centuries, partly to bypass the Ottoman blockade of the Europe-Far East trade route. Leaders: Portugal and Spain, then Holland, Britain, France, Russia. Motives of sponsors (economy, religion, glory): Prince Henry the Navigator (Portugal, 1394-1460) and Queen Isabella of Spain (1451-1504).
  • Drivers: interest in long-distance trade; compass; better maps and ships; growing geographic knowledge.
  • Vasco da Gama (Portugal): sea route to India and the Far East, 1498.
  • Christopher Columbus (for Spain): reached America 1492; died without knowing he had found new lands. Name America from mapmaker Amerigo Vespucci; also called the "New World".
  • Ferdinand Magellan (for Spain): circumnavigated the world 1519-1522.
  • Newly "discovered" lands were later conquered as European colonies. Voyages boosted profits, globalisation, and faster capitalist growth.
Matching tip

1492 Columbus (America). 1498 da Gama (India sea route). 1519-22 Magellan (world voyage). Ottoman block → search for new routes.

notes.title: 4.5 The Renaissance: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.5

The Renaissance

"Rebirth" of learning that began in Italy and reshaped European art, politics, and ideas about the individual.

Outcomes: compare Renaissance ideals with today's thinking

Key termRenaissance. Intellectual movement meaning "rebirth" of learning. Roughly 14th to 17th centuries. Began in Italy; spread to England, France, Germany, Spain, Holland.
  • Italy was essentially an urban society.
  • Age of recovery from 14th-century disasters; revival in politics and art.
  • New view of human beings: emphasis on individual ability.
Exam tip

Renaissance = rebirth of learning, Italy first, individual ability. Do not confuse with Reformation (religious split).

notes.title: 4.6 The Reformation: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.6

The Reformation

A 16th-century religious movement that produced Protestantism and forced Catholic reform.

Outcomes: compare Reformation ideals with today's thinking

Key termReformation. Religious movement that led to Protestantism breaking from the Catholic Church in the early 16th century. Began in Germany with Martin Luther (1517). Causes: social, political, religious, and economic. Reformers supported capitalism, individualism, and nation-states.
  • Jean Calvin (French, in Switzerland): Calvinist church. French Calvinists called Huguenots.
  • John Knox (Scotland): Presbyterian Calvinism, 1560.
  • England: Henry VIII and Elizabeth I separated from Rome; national church = Anglican Church.
Key termCounter-Reformation. Catholic Church's own reform response to Protestant challenge (including missionary organisations such as the Jesuits).
True/false trap

French Calvinists = Huguenots (not Presbyterians). English national Protestant church = Anglican. Luther starts Reformation in 1517.

notes.title: 4.7 Industrial Revolution: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.7

Industrial Revolution

Machines and steam power shifted economies from farm and handicraft to factory manufacturing.

Outcomes: define industrial revolution; list contributions to the modern world

Key termIndustrial Revolution. Invention and use of machines in place of hard hand labour. Shift from farming/handicrafts to manufacturing by machine in factories. Began in Great Britain in the 1780s; spread over decades to other Western nations. By mid-19th century Britain was the world's first and richest industrial nation (1850 cotton industry alone ≈ all other European countries combined).
  • New power: steam (replaced wind/water). Early engines: Savery (1698), Newcomen (c. 1705-1711). James Watt (1782-84) improved steam engines for factory machinery.
  • Steam then applied to transport: steamboats, steamships, railways. First railway locomotive 1804.
  • Also in the United States from about 1800; later the US surpassed Britain in industrial production.
  • On the continent, early industrialisers: Belgium, France, Germany.
  • Britain's advantages often tested: natural resources, labour force, readiness to invest in machines.
Exam tip

Define = machines replace hand labour; factories; steam. Start = Britain, 1780s. Watt improves steam; locomotive 1804.

notes.title: Peoples and States of Africa to 1500: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 5

Peoples and States of Africa to 1500

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Language families, major pre-colonial states, Islam in West Africa, Trans-Saharan trade, and early outside contacts.

Study lessons 5.1 to 5.9. Match each empire to its trade base and one reason it rose or fell.

Focus for exams
  • Outline major economic, cultural, social and political developments in pre-colonial Africa
  • Describe the peoples and language families of Africa
  • Analyse inter-connections among Africans from trade, population movements and wars
  • Evaluate factors for the rise and decline of empires in Africa to the early 16th century
  • Explain the origin of Islam and its role in the expansion of West African empires

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Four language super-families: Congo-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan, Khoisan. Not all African languages are native (Arabic, colonial European languages).
  • Mamluk Egypt: Turkish origin; dynasty 1250-1517; Ottomans take Egypt 1517.
  • Funj Sultanate: 1504, capital Sennar (Sudan); rivalry with Ethiopia; conquered by Egypt in 1820s.
  • West Africa: Ghana (Soninke; ends 1076 Almoravids) → Mali (Sundiata; Mansa Musa; Timbuktu) → Songhai (Gao; ends 1591 Tondibi). Also Kanem-Bornu, Hausa states.
  • Kongo (late 14th c.); Swahili city-states (Kilwa, Mombasa, Mogadishu…); Great Zimbabwe (Shona, gold trade).
  • Trans-Saharan trade (camels; gold, salt, later enslaved people) built Ghana, Mali, Songhai power and spread Islam.

notes.title: 5.1 Languages and peoples of Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.1

Languages and peoples of Africa

Over 1000 languages on the continent group into four major super-families.

Outcomes: describe languages and peoples; appreciate diversity

Key termFour language super-families. Linguists classify African peoples mainly as speakers of Congo-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan, and Khoisan.
  • Congo-Kordofanian: Niger-Congo (much of West Africa and all of Bantu Africa; 450+ Bantu languages; Kiswahili is Bantu) and Kordofanian (small area in the Nuba hills, Sudan).
  • Afro-Asiatic: northern Africa, Sahara, Horn, around Lake Chad. Six sub-groups: Berber, Chadic, Coptic (Ancient Egyptian), Cushitic, Omotic, Semitic. Omotic spoken only in Ethiopia; Semitic mainly in the Horn.
  • Nilo-Saharan: six subgroups including Chari-Nile, Songhay, Saharan, Meban, Koman, Fur.
  • Khoisan: Khoikhoi and San; around the Kalahari (northern South Africa, SW Botswana, Namibia).
True/false trap

Not all languages spoken in Africa are native. Arabic arrived with Muslim Arabs (7th-11th c.); colonial powers later brought European languages.

notes.title: 5.2 States in North Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.2

States in North Africa

Mamluk Egypt and the Funj Sultanate shaped northeast Africa and often clashed with Ethiopia over trade.

Outcomes: explain Mamluk Egypt; discuss the Funj Kingdom

Key termMamluk Egypt. Fatimids used Turkish-origin Mamluk soldiers and declared Egyptian independence from Baghdad in 969. Mamluks later took power and ruled Egypt 1250-1517; expanded into Palestine, Syria, and beyond. Economic growth under Mamluks. Ethio-Egyptian relations often conflictual; Zera Yacob (r. 1434-1468) tried smoother ties (short-lived). Decline: corruption, falling agriculture, cattle plague, drought. Ottomans defeated Mamluks with firearms and occupied Egypt in 1517.
Key termFunj Sultanate. Founded 1504 by cattle-keeping nomads in today's Sudan; capital Sennar. Fought Ethiopia over trade routes; King Susenyos's army hit them hard ~1620. Continued until Muhammed Ali of Egypt conquered it in the 1820s.
Exam tip

Mamluk dynasty dates: 1250-1517. Funj capital = Sennar (1504). Both rivalled Christian Ethiopia over trade.

notes.title: 5.3 Spread of Islam and its impact in West Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.3

Spread of Islam and its impact in West Africa

Islam moved from Arabia into Egypt and North Africa, then helped reshape West African empires.

Outcomes: explain Islam's origin and role in West African empire expansion

Key termIslam into Africa. After Islam's rise in the early 7th century, Muslim Arabs conquered Egypt in 642, then the rest of North Africa; by century's end they reached Morocco and southern Spain. After 11th-century rivalries, Islam revived in North Africa with more Arab immigration, then expanded with West African empires.
  • Islam linked West African rulers to North African and wider Muslim trade and learning networks.
  • Control of Trans-Saharan routes helped small states grow into empires (Ghana, Mali, Songhai, and others).
  • Islamization spread along with trade across West and West-Central Africa.
Exam tip

Egypt conquered 642. Islam + Trans-Saharan trade = key combo for West African imperial rise.

notes.title: 5.4 States in Western Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.4

States in Western Africa

Ghana, Mali, and Songhai rose on Trans-Saharan trade; Kanem-Bornu and Hausa states also mattered.

Outcomes: write origin, rise and fall of West African empires; recognise Islam's role

Key termGhana Empire. Soninke people; parts of today's Mauritania, Mali, Senegal. Founded 4th century AD; height ~1000 AD. Relied on Trans-Saharan trade. Rise of Islam was central to both greatness and decline. Ended 1076 when Almoravids captured capital Kumbi Saleh.
Key termMali Empire. Emerged after Ghana. Founded by Sundiata Keita (Mandinka). Greatest king: Mansa Musa (1312-1337), pilgrimage to Mecca; Islam expanded widely. Capital Timbuktu: major Islamic learning centre. Weakened by poor leadership and attacks (e.g. Tuareg); Songhai rose after.
Key termSonghai Empire. Capital Gao. Threw off Mali's overlordship late 14th century. Controlled Trans-Saharan trade; ties with Berbers; kings accepted Islam early 11th century; gold from forest region. Ended 1591 when Morocco defeated Songhai at Tondibi.
  • Kanem-Bornu: Muslim ruling dynasty; army protected routes and taxed traders; declined as trade shifted to the Atlantic coast.
  • Hausa city-states (Nigeria, ~1000-1200): Kano, Katsina, Zazzau (Zaria), Gobir, Kebbi, Rano, Zamfara; pastoralists and farmers; agriculture-based economy.
Matching tip

Kumbi Saleh → Ghana. Timbuktu / Mansa Musa → Mali. Gao / Tondibi 1591 → Songhai. Main greatness factor for Ghana often = Trans-Saharan trade.

notes.title: 5.5 Equatorial, Central and Eastern Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.5

Equatorial, Central and Eastern Africa

Bantu migrations, the Kingdom of Kongo, and Swahili coastal cities linked inland Africa to Indian Ocean trade.

Outcomes: analyse relationships among African regions

Key termBantu migrations. From the 1st millennium BC, farming peoples speaking Bantu dialects moved slowly from the Niger region into East Africa and the Congo basin as small communities (not invading hordes).
Key termKingdom of Kongo. Lower Zaire River; founded by Bantu people in the late 14th century. Hunters, warriors, skilled smiths; agriculture and trade. European explorers reached Kongo in 1482 and 1491; later Portuguese colonisation.
Key termSwahili city-states. Bantu coastal villages ~2000 years ago; after Islam rose, Arabic-speaking Muslim merchants married into local elites. Language Swahili ("coasters" in Arabic): African with Islamic/Arabic influence. Cultural diffusion of Arabic, Persian, and Bantu traditions. Key ports: Mogadishu; Malindi, Mombasa; Zanzibar, Kilwa; Brava, Pate, Pemba, Sofala. Kilwa (island): main East African gold and ivory trade centre. Wealthy Muslim elites ruled the cities.
Exam tip

Swahili = cultural mix (Bantu + Arabic/Persian/Islamic). Famous trade hub = Kilwa.

notes.title: 5.6 Southern Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.6

Southern Africa

States formed more slowly in the south; Great Zimbabwe became a famous trading power.

Outcomes: describe southern kingdoms; explain the nature of southern African peoples

Key termGreat Zimbabwe. Founded by Bantu-speaking Shona from about AD 1000. In the 13th-14th centuries: stone houses, large circular wall and tower. Wealthy trading empire linked to the East African coast (11th-15th centuries). Economy: cattle, crops, and gold trade on the Indian Ocean coast.
  • Independent villages consolidated into early states from about the 11th century.
  • Khoisan-speaking Khoikhoi and San peoples lived around the Kalahari region (see 5.1).
Exam tip

Great Zimbabwe = Shona + stone architecture + gold/cattle trade. Not a West African Trans-Saharan empire.

notes.title: 5.7-5.9 Relations, Trans-Saharan trade, early contacts: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.7-5.9

Relations, Trans-Saharan trade, early contacts

Camels, gold, and salt tied Africa together; the East African coast opened early windows to the wider world.

Outcomes: analyse inter-connections; evaluate trade impacts; describe early outside contacts

Key termIntra- vs inter-continental relations. Intracontinental = within Africa. Intercontinental = between continents. North-south Sahara contact became regular Trans-Saharan caravan trade from the 4th century after the camel; Islam later strengthened North-tropical African ties.
Key termTrans-Saharan trade. Routes linked West/West-Central Africa with North Africa; another crossed the central Sahara to Kanem; a branch linked West Africa and Egypt. Goods included gold and salt; after the 7th century, enslaved people also became important. Empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai grew powerful by controlling routes. Trade spread Islam in West and West-Central Africa.
Key termEarly outside contacts. East African coast interacted with Arabs, Greeks, Persians, Romans, Chinese, Indians, Spain, and Portuguese. From the mid-15th century, Portugal and Spain pushed to dominate international trade through sponsored navigators. European images of Africa often framed Europe as superior by contrast.
Exam tip

Camel + Trans-Saharan routes → imperial power in West Africa. First European push to dominate African trade links: Portugal and Spain (not Britain/France first).

notes.title: Africa and the Outside World: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 6

Africa and the Outside World, 1500-1880s

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Coastal contact with Europe, slavery and the Trans-Atlantic trade, "legitimate" commerce, white settlement in South Africa, explorers and missionaries.

Study lessons 6.1 to 6.5. Be ready to define Triangular Trade and list economic, political, and social effects on Africa.

Focus for exams
  • Evaluate the nature of African-European relationships in the period
  • Analyse political, social and economic impacts of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
  • Examine living conditions under Trans-Atlantic and Trans-Saharan slave trades
  • Compare consequences of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade on Africa
  • Explain motives of white settlers in southern Africa

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Portugal first along West Africa: bypass Muslim North Africa; reach gold regions (then India).
  • Trans-Atlantic slavery dwarfed earlier slave trades; 12+ million Africans deported.
  • Phases: piratic (to 1580s) → monopolistic companies / Triangular Trade → free trade (from 1690s).
  • Triangle: Europe (cloth, guns, alcohol, metals) → Africa (enslaved people) → Americas (sugar, tobacco) → Europe.
  • "Legitimate" trade: cash crops/raw materials for European goods after slave trade outlawed.
  • Dutch Cape settlement 1652; Boers; Great Trek from 1835 against British equality/abolition policy.
  • Explorers (1780s-1870s) and missionaries often paved the way for colonial expansion.

notes.title: 6.1 Contact with the outside world: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1

Contact with the outside world

Portugal opened lasting European contact with West Africa's coast while hunting gold and a route to India.

Outcomes: evaluate African-European relationships

Key termPortuguese coastal contact. Portugal was the first European power to establish early contacts with West African coasts. Distant goal: reach India. Immediate goal: bypass Muslim North Africa and gain direct access to West African gold, a major source of national wealth that funded further voyages. Spain also built coastal relations in the period.
Exam tip

First European coastal power in West Africa = Portugal. Immediate motive = gold access, not only India.

notes.title: 6.2 Slavery and the Trans-Atlantic slave trade: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.2

Slavery and the Trans-Atlantic slave trade

Slavery was old in Africa, Europe, and Asia, but the Atlantic trade was far larger and more destructive.

Outcomes: explain factors; analyse political, social, economic impacts; examine living conditions

Key termEarlier slave trades. Steady traffic continued in the 15th century. Main earlier market for enslaved Africans: Southwest Asia (often domestic servants). Older routes: Nile to Egypt; Sahara to North Africa; northeast Africa to Persian Gulf and India. Numbers were small beside the Trans-Atlantic trade.
Key termWhy West Africa supplied the Atlantic trade. (1) Fragmentation of large states (Ghana, Mali, Songhai). (2) Region became a major source of enslaved people. (3) Endemic conflict among small coastal states willing to exchange captives for European arms.
Key termDemand in the Americas. Plantations needed labour. Native Americans died from disease and harsh treatment; European "white" slaves failed in the tropical climate. From the 15th century into the early 19th, Europeans transported Africans across the Atlantic.
Key termThree phases. Piratic (15th c. to 1580s): individual merchants, adventurers, pirates. Monopolistic (from 1580s): government-backed companies with armed support; wider hunting grounds; huge profits; includes Triangular Trade linking three continents. Free trade (from 1690s): many individual traders compete with companies.
  • Triangular Trade path: Europe → Africa (cotton cloth, alcohol, firearms, metal wares) exchanged for enslaved people → Americas (sold for sugar, tobacco, other plantation goods) → Europe for manufacture.
  • Economic: undermined African craft technology and distorted development; violence disrupted farming.
  • Political: confusion, insecurity, discouraged political development, encouraged violence; wars destroyed states.
  • Social: undermined morality and dignity; people treated as property; depopulation of productive young men and women; huge family suffering. Over 12 million Africans enslaved and deported.
  • Most captives were sold by other Africans (exam favourite), not only by European inland raids.
Matching tip

Triangular Trade = three continents. Ships to Africa often carried cloth and guns. Americas → Europe: sugar (and similar). Slave Coast = West Africa.
