notes.title: 6.3 The "legitimate" trade: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.3

The "legitimate" trade

After Europe outlawed the slave trade, commerce shifted to cash crops and raw materials.

Outcomes: explain political and economic influences of other continents on Africa

Key termLegitimate trade / legitimate commerce. Trade in commodities between Africans and European merchants after the slave trade was gradually outlawed. African raw materials, especially cash crops, were exchanged for European goods. Europeans saw West Africa as a fertile field for this commerce after centuries of slave-trade distortion.
Exam tip

"Legitimate" here means non-slave commodity trade (cash crops/raw materials ↔ European goods), not "morally perfect" trade.

notes.title: 6.4 White settlement in South Africa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.4

White settlement in South Africa

Dutch farmers (Boers) settled the Cape from 1652; conflict with Khoisan and later British policy triggered the Great Trek.

Outcomes: explain motives of white settlers in southern Africa

Key termDutch Cape settlement. In 1652 a Dutch trading company founded a permanent settlement on South Africa's southern shore to regulate trade with the Khoisan. In 1657, commander Van Riebeck released soldiers to farm as Boers (farmers), supplied with enslaved West Africans. Settlement on Khoisan grazing land sparked the first Khoi-Dutch war (1659); Khoisan drove Boers back temporarily. Second war (1673-77): Dutch won; Khoisan withdrew inland.
Key termBritish expansion and the Great Trek. Britain cleared Xhosa from Zuurveld (1818-19) and later pushed them beyond rivers (wars including 1834-35). Britain abolished slavery in the Cape and returned some land to the Xhosa, angering Boers who used slave labour and opposed equality with Black people. From 1835, Boers left the Cape northward in the Great Trek (thousands of families in the late 1830s).
Exam tip

1652 Dutch Cape. Boers = farmers. Great Trek motives: reaction to laws freeing Africans/coloured people and opposition to Black-White equality ideas; also anger at abolition of slavery.

notes.title: 6.5 European explorers and missionaries: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.5

European explorers and missionaries

Abolition interest and profit hopes sent explorers inland; missionaries often mixed conversion with politics.

Outcomes: describe political and economic influences of other continents

Key termEuropean explorers (c. 1780s-1870s). Despite coastal trade, Europeans remained largely ignorant of Africa's interior, peoples, and history. Abolition of the slave trade stimulated new interest. Some claimed pure scientific motives or adventure/fame; those who financed journeys often sought future trading profit. Explorers were generally direct agents of later colonial expansion.
Key termMissionaries. Portuguese Catholic missionaries followed early coastal penetration (late 15th-early 16th c.), hoping converted rulers would become Portuguese allies. When African rulers saw the political motive, relations soured.
Exam tip

Do not treat explorers as only "curious scientists." Textbook links them to trade profit and colonial expansion.

notes.title: The Age of Revolutions: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 9

The Age of Revolutions, 1750s to 1815

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Industrial capitalism, the French Revolution, Napoleon, American independence, and the Congress of Vienna.

Study lessons 9.1 to 9.5. Link each revolution to one cause, one turning date, and one lasting effect.

Focus for exams
  • Identify factors that consolidated capitalism in modern Europe
  • Describe political, economic and social effects of the Industrial Revolution
  • Explain causes, course and consequences of the French Revolution
  • State Napoleonic reforms and contributions
  • Outline the American War of Independence
  • Point out aims and consequences of the Congress of Vienna (1815)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Industrial capitalism: machines, factories, wage labour, private property, free markets; Britain as "workshop of the world"; railways integrate space.
  • French Revolution: feudal Estates; Bastille 14 July 1789; ends 1799 with Napoleon; causes include bankrupt monarchy, philosophers, Third Estate injustice.
  • Napoleon: Consulate; Napoleonic Code 1804 (civil equality); final defeat Waterloo 1815; exile St Helena (d. 1821).
  • American independence: 13 British colonies; war 1775-1783; Declaration 4 July 1776; constitution 1787; three-branch limited government.
  • Congress of Vienna (1814-15): long-term peace after French wars; balance of power; Metternich; ignored nationality; relative peace but no flexible international organ.

notes.title: 9.1 Industrial capitalism in Europe: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
9.1

Industrial capitalism in Europe

Machine production turned early capitalism into industrial capitalism centred first in Britain.

Outcomes: identify factors consolidating capitalism; describe IR consequences

Key termIndustrial Revolution. New manufacturing processes in Europe and the US (18th-19th centuries). Shift from farming and handmade goods to machinery and factories (e.g. cloth). Britain had coal and iron to power and build machines. Began late 1700s in Britain and spread globally.
Key termIndustrial capitalism. Mode of production with large, centrally controlled capital financing commodity production. Capitalism roots in 16th-17th century NW Europe (especially Britain). Features: capital accumulation, competitive markets, price system, private property/property rights, voluntary exchange, wage labour. Technology (telephone, typewriter, electricity) sped coordination and record-keeping.
  • Challenged mercantilist trade barriers and monopolies; by mid-19th century Britain embraced laissez-faire (free-market liberalism and competition).
  • Britain seen as the world's workshop; similar forces remade landscapes across Europe and North America.
  • Steam locomotives and railways integrated vast spaces politically, culturally, and economically.
Exam tip

Industrial capitalism = large capital + machines + wage labour + markets. Britain first; laissez-faire by mid-1800s.

notes.title: 9.2 French Revolution: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
9.2

French Revolution

A decade of upheaval (1789-1799) destroyed feudal privilege in France and opened the door to Napoleon.

Outcomes: point out and explain causes, course, and consequences

Key termFrench Revolution. Major social upheaval beginning 1787/1789 and ending 1799. Storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. Ended when Napoleon overthrew the revolutionary government and set up the Consulate.
Key termThree Estates. First: royal family and clergy. Second: nobility. Both owned vast land, held privileges, paid no tax. Third: largest section (peasants and bourgeoisie); little land/rights; heavy taxes. Estates General not called since 1614 until Louis XVI summoned it on 5 May 1789 amid bankruptcy. Absolute monarchy concentrated power in the king.
  • Three main causes: bankrupt, inefficient autocratic monarchy; influence of French philosophers against feudal injustice; deep exploitation of the Third Estate.
  • Fundamental cause often tested as injustices under the old feudal order (privileged clergy and nobility vs Third Estate).
True/false trap

Two privileged classes = nobility and clergy (not bourgeoisie). Bastille date = 14 July 1789.

notes.title: 9.3 Napoleonic Era: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
9.3

Napoleonic Era

Napoleon built a vast empire, reformed French law, then fell to a coalition at Waterloo.

Outcomes: explain major reforms; state contributions to contemporary society

Key termNapoleon Bonaparte. French general who took power in 1799 (Consulate). Aimed to build an empire larger than Rome's; appointed officials and unified law on a Roman-inspired model.
Key termNapoleonic Code (1804). Law code guaranteeing civil equality to all persons regardless of birth, wealth, and rank. Influenced Europe widely.
  • Final defeat at Waterloo (Belgium, 1815): Duke of Wellington (Britain) and Prussian Blucher. Forces of conservatism and rising nationalism prevailed.
  • Exiled to St Helena in the southern Atlantic; died 1821.
Exam tip

Napoleonic Code = civil equality (1804). Final defeat = Waterloo (not Jena or Trafalgar alone).

notes.title: 9.4 American War of Independence: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
9.4

American War of Independence

Thirteen British colonies fought free (1775-1783) and built a limited constitutional republic.

Outcomes: explain the war and its wider influence

Key termAmerican Revolution / War of Independence. Insurrection 1775-1783 in which 13 British North American colonies threw off British rule to form the USA. Britain had established the thirteen colonies between 1607 and 1682.
  • Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776): justified rebellion; announced the new nation; set out a philosophy of human freedom influential in the Western world. (Textbook may misprint the date as July 14; standard exam date is 4 July.)
  • Britain accepted defeat in 1783. Constitution signed by majority of delegates on 17 September 1787.
  • Founders admired Roman limits on power: constitution balances government among three branches to restrain elected leaders.
Exam tip

War 1775-1783. Independence declared 1776. Effect: liberated Americans from Britain and influenced later revolutions (including France).

notes.title: 9.5 The Congress of Vienna: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
9.5

The Congress of Vienna

After Napoleon, European statesmen redesigned the map to restore peace and a balance of power.

Outcomes: point out aims and consequences of the Congress of Vienna (1815)

Key termCongress of Vienna. Began September 1814 (after Napoleon's first abdication); Final Act June 1815, just before Waterloo. Most comprehensive European settlement yet. Aim: long-term peace plan by settling issues from the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars.
  • Host atmosphere dominated by Austria's Metternich; Friedrich Gentz managed protocol/secretariat.
  • Friction over Poland and Saxony; claims of Sweden, Denmark, Russia; German borders. Russia/Prussia often opposed by Austria, France, England (secret defensive alliance 3 Jan 1815).
  • Pursued balance of power; largely ignored nationality (territories traded without inhabitants' wishes).
  • Secured a long period of relative European peace (cardinal need). Failed to create a flexible international organ for 19th-century new forces; later criticised then partly rehabilitated by historians.
Exam tip

Vienna = peace + balance of power after Napoleon. Metternich = key Austrian host figure. Nationality largely ignored.

notes.title: Ethiopia 13th to mid-16th C.: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 7

States, Principalities, Population Movements and Interactions in Ethiopia, 13th to mid-16th C.

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. "Solomonic" restoration, Muslim sultanates, Christian-Adal wars, southern states, Oromo expansion, Gadaa, and local egalitarian systems.

Study lessons 7.1 to 7.8. Tie trade-route rivalry to the Adal wars, then link Oromo success to the Gadaa system.

Focus for exams
  • Examine major characteristics of peoples, states and principalities in Ethiopia, 13th-16th centuries
  • Explain major population movement, expansion, and integration
  • Identify features of the relationship between the Christian kingdom and Muslim sultanates
  • Discuss the Oromo Gadaa system

Unit summary · Must remember

  • "Solomonic" dynasty from 1270 under Yekuno-Amlak (Amhara); claim via Kibre Negest is legendary (quotation marks).
  • Expansion under Amde-Tsion; mobile courts; rist (hereditary land claim) and gult (tribute right as salary).
  • Muslim sultanates on Zeila route: Ifat (Walasma), Fatigar, Dawaro, Bali, Hadiya, Adal, and others.
  • Imam Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi: Shimbra Kure 1529; empire Zeila to Massawa by 1535; killed Woyna-Dega 25 Feb 1543 (Gelawdewos + Portuguese).
  • Oromo movement: largest 16th-c. expansion; Gadaa (8-year grades); Guddifacha and Moggasa adoption.
  • Egalitarian examples: Sidama (Mote, Songo, Luwa), plus Gedeo, Konso, Burji.

notes.title: 7.1 The "Solomonic" Dynasty and the Christian Kingdom: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.1

The "Solomonic" Dynasty and the Christian Kingdom

From 1270 a new Christian dynasty claimed Solomon-Sheba descent to replace the Zagwe and expand for trade and territory.

Outcomes: outline restoration factors; analyse social, economic, political features

Key term"Solomonic" dynasty. Restored by Amhara ruler Yekuno-Amlak in 1270. Claimed descent from Aksumite kings and used the Queen of Sheba-King Solomon legend to call Zagwe rulers illegitimate. Name is in quotation marks because Solomon descent is legendary, not historically proven. Elaborated in the 14th-century Kibre Negest ("Glory of Kings"): Ethiopian rulers from Menilek I (son of Sheba and Solomon) down to Haile Selassie I.
  • In 1270 the kingdom was confined; Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-44) led rapid expansion north, west, south, and east (including Ifat, Fatagar, Dawaro, Hadiya, Bali).
  • Motives: control trade routes (esp. Zeila) and seize territory. Trade wealth funded a strong army.
  • Mobile courts: capitals moved for food, firewood, and military needs (from Lake Haiq toward northern then eastern Shewa).
Key termRist and gult. Rist: hereditary/communal birthright claim to land; peasants pay tribute (gibber). Gult: right given to an official (bale-gult) to collect peasant produce; medieval substitute for salary; not hereditary; lasts while loyal. Helped administer the empire and maintain a territorial army. Predominant feature of Ethiopian feudalism for a long period.
Exam tip

1270 = Yekuno-Amlak. Kibre Negest = legendary legitimacy text. Gult ≠ hereditary; rist is the hereditary land claim.

notes.title: 7.2 The Muslim principalities: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.2

The Muslim principalities

Islam and the Zeila trade corridor produced a chain of sultanates that rivalled the Christian highlands.

Outcomes: explain Muslim-Christian relations; identify trade-route links

Key termMuslim sultanates. Formed along long-distance trade routes after Islam entered Ethiopia and the Horn. Along the Zeila route (main gateway of Islam inland): Ifat, Fatigar, Dawaro, Dara, Bali, Hadya (Hadiya), Arbabini, Sharka, and Adal.
Key termIfat / Walasma. Mid-13th century south of Shewa; founder Umar Walasma (Walasma dynasty). In 1285 destroyed the older Makhzumite dynasty and became the strongest Muslim sultanate, controlling Zeila trade territory. Strongest rival of the Christian highland state. After Christian pressure (Ifat defeated 1332 in later tradition), Walasma family helped found Adal around Harar (~1380).
Exam tip

Zeila route = Islam + wealth + rivalry. Ifat = Walasma; Adal later centres on Harar.

notes.title: 7.3 Christian Kingdom and the Sultanate of Adal: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.3

Christian Kingdom and the Sultanate of Adal (1520s-1559)

Competition for long-distance trade and territory peaked in the wars of Imam Ahmed.

Outcomes: identify features of Christian-Muslim sultanate relations

Key termSources of conflict. Desire to monopolize long-distance trade (wealth and links among peoples) and territorial expansion. Height of war: 1529-1543.
Key termImam Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi. Also called "the left-handed"; born Hubet (between Dire Dawa and Jigjiga). Mobilized Afar, Argoba, Somali, Harari and others. Campaigns against Lebne Dengel from 1527; victory at Shimbra Kure (March 1529, near Mojjo). By 1535 his empire stretched Zeila to Massawa and deep inland; set up bureaucracy including recruits from Christian lands. Wife Bati Del Wanbara accompanied expeditions.
  • Internationalised: Ottomans backed Imam Ahmed (Turkish musketeers 1540); Portugal backed the Christian kingdom (soldiers arrived 1541 after Lebne Dengel's 1535 request).
  • Aug 1542: Christian defeat at Ofla (southern Tigray); ~200 Portuguese including Christopher da Gama killed.
  • 25 Feb 1543, Battle of Woyna-Dega near Lake Tana: Imam Ahmed killed; Adal defeated by Gelawdewos with Portuguese help (Queen mother Seble-Wongel advised preparations).
  • Later: Oromo expansion and Adal's decline; capital moved to Awsa (Afar) 1576/7.
Date drill

Shimbra Kure 1529. Woyna-Dega / death of Imam Ahmed 1543. Portugal vs Ottoman proxy dimension.

notes.title: 7.4 Southern and central states: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.4

Southern and central states

Indigenous-religion polities south of the Blue Nile dealt with Solomonic pressure long before the 16th-century wars.

Outcomes: describe peoples and states of the period

Key termCentral and southern states. Examples: Damot, Kafa, Ennarya, Bizamo, Walaita, Yem, Kambata, Gurage chiefdoms, Agaw kingdom of Gojjam. Many practiced indigenous religions.
  • Damot: probably earliest; may date to Aksumite times south of the Blue Nile; possibly linked to Enareya, Bizamo, Walaita. Famous ruler Motalami, converted to Christianity by Abune Tekle Haymanot in the late 13th century.
  • Solomonic rulers tried to bring Damot under control from the late 13th century onward.
Exam tip

Damot + Motalami + Tekle Haymanot conversion is a frequent local-state example.

notes.title: 7.5 Population movements, expansion, and integration: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.5

Population movements, expansion, and integration

Sixteenth-century wars and migrations remade the Horn; the Oromo movement was the largest.

Outcomes: explain major population movement, expansion, and integration

  • Argoba, Afar, Somali movements linked to Christian-Adal conflict in the late 15th-early 16th centuries. Argoba lived on caravan routes to Zeila: agents of trade and Muslim sultanate formation.
  • Oromo movement and expansion: largest of the period; reshaped Christian and Muslim politics (helped push Adal capital to Awsa).
  • Success factors included Gadaa military organisation, broad social participation in war, and effective use of the horse; Christian and Adal forces were already weakened by decades of fighting.
Exam tip

Largest movement = Oromo. Smaller linked movements = Argoba, Afar, Somali around the Adal wars.

notes.title: 7.6-7.7 Gadaa, Moggasa and Guddifacha: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.6-7.7

Gadaa, Moggasa and Guddifacha

Gadaa organised Oromo politics and war; adoption customs integrated newcomers as equals.

Outcomes: describe the Gadaa system; point out adoption features

Key termGadaa system. Age-grade egalitarian system. Assembly (chaffe) of the ruling Gadaa class led the nation. Regulates political, economic, social, and religious life: conflict resolution (arara), reparation (Guma), women's rights, moral conduct, cohesion. Practiced long before the 16th-century movement. One Gadaa period = 8 years; five periods (40 years) = one generation; nine generations = an era. Philosophy: eight-year terms, balanced opposition, power-sharing across levels. Guided by generation, age, sex, and class.
Key termGuddifacha. Parent adopts a child; adopted child has equal rights with a biological child.
Key termMoggasa (Oromsu). Adopting non-Oromos / incorporating individuals or groups into a clan by oath of allegiance; full rights and obligations. Undertaken by the Abba Gadaa.
Exam tip

Gadaa = 8-year grades + chaffe leadership. Guddifacha = child adoption. Moggasa = clan incorporation of non-Oromos.

notes.title: 7.8 Egalitarian systems of governance: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.8

Egalitarian systems of governance

Sidama, Gedeo, Konso, and Burji illustrate indigenous democratic and consultative rule.

Outcomes: explain egalitarian democracy among Sidama, Gedeo, Konso, Burji

Key termSidama governance. Political authority under the Mote (king) in consultation with elders' council Songo (agenda discussed, decisions submitted for Mote approval). Unwritten rules known and practiced across generations. Woma: cultural/ritual leader (peacemaker; no war/raiding; sacrifices, circumcision, marriage rituals). Luwa: age-grade system with 8-year cycle; five named generations (Fulasa, Wawasa, Darara, Hirbora, Mogisa); strong bonding; each group selects a Gadaanna leader.
  • Textbook also points to related egalitarian or consultative traditions among Gedeo, Konso, and Burji (map these regions for exams).
Exam tip

Sidama trio: Mote (political), Songo (council), Woma (ritual). Luwa = 8-year age grades.

notes.title: Ethiopia mid-16th to mid-19th C.: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · History · Unit 8

Political, Social and Economic Processes in Ethiopia, mid-16th to mid-19th C.

Based on the MoE Grade 9 History student textbook. Autonomous regional polities, the Gondarine capital, Zemene-Mesafint warlords, the Yejju Dynasty, and the rise of Shewa.

Study lessons 8.1 to 8.5. Connect Gondar's permanent capital to later warlord politics ending only in 1855.

Focus for exams
  • Describe peoples and states of Ethiopia from mid-16th to mid-19th century
  • Explain major socio-economic and political structures of the period
  • Explain major features and achievements of the Gondarine period
  • Identify main features of the Zemene-Mesafint and the Yejju Dynasty

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Many southern, western, and eastern polities stayed largely autonomous (trade, marriage, conflict links).
  • Southern titles/examples: Tato (Kafa), Kawo, Sera; Omotic and Cushitic structures; Gibe Oromo monarchies (e.g. Jimma under Abba Jifar I).
  • Gondar permanent capital ~1636 under Fasiladas; castles, churches, bridges; ended mobile-camp tradition.
  • Zemene-Mesafint (Era of Warlords) roughly 1769-1855: Mikael Sehul kills Iyoas (1769); Mentewab earlier as regent.
  • Yejju / Warra Sheh from Ali Gwangul (Ali I), 1786; relative stability with strong regional lords.
  • Shewa detaches from Gondar orbit; Sahle Sellase (r. 1813-47) expands and deals with Britain and France.

notes.title: 8.1 Peoples and states (E/C/S/W regions): Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.1

Peoples and states of eastern, central, southern and western regions

From the mid-16th to mid-19th century many Ethiopian polities stayed independent of both the Christian kingdom and rival powers.

Outcomes: describe sources of power; explain Omotic, Cushitic, Semitic, Nilotic structures

Key termAutonomous polities. Peoples maintained ties through trade, marriage, and resource conflicts; borders expanded or shrank. Key terms in the unit opener: Tato, Kawo, Sera.
  • Southern states: Kafa (rulers titled tato, from Ennarya tradition; Kuripo trenches; trade in ivory, musk, honey, coffee, enslaved people, gold). Wolaita, Gamo, Gofa, Dawuro, Konta share similar Omotic-style structures. Hadiya, Kambata, Sidama, Tambaro, Halaba, Gedeo, Konso, Burji often governed through sera traditions.
  • Western / Gibe Oromo monarchies: Gadaa roots shifted toward kingship. Limmu-Ennarya; Jimma under Abba Jifar I (Sanna, r. 1830-1855) using Islam plus coffee and slave-trade wealth; Gumma and other Gibe states.
  • Gambella / Nilotic: Anywaa, Nuer, Majang, Komo, Opuo. Often no strong centralised state; Anywaa villages led by nobles (nyieye) or headmen (kuaari) for peace and wealth redistribution; Majang highly egalitarian.
  • Eastern: Harar as Adal centre from ~1380; reduced to walled town by Oromo expansion. After Imam Ahmed, Emir Nur Mujahid reorganised Muslims; defeated Christian forces in 1559. Afar and Somali pastoral communities remained important in regional politics and trade.
Exam tip

Tato → Kafa. Jimma / Abba Jifar I → strongest later Gibe state. Harar → Adal's later political core.

notes.title: 8.2 Gondarine period: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.2

Gondarine period

The Christian kingdom made Gondar a permanent capital and a showcase of castle architecture.

Outcomes: explain major features and achievements of the Gondarine period

Key termGondarine period. Years when highland Christian rulers governed from Gondar. From the mid-16th century the political centre shifted from Shewan highlands to the Lake Tana region because of Adal's threat and Oromo expansion. After Gelawdewos died (1559), Minas retreated north of the Abay; later rulers consolidated around Tana.
  • Permanent capital founded under Fasiladas around 1636. Strategic site on long-distance routes linking the southwest with Massawa (Red Sea) and Mettema (Ethio-Sudanese border).
  • Ended the older tradition of ruling from temporary camps.
  • Achievements: magnificent castles/palaces, churches, bridges, swimming pools; architectural fame (e.g. Fasiladas castle).
  • Gondar remained a political centre for about two centuries.
Exam tip

Gondar ~1636 Fasiladas = permanent capital; architecture is the classic "achievement" answer.

notes.title: 8.3 The Zemene-Mesafint (Era of Warlords): Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.3

The Zemene-Mesafint (Era of Warlords)

Political and church disputes shattered central control; regional lords ruled Ethiopia's north for decades.

Outcomes: identify main characteristic features of the Zemene-Mesafint

Key termMentewab. Wife of Emperor Bakafa (r. 1721-30). Ruled as regent for her son Iyasu II (r. 1730-55); backed by brother Welde Leul (Ras Bitweded) until 1767. Lost power in 1769.
Key termZemene-Mesafint. "Era of Warlords," commonly dated 1769-1855. Trigger: Tigrean warlord Ras Mikael Sehul came to Gondar, killed King Iyoas (1755-1769), and took Ras Bitweded. Combined with Orthodox Church doctrinal/regional splits. Warlords competed for Ras Bitweded and regional power (Tigray, Semen, Begemedir, Lasta, Yejju, Wollo, Gojjam, Shewa, and others), expanding territory and controlling the nominal emperor.
Exam tip

Dates 1769-1855. Mikael Sehul + death of Iyoas open the era. Mentewab = powerful queen/regent before the collapse.

notes.title: 8.4 The Yejju Dynasty: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.4

The Yejju Dynasty

After Mikael Sehul's fall, Yejju Oromo leaders dominated Gondarine politics as the Warra Sheh.

Outcomes: identify main features of the Yejju Dynasty

Key termYejju Dynasty (Warra Sheh). Founded by Ali Gwangul (Ali I) from a Yejju Oromo family in 1786. Brought relative stability compared with pure chaos, yet strong regional lords remained across Tigray, Semen, Begemedir, Lasta, Wollo, Gojjam, Shewa, and elsewhere.
  • Yejju rulers usually held the powerful title of Ras Bitweded and controlled successive puppet emperors at Gondar.
  • Dominated northern politics through much of the Zemene-Mesafint until mid-19th-century reunification (context for Grade 10).
  • Shows Oromo integration into the highest levels of Christian highland politics after the 16th-century movements.
Exam tip

Yejju = Warra Sheh = Ali Gwangul, 1786. Oromo family at the centre of Gondar politics.

notes.title: 8.5 The Kingdom of Shewa: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
8.5

The Kingdom of Shewa

Once the Christian political heartland, Shewa rebuilt itself as a semi-independent kingdom during the warlord era.

Outcomes: describe Shewan developments and role in Zemene-Mesafint politics

Key termKingdom of Shewa. Central highlands had been the Christian centre, then lost primacy when the capital moved to the Lake Tana area under Adal and Oromo pressure. Gondarine rulers (e.g. Iyassu I, r. 1682-1706) tried military control, but Shewa gradually detached from the new centre.
  • Sahle Sellase (r. 1813-47): brought several regions under Shewan control; maintained law and order; attracted foreign travellers; built independent relations with Britain and France.
  • Shewa's relative stability and foreign ties made it a key player during and after the Zemene-Mesafint.
Exam tip

Shewa detaches after capital shift to Gondar/Tana. Sahle Sellase = expansion + Britain/France contacts.

notes.title: Physics and Human Society: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 1

Physics and Human Society

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. What physics is, its main branches, links to other fields, and key scientists who shaped the subject.

Study lessons 1.1 to 1.4. Be ready to define, describe, and discuss contributions and change over time.

Learning competencies · Unit 1
  • Define physics in different ways (lesson 1.1)
  • Describe the different branches of physics (lesson 1.2)
  • Describe the relationships between physics and other fields of study (lesson 1.3)
  • Describe how aspects of physics are used in other sciences and everyday technology (lessons 1.1, 1.3)
  • Discuss the contributions of prominent scientists in advancing physics (lesson 1.4)
  • Discuss how physics knowledge was evolving and changing in history (lesson 1.4)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Physics (from Greek phusis, nature): natural science that describes the basic mechanisms of the universe.
  • A person who studies physics is a physicist.
  • Main branches: mechanics, acoustics, optics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, nuclear physics, astrophysics.
  • Physics underpins chemistry, engineering, geology, biophysics, geophysics, and medical physics.
  • Classical physics: Renaissance to end of 19th century. Modern physics: revolutionary discoveries from the early 20th century onward.
  • Key names: Newton (mechanics/gravitation), Faraday (electromagnetism/generator), Joule (heat and work), Curie (radioactivity), Einstein (relativity, quantum ideas).

notes.title: 1.1 Definition and nature of physics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.1

Definition and nature of physics

Physics explains how nature works, from phones and planes to heritage buildings that stay standing.

Outcome: define physics in different ways

Key termPhysics. Branch of natural science that describes the fundamental aspects of the universe: what things are in it, what properties we notice, and what processes those things (or their properties) undergo. In short: it describes the basic mechanisms that make the universe behave as it does.
Key termPhusis. Greek word meaning nature. The name "physics" comes from this root.
Key termPhysicist. A person who studies physics.

Everyday and local links:

  • Modern tech (computers, smartphones, tablets) and heritage structures (Harar Jugol, Fasilides Castle, Axum Obelisk, Lalibela rock churches) all rely on physics for how they work or stay balanced.
  • Physics helps you understand cars, airplanes, rockets, refrigerators, radios, TVs, and many tools.
  • It explains phenomena such as why walking on a smooth surface is hard, or why an electric fan rotates.
  • It supports ideas in biology, chemistry, geology, astronomy, and other subjects.

Career-linked fields where physics applies: transportation; aviation and space science; medicine; forensic and military science; meteorology and metrology.

Exam tip

Best MCQ fit for "phusis / nature": physics is a natural science that studies the laws and principles of our universe (not life/organisms alone, not chemistry's matter changes, not social behaviour).

notes.title: 1.2 Branches of physics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.2

Branches of physics

As technology grew, physics split into specialized branches. Match each everyday event to its branch.

Outcome: describe the different branches of physics

Key termMechanics. Motion of objects, with or without reference to force. Split into classical mechanics (laws of motion for ordinary objects and forces) and quantum mechanics (behaviour of the smallest particles: electrons, protons, neutrons).
Key termAcoustics. Sound: production, transmission, and effects.
Key termOptics. Light: behaviour, propagation, and properties.
Key termThermodynamics. Thermal energy and heat transfer.
Key termElectromagnetism. Electromagnetic force: electric fields, magnetic fields, light. Two linked aspects: electricity and magnetism.
Key termNuclear physics. Structure, properties, and reactions of atomic nuclei.
Key termAstrophysics. Applies physics methods and principles to astronomical objects and phenomena.
Exam tip

Car braking to a stop → mechanics. Nature of light → optics. "Evolution" is not a physics branch. "Classical physics" is a historical era, not one branch like optics.

notes.title: 1.3 Related fields to physics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3

Related fields to physics

Physics is a foundation science. Other subjects and technologies borrow its laws and methods.

Outcomes: describe relationships with other fields; how physics is used in other sciences and technology

Key termChemistry link. Chemistry studies atoms and molecules, but it is rooted in atomic and molecular physics.
Key termEngineering. Most engineering uses physics. In architecture: structural stability, acoustics, heating, lighting, and cooling of buildings.
Key termGeology. Study of Earth's nonliving parts; relies on physics for radioactive dating, earthquake analysis, and heat transfer across Earth's surface.
Key termBiophysics. Applies physics principles and methods to biological phenomena and systems.
Key termGeophysics. Applies physics to the study of the Earth.
Key termMedical physics. Diagnostics and therapy using physics: X-rays, MRI, ultrasonic blood-flow measurements.
  • Also think transport, traffic, quality control, and standards: institutions like aviation industry, dams (e.g. GERD), quality/standards bodies, and radiation protection all apply physics principles.
Exam tip

If asked which project does not use physics: usually the answer is none of the above when every listed institution uses physics in some way.

notes.title: 1.4 Historical issues and contributors: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.4

Historical issues and contributors

Physics grew from classical ideas into modern theories that reshaped technology and our view of the universe.

Outcomes: discuss prominent scientists' contributions; discuss how physics knowledge evolved

Key termClassical physics. Physics as developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century.
Key termModern physics. Physics transformed by revolutionary discoveries starting at the beginning of the 20th century. Many classical laws were modified; technology, society, and our picture of the universe changed dramatically.
Key termIsaac Newton. Foundations of classical mechanics: three laws of motion and universal gravitation (falling bodies on Earth and planets in the heavens). Key figure in the Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries.
Key termMichael Faraday. Electromagnetism. In 1821: mechanical motion from a magnet and electric current. About ten years later: converted magnetic force into electrical force and invented the world's first electric generator.
Key termJames Prescott Joule. Studied heat and its link to mechanical work; helped establish the law of conservation of energy and foundations for the first law of thermodynamics (energy transfer and transformation).
Key termMarie Curie. Pioneering work on radioactivity (nuclear physics). Discovered polonium and radium. Often called the mother of modern nuclear physics.
Key termAlbert Einstein. Theory of relativity (deep impact on classical mechanics and the philosophy of physics). Also contributed to quantum mechanics. Widely seen as one of the greatest physicists of all time.
Exam tip

Charles Darwin is a biologist (evolution), not a historical physics contributor in the textbook sense. Galileo's Pisa tower idea: objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass (not "heavier falls faster").

notes.title: Physical Quantities: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 2

Physical Quantities

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. Scales and SI standards, how to measure safely, how quantities are classified, and how to convert units.

Study lessons 2.1 to 2.4. Practise reading scales, naming SI units, and converting length, mass, and time.

Learning competencies · Unit 2
  • List physical quantities (lessons 2.1, 2.3)
  • Identify measurement scales; state and use standard units and prefixes (lesson 2.1)
  • Measure physical quantities with accuracy; list instruments for length, mass, and time (lesson 2.2)
  • Perform measurement activities using different units; follow lab safety rules (lesson 2.2)
  • Classify quantities as fundamental/derived and as scalar/vector (lesson 2.3)
  • Convert units of length, mass, and time (lesson 2.4)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Measurement: compare an unknown quantity with a known standard unit.
  • Seven fundamentals: length, mass, time, temperature, current, amount of substance, luminous intensity. Units: m, kg, s, K, A, mol, cd.
  • Traditional units (palm, footsteps, sundial) lack a shared standard; SI units allow the same result everywhere.
  • Prefixes: kilo $10^{3}$, milli $10^{-3}$, micro $10^{-6}$, nano $10^{-9}$, etc.
  • Derived examples: speed $v=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$, density $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$, force (N), work (J), pressure (Pa).
  • Scalars: magnitude only (mass, time, energy). Vectors: magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
  • Key conversions: $1\,\mathrm{km}=1000\,\mathrm{m}$; $1\,\mathrm{m}=100\,\mathrm{cm}=1000\,\mathrm{mm}$; $1\,\mathrm{kg}=1000\,\mathrm{g}$; $1\,\mathrm{h}=3600\,\mathrm{s}$.

notes.title: 2.1 Scales, standards, units (prefixes): Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.1

Scales, standards, units (prefixes)

You cannot compare time with length. Each quantity needs a scale, a standard, and a unit.

Outcomes: identify scales; state and use standard units; use prefixes and scientific notation

Key termScale. Markings on a measuring device that show how much is being measured. More marks → greater precision. Often the last digit is estimated (e.g. a line between 3.3 and 3.4 read as 3.35).
Key termStandard. An agreed reference so different people in different places get the same result. It must be accessible and reliably measurable. Palm size or footsteps are not standards (unfair and inaccurate).
Key termSI system. International System of Units (metric adaptation; standards revised in 2019). Seven basic quantities: length ($l$), mass ($m$), time ($t$), temperature ($T$), current ($I$), amount of substance ($n$), luminous intensity ($I_v$).
  • Meter (m): distance light travels in vacuum in $\dfrac{1}{299792458}\,\mathrm{s}$.
  • Second (s): $9\,192\,631\,770$ periods of radiation from the caesium-133 atom.
  • Kilogram (kg): defined using the fixed Planck constant $h$ (with metre and second).
Key termScientific notation. Write large or small values as $d \times 10^{n}$, where $d$ is between 1 and 10 (or 0 and 10 as rounded) and $n$ is an integer. Example: $3.24 \times 10^{3}=3240$; $3.24 \times 10^{-3}=0.00324$.
Key termSignificant figures. Each non-zero digit counts. Zeros count if between non-zero digits or at the end of a decimal part.
Key termPrefix. Letter/syllable placed directly before a unit name (no space) to scale it. Examples: tera (T, $10^{12}$), giga (G, $10^{9}$), mega (M, $10^{6}$), kilo (k, $10^{3}$), centi (c, $10^{-2}$), milli (m, $10^{-3}$), micro ($\mu$, $10^{-6}$), nano (n, $10^{-9}$), pico (p, $10^{-12}$). So $1\,\mathrm{kg}=10^{3}\,\mathrm{g}$.
Exam tip

Ratio scales allow $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$ (most physics scales). A nanosecond is $10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}$, not $10^{9}\,\mathrm{s}$. SI time standard → caesium-133 vibrations.

notes.title: 2.2 Measurement and safety: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.2

Measurement and safety

Measurement compares an unknown with a known unit. Do it with the right tool, and stay safe in the lab.

Outcomes: list instruments; measure length, mass, time; follow safety rules

Key termMeasurement. Comparing an unknown quantity with another quantity of the same kind (the unit). Three elements: the quantity, the measuring tools, and standard units.
Key termLength. SI unit metre (m). Also mm, cm, km. Instruments: metre rule/stick, tape, vernier caliper, micrometer (for small diameters such as a marble).
Key termMass. Amount of matter in a body. SI unit kilogram (kg). Also g, mg, tonne. Scientific instrument: beam balance (and other modern balances).
Key termTime. Duration between the start and end of an event. SI unit second (s). Also min, h, day, week, month, year. Traditional sundials or shadow positions are useful locally but not accurate standards. Prefer digital/analogue clocks and watches for reliable daily timing.

Laboratory safety (physics lab):

  • Always wear lab safety goggles.
  • Avoid baggy clothes, bulky/dangling jewellery, open-toed shoes or sandals.
  • Never work alone in the laboratory.
  • Bring only books/notebooks needed for the experiment.
  • Read about the experiment before you start.
Exam tip

Most reliable everyday time method among typical options: a digital watch, not star rotation or tree shadows.

notes.title: 2.3 Classification of physical quantities: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.3

Classification of physical quantities

Sort every quantity two ways: fundamental vs derived, and scalar vs vector.

Outcomes: classify fundamental/derived; describe derived in terms of fundamentals; distinguish scalar and vector

Key termPhysical quantity. Anything you can measure (directly or indirectly), described by a number and a unit.
Key termFundamental (basic) quantities. Measured directly; not defined in terms of other physical quantities. Seven with SI units:
  • Length $l$: metre (m)
  • Mass $m$: kilogram (kg)
  • Time $t$: second (s)
  • Temperature $T$: kelvin (K)
  • Current $I$: ampere (A)
  • Amount of substance $n$: mole (mol)
  • Luminous intensity $I_v$: candela (cd)
Key termDerived quantities. Depend on one or more fundamentals. Their units are derived units. Examples:
  • Speed $v=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$ → $\mathrm{m/s}$
  • Density $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$ → $\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
  • Acceleration $a=\dfrac{\text{velocity}}{\text{time}}$ → $\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$
  • Force $F=ma$ → newton (N) $= \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^{2}}$
  • Work $W=F \times$ displacement → joule (J) $= \mathrm{kg\cdot m^{2}/s^{2}}$
  • Pressure $P=\dfrac{F}{A}$ → pascal (Pa) $= \mathrm{kg/(m\cdot s^{2})}$
Key termScalar. Magnitude only (number + unit). Examples: distance, mass, time, temperature, energy, work, speed, pressure, area.
Key termVector. Magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. Notation: bold or arrow, e.g. $\vec{S}$ or $\mathbf{S}$. Example: $50\,\mathrm{km/h}$ east is a full velocity.
Exam tip

Density is not fundamental. Joule is a derived SI unit. Speed is scalar; velocity is vector.

notes.title: 2.4 Unit conversion: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.4

Unit conversion

Same quantity, different units: multiply by a conversion factor so units cancel correctly.

Outcomes: convert length, mass, and time between SI and non-SI units

Key termUnit conversion. Changing between units of the same physical quantity using multiplicative conversion factors.

Length

  • $1\,\mathrm{km}=1000\,\mathrm{m}$
  • $1\,\mathrm{m}=100\,\mathrm{cm}=1000\,\mathrm{mm}$
  • $1\,\mathrm{cm}=10\,\mathrm{mm}=0.01\,\mathrm{m}$
  • $1\,\mathrm{mm}=0.001\,\mathrm{m}$

Example: $200\,\mathrm{m}=20000\,\mathrm{cm}=0.2\,\mathrm{km}=2\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{mm}$.

Mass

  • $1\,\mathrm{kg}=1000\,\mathrm{g}$
  • $1\,\mathrm{mg}=0.001\,\mathrm{g}$
  • $100\,\mathrm{kg}=1$ quintal; $1000\,\mathrm{kg}=1$ tonne

Example: $1.5\,\mathrm{kg}+500\,\mathrm{g}+250\,\mathrm{g}+25\,\mathrm{g}+0.8\,\mathrm{g}=2275.8\,\mathrm{g}=2.2758\,\mathrm{kg}$.

Time

  • $1\,\mathrm{min}=60\,\mathrm{s}$
  • $1\,\mathrm{h}=60\,\mathrm{min}=3600\,\mathrm{s}$
  • $1$ day $=24\,\mathrm{h}$; $1$ week $=7$ days; $1$ year $\approx 365.25$ days

Examples: $2\,\mathrm{h}=7200\,\mathrm{s}$; $0.5\,\mathrm{h}=1800\,\mathrm{s}$; $\dfrac{3}{5}\,\mathrm{h}=2160\,\mathrm{s}$.

Exam tip

Earth to Moon distance → km. Thin wire diameter → mm. Prefix check: nano $=10^{-9}$.

notes.title: Motion in a Straight Line: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 3

Motion in a Straight Line

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. One-dimensional (rectilinear) motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, and graphs.

Study lessons 3.1 to 3.6. Always say whether a quantity is scalar or vector, and name your reference frame.

Learning competencies · Unit 3
  • Describe motion in terms of frame of reference, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration (lessons 3.1 to 3.4)
  • Draw diagrams to locate objects with respect to a reference (lesson 3.1)
  • Solve problems involving distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration (lessons 3.2 to 3.4)
  • Make practical measurements of distance, displacement, average speed, average velocity, and acceleration (lessons 3.1 to 3.4)
  • Define uniform motion and give examples (lesson 3.5)
  • Plot $s$-$t$ and $v$-$t$ graphs; find velocity and acceleration from slopes (lesson 3.6)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Motion: continuous change of position relative to a fixed reference frame.
  • Distance $s$: total path length (scalar). Displacement $\vec{S}=\vec{X}_f-\vec{X}_i$ (vector).
  • Speed $v=s/t$ (scalar). Velocity: rate of change of displacement (vector).
  • Average speed $= s_{\mathrm{tot}}/t_{\mathrm{tot}}$. Instantaneous speed: speed at one instant (speedometer).
  • $\vec{a}_{\mathrm{av}}=(\vec{v}_f-\vec{v}_i)/(t_f-t_i)$. Unit: $\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$. Speeding up / slowing down / changing direction.
  • Uniform motion: constant velocity; $a=0$; average = instantaneous velocity.
  • Slope of $s$-$t$ → velocity. Slope of $v$-$t$ → acceleration. Area under $v$-$t$ (uniform) → distance.

notes.title: 3.1 Position, distance and displacement: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.1

Position, distance and displacement

Home to school is the classic example: your home can be the origin; the school is a later position.

Outcomes: define motion, position, displacement; use a reference frame; contrast distance and displacement

Key termFrame of reference. A set of coordinates (fixed objects) used to decide positions. Origin is often the fixed reference point for straight-line motion.
Key termMotion. Continuous change in position of an object relative to a fixed reference frame as time passes. Rest: position does not change in that frame. Rest and motion are relative (e.g. still on a moving horse vs ground).
Key termPosition. Location with respect to a reference point (often the origin). On a 1D $x$-axis, positions can be positive or negative.
Key termDistance ($s$). Total path length travelled. Scalar (no direction). Always non-negative. SI unit: metre (m).
Key termDisplacement ($\vec{S}$). Change of position in a direction: $\vec{S}=\vec{X}_f-\vec{X}_i$. Vector. Independent of path. Home → school → home gives displacement zero even if distance is large.
  • Distance depends on the path; displacement depends on initial and final positions.
  • Distance $\ge$ magnitude of displacement.
Exam tip

Negative displacement pairs: final position left of initial on your chosen axis (e.g. $7\,\mathrm{m}$ to $-3\,\mathrm{m}$, or $-3\,\mathrm{m}$ to $-7\,\mathrm{m}$).

notes.title: 3.2 Average speed and instantaneous speed: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.2

Average speed and instantaneous speed

Speed says how fast, not which way. A speedometer shows the value right now.

Outcomes: differentiate average vs instantaneous speed; compute average speed

Key termSpeed. Rate at which an object changes location; distance per unit time. Scalar. Symbol often $v$. SI: $\mathrm{m/s}$ (also $\mathrm{km/h}$, $\mathrm{mi/h}$).

$$v=\dfrac{s}{t}$$

Key termAverage speed. Total distance divided by total time for the whole trip:

$$v_{\mathrm{av}}=\dfrac{s_{\mathrm{tot}}}{t_{\mathrm{tot}}}$$

Key termInstantaneous speed. Speed at one specific instant. Car speedometer reading. For a very short interval: $v_{\mathrm{ins}}=\dfrac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$ as $\Delta t \to 0$.

Worked idea: $80\,\mathrm{km}$ in $1.5\,\mathrm{h}$ → $v_{\mathrm{av}}=53.33\,\mathrm{km/h}$. Convert: $\times\dfrac{1000}{3600}$ → about $14.81\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Distance from speed: $s=v_{\mathrm{av}}t$. Example: $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $1.5\,\mathrm{h}=5400\,\mathrm{s}$ → $s=27000\,\mathrm{m}$.

Exam tip

Average of all instantaneous speeds over a trip gives the average speed. Both are scalars.

notes.title: 3.3 Average velocity and instantaneous velocity: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.3

Average velocity and instantaneous velocity

Velocity is speed with direction. Same path length can give zero velocity if you end where you started.

Outcomes: differentiate average vs instantaneous velocity; compute average velocity

Key termVelocity. Rate of change of displacement. Vector. Symbol $\vec{v}$. SI: $\mathrm{m/s}$.
Key termAverage velocity. Total displacement divided by total time:

$$\vec{v}_{\mathrm{av}}=\dfrac{\vec{X}_f-\vec{X}_i}{t_f-t_i}=\dfrac{\Delta\vec{X}}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{\vec{S}}{\Delta t}$$

  • $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{av}}$ has the same direction as the displacement.
  • Positive $x$ displacement → positive average velocity on that axis.
Key termInstantaneous velocity. Velocity at one instant (limit of average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$). In uniform motion it equals average velocity at all times.
Exam tip

Speed uses distance; velocity uses displacement. Returning home: average speed > 0, average velocity $=0$.

notes.title: 3.4 Acceleration: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.4

Acceleration

Acceleration tracks how velocity changes: faster, slower, or a new direction.

Outcomes: define acceleration; calculate average acceleration

Key termAcceleration. Rate of change of velocity. Vector $\vec{a}$. SI unit: $\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$.

$$\vec{a}_{\mathrm{av}}=\dfrac{\vec{v}_f-\vec{v}_i}{t_f-t_i}$$

  • Occurs when speed increases, decreases, or direction changes (or both).
  • From rest: $\vec{v}_i=0$. Coming to rest: $\vec{v}_f=0$.
  • Deceleration: speeding down; often treated as negative acceleration when slowing on a chosen axis.
  • If $\vec{v}_i=\vec{v}_f$, then $\vec{a}_{\mathrm{av}}=0$ (even if the object is still moving).

Example: train from rest to $36\,\mathrm{km/h}=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $20\,\mathrm{s}$ → $a_{\mathrm{av}}=+0.5\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ east.

Example: $v_i=7.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v_f=12.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $a=2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ → $\Delta t=\dfrac{v_f-v_i}{a}=2\,\mathrm{s}$.

Exam tip

Positive acceleration: speeding up in the positive direction (or velocity change positive). Negative: often slowing down on that axis. Direction of $\vec{a}$ matches the change in velocity, not always the velocity itself.

notes.title: 3.5 Uniform motion: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.5

Uniform motion

Equal distances in equal times, same direction: constant velocity on a straight line.

Outcomes: define uniform motion; give examples

Key termUniform motion (uniform rectilinear motion). Motion along a straight line with constant velocity (constant speed in a fixed direction). Position changes at a steady rate. Equal distances in equal time intervals.
  • Acceleration $a=0$ (magnitude and direction of velocity unchanged).
  • Average velocity $=$ instantaneous velocity at all times.
  • Examples: car on a straight road at fixed speed; airplane flying at constant speed in one direction.

Real trips often speed up and slow down, so averages matter when motion is not uniform.

Exam tip

On a $v$-$t$ graph, uniform motion is a horizontal line (zero acceleration / constant speed).

notes.title: 3.6 Graphical representation of motion: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.6

Graphical representation of motion

Graphs show the whole story of a 1D trip: stop, reverse, speed up, or coast.

Outcomes: plot $s$-$t$ and $v$-$t$; define slope; find velocity and acceleration from graphs

Key termPosition-time ($s$-$t$ or $x$-$t$) graph. Time on horizontal axis; position on vertical axis. Slope $=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}=\vec{v}_{\mathrm{av}}$. Steeper line → faster motion. Zero slope → object at rest.
Key termVelocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph. Shows how velocity changes with time. Slope $=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=$ acceleration. Straight sloping line → constant acceleration.
  • Uniform motion: $v$-$t$ is horizontal; area under the line $=v\cdot t=s$ (distance covered).
  • Speed limit / traffic: keep within posted limits (e.g. $80\,\mathrm{km/h}$). Speedometer reads instantaneous speed; high speed raises crash risk.
Exam tip

Memorise: slope of $s$-$t$ → velocity; slope of $v$-$t$ → acceleration; area under uniform $v$-$t$ → distance.

notes.title: Force, Work, Energy and Power: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 4

Force, Work, Energy and Power

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. Dynamics: what causes motion (forces and Newton's laws), then work, energy, and power.

Study lessons 4.1 to 4.6. Separate everyday "effort" from the physics meaning of work.

Learning competencies · Unit 4
  • Understand different types of forces (contact / non-contact) (lesson 4.1)
  • Practically measure forces; differentiate mass and weight (lessons 4.1, 4.2)
  • Explain Newton's laws of motion (lesson 4.2)
  • Define friction; explain advantages and disadvantages (lesson 4.3)
  • Know about work and energy; calculate $W$, $E_k$, $E_p$ (lessons 4.4, 4.5)
  • Relate work and power (lesson 4.6)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Force: push or pull (vector). SI unit newton (N). $1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^{2}}$.
  • Contact vs non-contact (e.g. friction vs gravity / magnetism).
  • Newton 1: inertia / net force zero → rest or constant velocity. Newton 2: $\vec{F}=m\vec{a}$. Newton 3: $\vec{F}_{12}=-\vec{F}_{21}$.
  • Weight $W=mg$; mass is inertia (constant); weight can change with $g$.
  • Work $W=F_{\parallel}S$ (J). Kinetic $E_k=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$. Gravitational $E_p=mgh$.
  • Mechanical energy $=E_k+E_p$. Power $P=W/t$ (watt).

notes.title: 4.1 The concept of force: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.1

The concept of force

Kinematics describes motion. Dynamics asks what causes the motion: forces.

Outcomes: define force; give examples; measure gravitational force

Key termForce. A push or pull on a body that can change its state of motion (velocity) or cause deformation (shape/size). Vector: magnitude and direction. Symbol $\vec{F}$ or bold $\mathbf{F}$. SI unit: newton (N). Often measured with a spring scale (elongation).
  • Examples: friction, normal force, gravity, springs, kicks, lifts.
  • A force does not always produce motion (balanced forces can cancel).
Key termContact forces. Need physical contact: applied force, normal force, friction, spring force.
Key termNon-contact forces. Act without touching: magnetic force, gravitational force (object falls back to Earth).
Key termWeight. Magnitude of the gravitational force on a body, measured in newtons, directed toward Earth's centre. Bathroom/roadside scales often display a mass reading, but the underlying effect is weight ($W=mg$).
Exam tip

Force is a vector. Weight is in newtons, not kilograms.

notes.title: 4.2 Newton's laws of motion: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.2

Newton's laws of motion

Three laws: keep going (inertia), accelerate with net force, and forces come in pairs.

Outcomes: state all three laws; link $a$ to $F$ and $m$; relate gravity and weight

Key termNewton's first law (inertia). A body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced (net) force acts. Inertia: tendency to resist velocity change. Mass measures inertia (larger mass → harder to change motion).
Key termInertial frame. Reference frame where Newton's first law holds. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial.
Key termMass vs weight. Mass: amount of matter / inertia; constant everywhere. Weight: $W=mg$; depends on local $g$ (Moon ~1/6 of Earth's $g$; $g$ changes with height).
Key termNewton's second law. Acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass:

$$\vec{F}=m\vec{a},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^{2}}$$

On Earth, gravitational force / weight: $F_g=W=mg$ (toward Earth's centre; often use $g\approx 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$).

Key termNewton's third law. Forces act in pairs on different objects: $\vec{F}_{12}=-\vec{F}_{21}$ (equal magnitude, opposite direction). Example: block on table: weight down on table; normal force up on block.
Exam tip

$a=F/m$. Example: $50\,\mathrm{N}$ on $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ → $a=5\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$. Weight of $50\,\mathrm{kg}$: $W=50\times 9.8=490\,\mathrm{N}$ (or $500\,\mathrm{N}$ if $g=10$).

notes.title: 4.3 Forces of friction: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.3

Forces of friction

Friction opposes sliding. Without it, walking and braking fail; with too little grip, vehicles stick in mud or skid.

Outcomes: define friction; link to surface roughness; advantages and disadvantages

Key termForce of friction ($f$). Resistance from a surface to motion (or attempted motion) of an object. Contact force. Larger on rough surfaces than smooth. Directly related to the normal force.
Key termStatic friction. Acts when one body tends to slide over another but has not yet moved. Usually needs a larger force to overcome than kinetic friction.
Key termKinetic friction. Acts while surfaces slide (or when one body rolls over another). Effect on motion is generally less than static friction for the same surfaces.
  • Useful: walking, running, tyre grip, stopping a car.
  • Problem: hard to walk on ice; machines waste energy as heat; mud can leave cars "stuck" when grip is wrong for the surface.
Exam tip

Smooth surface → small friction → hard to walk. Brakes and road friction stop a car.

notes.title: 4.4 The concept of work: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.4

The concept of work

Everyday "hard work" is not always physics work. You need force and displacement along that force.

Outcomes: define scientific work; relate $W$, $F$, $S$; calculate work

Key termWork ($W$). Done when a force component parallel to the displacement moves an object through displacement $S$:

$$W=F_{\parallel}S$$

  • Scalar. SI unit: joule (J). $1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$ (1 N moving through 1 m along the force).
  • Force perpendicular to displacement (holding a chair still; carrying a bucket horizontally at constant velocity with vertical lift force) → zero work by that force.
  • Pushing a wall with no displacement → zero work.
  • Lifting a box upward: force and displacement both up → work done.

Example: $F_{\parallel}=60\,\mathrm{N}$, $S=12\,\mathrm{m}$ → $W=720\,\mathrm{J}$.

Exam tip

Holding a book at fixed height for two hours: displacement zero → work by your hand on the book is zero.

notes.title: 4.5 Kinetic and potential energies: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.5

Kinetic and potential energies

Energy is the capacity to do work. Motion stores kinetic energy; height stores gravitational potential energy.

Outcomes: define $E_k$ and $E_p$; solve related problems

Key termEnergy. Capacity to do work. Scalar. SI unit joule (J). Work transfers energy.
Key termKinetic energy ($E_k$). Energy due to motion:

$$E_k=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{2}/s^{2}}$$

  • Double mass (same $v$) → $E_k$ doubles.
  • Double speed (same $m$) → $E_k$ becomes $4\times$. Triple speed → $9\times$.

Example: $m=0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v=20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ → $E_k=40\,\mathrm{J}$. For $E_k=50\,\mathrm{J}$, $m=1\,\mathrm{kg}$: $v=\sqrt{2E_k/m}=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Key termPotential energy. Stored energy due to position or configuration (gravitational; elastic in a stretched spring).
Key termGravitational potential energy ($E_p$).

$$E_p=mgh$$

Heavier and higher → more $E_p$. Example: $m=30\,\mathrm{kg}$, $h=50\,\mathrm{m}$, $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ → $E_p=15000\,\mathrm{J}$.

Key termMechanical energy. Sum of kinetic and potential energies.
Exam tip

Always convert grams to kilograms before $E_k=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$.

notes.title: 4.6 Power: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
4.6

Power

Same work done faster means greater power.

Outcomes: define power; relate work, energy, and power

Key termPower ($P$). Rate of doing work, or rate of transferring energy. Scalar.

$$P=\dfrac{W}{t}=\dfrac{E}{t}$$

  • SI unit: watt (W). $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.
  • Example: $1500\,\mathrm{J}$ in $5\,\mathrm{s}$ → $P=300\,\mathrm{W}$.
  • Lifting against gravity: work/energy $\approx mgh$, so $P=\dfrac{mgh}{t}$.

Example: pump lifts $500\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water by $10\,\mathrm{m}$ in $5\,\mathrm{s}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$): $P=\dfrac{500\times 10\times 10}{5}=10000\,\mathrm{W}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Exam tip

Same work in half the time → twice the power.

notes.title: Simple Machines: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 5

Simple Machines

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. What simple machines do, the six types, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, efficiency, and local design ideas.

Study lessons 5.1 to 5.6. Machines make work easier. They do not create energy.

Learning competencies · Unit 5
  • Know the types of simple machines (lessons 5.1 to 5.4)
  • Define mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, and efficiency (lesson 5.5)
  • Solve problems related to simple machines (lesson 5.5)
  • Construct / design simple machines for local problems (lesson 5.6)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Purposes: change direction, multiply force, or multiply distance/speed (not energy).
  • Six types: inclined plane, wedge, screw | lever, wheel and axle, pulley.
  • Effort = force you apply. Load = force the machine exerts on the object.
  • $W_{\mathrm{in}}=F_E \times d_E$; $W_{\mathrm{out}}=F_L \times d_L$.
  • $\mathrm{MA}=F_L/F_E$; $\mathrm{VR}=d_E/d_L$; $\eta=W_{\mathrm{out}}/W_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{MA}/\mathrm{VR}$ (often as %).
  • Ideal (no friction): $\mathrm{AMA}=\mathrm{IMA}=\mathrm{VR}$. Real world: $\mathrm{IMA}>\mathrm{AMA}$; $\eta<1$.

notes.title: 5.1 Simple machines and their purposes: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.1

Simple machines and their purposes

A stapler, axe, knife, or well pulley all use one main effort to make a hard job easier.

Outcomes: define simple machines; identify force / distance / direction roles

Key termSimple machine. Device that helps you do mechanical work more easily, usually with a single effort against a load. Energy-transferring device: it does not create energy or multiply energy.
Key termEffort ($F_E$). Force you (or another source) apply to the machine.
Key termLoad ($F_L$). Force the machine exerts on the object being moved or lifted.

$$W_{\mathrm{in}}=F_E \times d_E,\qquad W_{\mathrm{out}}=F_L \times d_L$$

Three ways machines help:

  • Direction changer: e.g. fixed pulley on a flagpole (pull down, flag goes up).
  • Distance / speed multiplier: load moves farther than effort in the same time (e.g. bicycle pedals vs wheels).
  • Force multiplier: small effort moves a large load (e.g. inclined plane into a truck; bottle opener). Load moves a shorter distance than the effort.

Trade-off: gain force → lose distance (or reverse). Input energy ≈ output energy (ideally); you cannot multiply force and distance at the same time.

Exam tip

Machines do not create energy. Wrong MCQ choice: "machines multiply energy."

notes.title: 5.2 Simple machines at home: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.2

Simple machines at home

Break everyday tools into pulleys, wheels, levers, wedges, and screws.

Outcomes: list home simple machines and state their purpose

Key termBuilding blocks. Complex machines are combinations of simple ones. At home you still meet the same six types.
  • Stapler, scissors, bottle opener, claw hammer: levers (force or speed roles).
  • Knife, axe, door wedge: wedges (split or hold).
  • Screw lids, jar screws, corkscrew: screws (inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder).
  • Doorknobs, rolling pins, some taps: wheel and axle.
  • Curtain / blind cords, some wells: pulleys.
  • Ramps into a house or truck: inclined planes.

Functions still fall into: change direction, multiply force, or multiply speed/distance. Force multipliers: load > effort. Distance multipliers: load moves farther than effort.

Exam tip

For any listed tool, name type + purpose (force / distance / direction).

notes.title: 5.3 Simple machines at workplace: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.3

Simple machines at workplace

Cars and airplanes started from levers, ramps, and wheels. Workplace tools still do one clear movement.

Outcomes: categorize workplace machines by type

Key termWorkplace simple machine. Mechanical device that does a task with essentially one movement (e.g. a lever that moves a rock many times your weight).
  • Farm / site: shovel, spade, crowbar, wheelbarrow, pulley well, ramp for loading.
  • Workshop: hammer, pliers, screwdriver, wedge, screw clamp.
  • Compound machines at work: bicycle (wheel and axle, levers, screws, pulleys); wire cutters (two levers + two wedges); vehicles (many machines together).

Practice: for each tool, fill name → description → how it makes work easier (force, distance, or direction).

Exam tip

A lever can move a load much heavier than you if arrangement gives $\mathrm{MA}>1$.

notes.title: 5.4 Classification of simple machines: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.4

Classification of simple machines

Six types in two families: inclined-plane family and lever family.

Outcomes: list and identify the six types; sort home/work examples

Key termSimple vs compound. Simple: work with one movement. Compound: combination of simple machines (bicycle, wire cutter, car).

Inclined-plane group

  • Inclined plane / ramp
  • Wedge
  • Screw

Lever group

  • Lever
  • Wheel and axle
  • Pulley

Also classify by role:

  • Force multiplier: load > effort (load travels less distance).
  • Speed/distance multiplier: load travels farther than effort in same time.
  • Direction changer: load moves in a different direction from the effort (fixed pulley, some wedges).
Exam tip

Memorise the six names and which family each belongs to.

notes.title: 5.5 MA, velocity ratio and efficiency: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.5

Mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency

Three ratios tell you what a machine gains and what friction costs.

Outcomes: define MA, VR, $\eta$; calculate; know lever classes and key formulas

Key termMechanical advantage (MA). $\mathrm{MA}=\dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}=\dfrac{F_L}{F_E}$ (no units). $\mathrm{MA}>1$ → force multiplier. Example: $400\,\mathrm{N}/160\,\mathrm{N}=2.5$.
  • AMA (actual): includes friction losses.
  • IMA (ideal): no energy losses. Real world: $\mathrm{IMA}>\mathrm{AMA}$. Ideal textbook cases often take $\mathrm{AMA}=\mathrm{IMA}=\mathrm{MA}$.
Key termVelocity ratio (VR). $\mathrm{VR}=\dfrac{d_E}{d_L}$ (no units). $\mathrm{VR}=3$ means effort moves 3× as far as the load. $\mathrm{VR}<1$ → distance/speed multiplier role; $\mathrm{VR}>1$ often with force gain.
Key termEfficiency ($\eta$). $\eta=\dfrac{W_{\mathrm{out}}}{W_{\mathrm{in}}}=\dfrac{P_{\mathrm{out}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{MA}}{\mathrm{VR}}$ (also as %). Always < 100% in real machines (friction → heat).

Lever classes (fulcrum F, load L, effort E):

  • 1st: fulcrum between load and effort (see-saw, crowbar, scissors). Can be force or speed multiplier.
  • 2nd: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener). $\mathrm{IMA}>1$.
  • 3rd: effort between fulcrum and load (tweezers, fishing pole, broom, forearm). $\mathrm{IMA}<1$ (favours distance).

For levers: $\mathrm{MA}=F_L/F_E$; $\mathrm{VR}=d_E/d_L$ (distances from fulcrum).

Other ideal shortcuts (no losses): inclined plane $\mathrm{VR}=l/h$; wedge $\mathrm{VR}=l/t$; screw $\mathrm{IMA}=\pi d/p$; wheel and axle $\mathrm{VR}=R_{\mathrm{wheel}}/R_{\mathrm{axle}}$; pulley $\mathrm{VR}=\mathrm{IMA}=N$ (rope segments supporting the load).

Exam tip

If effort moves $2\,\mathrm{m}$ and load rises $8\,\mathrm{m}$, $\mathrm{VR}=2/8=0.25$ → distance multiplier.

notes.title: 5.6 Designing simple machines: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
5.6

Designing simple machines

Match a local hard job (well water, heavy loads) to the right machine and VR.

Outcomes: design/construct machines for real local problems; know pulley options

Key termDesign process. List hard community tasks → choose type (force / distance / direction) → sketch → aim for a useful VR (e.g. 3, 4, 5, 6 for pulley systems).
Key termFixed pulley. Axle fixed; mainly changes direction. Alone, effort is often ≥ load. Advantage: you pull from a convenient place. Disadvantage: little/no force gain.
Key termMovable pulley. Axle moves with the load. Roughly doubles force; $\mathrm{VR}=2$ (pull 2 m of rope to lift 1 m). Advantage: less effort. Disadvantage: you must move the pulley.
Key termCompound pulley (block and tackle). Fixed + movable. Effort can be less than half the load, but rope travels a long distance. Friction → $\mathrm{MA}<\mathrm{VR}$.
  • Local ideas: well bucket lift, loading ramp for a truck, wheelbarrow for market loads, screw press, lever to raise a heavy gate.
Exam tip

For pulley design questions, state whether you need direction change, force gain, or both, then pick fixed / movable / compound.

notes.title: Mechanical Oscillation and Sound Wave: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 6

Mechanical Oscillation and Sound Wave

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. Periodic motion, wave properties, pendulum and springs, how waves carry energy, sound, and interference.

Study lessons 6.1 to 6.6. Link $f$, $T$, $\lambda$, and $v$ before you touch sound or standing waves.

Learning competencies · Unit 6
  • Understand oscillation of strings, pendulum, and spring-mass systems (lesson 6.2)
  • Know propagation of different types of waves; distinguish wave types (lessons 6.1, 6.3)
  • Estimate speed of sound in different media and at different temperatures (lesson 6.4)
  • Explain superposition, standing waves, and sound characteristics / pollution (lessons 6.5, 6.6)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • $f=1/T$; $v=\lambda f$. Crest / trough; amplitude = max displacement.
  • Pendulum: $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ (independent of mass). Spring: $F=-kx$; $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.
  • Mechanical vs electromagnetic; transverse vs longitudinal (sound = longitudinal).
  • Sound needs a medium. Faster in solids than liquids than gases. Air: $v=331\sqrt{1+T_c/273}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
  • Echo = reflection; also refraction, diffraction, interference. Pitch↔$f$, loudness↔amplitude (dB), timbre = quality.

notes.title: 6.1 Common characteristics of waves: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.1

Common characteristics of waves

Every wave shares the same vocabulary: how tall, how long, how often, how fast.

Outcomes: define period, frequency, wavelength, amplitude; relate $f$, $T$, $\lambda$, $v$

Key termRest position. Undisturbed position of particles when not vibrating.
Key termCrest / trough. Highest point above / lowest point below the rest position.
Key termPeriod ($T$). Time for one complete cycle (or for one full wave to pass a point).
Key termFrequency ($f$). Number of complete waves per unit time. Unit: hertz (Hz). $1\,\mathrm{Hz}=1$ cycle/s.

$$f=\dfrac{1}{T},\qquad T=\dfrac{1}{f}$$

Key termAmplitude ($A$). Maximum displacement from equilibrium (metres).
Key termWavelength ($\lambda$). Distance between identical points on adjacent waves (crest to crest, or trough to trough).
Key termWave speed ($v$). Distance the wave travels per second ($\mathrm{m/s}$).

$$v=\lambda f$$

Exam tip

$2\,\mathrm{Hz}$ means 2 waves per second, so $T=0.5\,\mathrm{s}$.

notes.title: 6.2 String, pendulum and spring: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.2

String, pendulum and spring

A flick on a rope makes a pulse. A repeating swing or bounce is periodic motion.

Outcomes: pendulum and spring periods; Hooke's law; measure $g$

Key termPulse / wave. One travelling disturbance = pulse. A train of pulses = wave. On a string, the pulse can move along while particles move at right angles (transverse).
Key termPeriodic motion. To-and-fro motion that repeats in a fixed time (heartbeats, swings, clocks).
Key termSimple pendulum. Small bob on a light unstretchable string. Period:

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$$

  • Depends on length $L$ and $g$ only. Independent of mass.
  • Example: $L=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ → $T\approx 1.42\,\mathrm{s}$.
  • Rearrange to find local $g$: $g=\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^{2}L$.
Key termHooke's law. Restoring force of a spring is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction: $F_{\mathrm{res}}=-kx$. Spring constant $k$ in $\mathrm{N/m}$ (stiff → large $k$). Applied stretch force magnitude: $F_{\mathrm{app}}=kx$.
Key termSpring-mass period (smooth horizontal surface):

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$$

Example: $m=2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$ → $T=\pi/5\,\mathrm{s}$.

Exam tip

Pendulum: change mass → period unchanged. Change $L$ or location ($g$) → period changes.

notes.title: 6.3 Propagation of waves and energy transmission: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.3

Propagation of waves and energy transmission

Waves move energy. Some need a medium; some travel through empty space.

Outcomes: distinguish mechanical / EM and transverse / longitudinal; give examples

Key termWave. Disturbance that propagates through space or matter, carrying energy (sound from an instrument, water ripples, phone microwaves).
Key termMechanical waves. Need a material medium (particle vibrations). Examples: sound, water waves, waves on strings.
Key termElectromagnetic waves. Vibrating electric and magnetic fields; travel through vacuum. Examples: light, radio, X-rays.
Key termTransverse wave. Particle vibration perpendicular to wave travel / energy transfer. Examples: EM waves, waves on a string. Crests and troughs.
Key termLongitudinal wave. Particle vibration parallel to wave travel. Examples: sound, pressure waves. Compressions (particles close / high pressure) and rarefactions (particles apart / low pressure): like crests and troughs for longitudinal waves.
Exam tip

Vibrations parallel to propagation → longitudinal (sound). Perpendicular → transverse (string, light).

notes.title: 6.4 Sound waves: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.4

Sound waves

Vibrating objects make sound. It travels as a longitudinal wave through a medium, never through empty vacuum.

Outcomes: production; speed in media and with temperature; echo, refraction, diffraction

Key termSound. Longitudinal mechanical wave from vibrating sources (kirar/guitar string, tuning fork, voice). Needs a medium. Speed depends on compressibility and density.
  • Order of speed (typical): solids > liquids > gases (particles closer → easier collisions). Examples: air ~$331\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; water ~$1493\,\mathrm{m/s}$; iron ~$5950\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
  • Solids/liquids: temperature has little effect. Air: temperature matters.

$$v=331\sqrt{1+\dfrac{T_c}{273}}\,\mathrm{m/s}$$

($T_c$ in $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.) At $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: $v\approx 343\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Key termEcho. Reflection of sound from hard surfaces (walls, rocks, buildings). Soft materials absorb. SONAR uses echo timing (out and back) for depth/distance.
Key termRefraction of sound. Bending when speed changes (uneven wind or temperature). Day: warmer air near ground → sound bends away from ground. Night: colder near ground → bends toward ground (often clearer hearing).
Key termDiffraction. Spreading around openings/barriers. Lets you hear people in the next room. Stronger for longer wavelengths (low frequencies bend better).
Exam tip

Lightning before thunder: light is much faster than sound. Count seconds and use ~$343\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at ~$20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to estimate distance.

notes.title: 6.5 Superposition of waves: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.5

Superposition of waves

Where waves overlap, displacements add (with signs). That is interference.

Outcomes: superposition principle; constructive/destructive; standing waves

Key termSuperposition principle. At one point, resultant displacement = sum of individual displacements (signed). Also called interference.
  • Constructive: same $f$ and $\lambda$, in phase → larger amplitude.
  • Destructive: same $f$ and $\lambda$, out of phase → smaller (or zero) amplitude.
  • In phase: crests (and troughs) line up in time.
Key termStanding (stationary) wave. Two identical waves travelling opposite ways in the same medium. Oscillates in time but stays fixed in location (guitar string, bottle tone).
  • Nodes (N): zero displacement. Adjacent nodes: $\lambda/2$ apart.
  • Antinodes (A): maximum displacement. Adjacent antinodes: $\lambda/2$. Node to next antinode: $\lambda/4$.
Exam tip

Two identical waves of amplitude $4\,\mathrm{cm}$: constructive max $8\,\mathrm{cm}$; fully destructive $0$.

notes.title: 6.6 Characteristics of sound waves: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
6.6

Characteristics of sound waves

Same note on violin and piano can share pitch and loudness but still sound different (timbre).

Outcomes: pitch, loudness, timbre; sound pollution and standards

Key termPitch. Highness or lowness of sound. Depends on frequency. Higher $f$ → higher pitch (particles pass equilibrium more often per second).
Key termLoudness. How strong the sound seems; linked to amplitude (and energy). Measured in decibels (dB). Larger amplitude → louder.
Key termTimbre (quality). What makes two tones of the same pitch and loudness sound different (violin vs piano). Not "good" or "bad"; just distinctive character.
Key termSound pollution. Harmful elevated sound for humans or other organisms (hypertension, hearing loss, sleep disturbance). Harmful above about 75 dB; painful above about 120 dB.
  • Local causes: traffic, generators, loud music, construction. Solutions: distance, barriers, quieter machines, limits on night noise, better room sealing (watch diffraction through gaps).
Exam tip

Louder ↔ amplitude. Higher pitch ↔ frequency. Same note, different instrument ↔ timbre.

notes.title: Temperature and Thermometry: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Physics · Unit 7

Temperature and Thermometry

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Physics student textbook. What temperature is, safety and climate links, Celsius/Fahrenheit/Kelvin, thermometer types, conversions, and linear expansion.

Study lessons 7.1 to 7.7. Memorise fixed points and the conversion formulas before expansion problems.

Learning competencies · Unit 7
  • Understand temperature and different temperature scales (lessons 7.1, 7.4)
  • Describe extreme-temperature safety and effects of temperature change (lessons 7.2, 7.3)
  • Construct / use temperature scales and different thermometers (lessons 7.4, 7.5)
  • Convert between °C, °F, and K (lesson 7.6)
  • Calculate linear thermal expansion (lesson 7.7)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Temperature: hotness/coldness; linked to average kinetic energy of particles.
  • Scales: ice/steam points. °C: 0 / 100. °F: 32 / 212. K: 273.15 / 373.15. SI unit: kelvin (K). Absolute zero: $0\,\mathrm{K}=-273.15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • $T_C=\tfrac{5}{9}(T_F-32)$; $T_F=\tfrac{9}{5}T_C+32$; $T_K=T_C+273.15$.
  • $\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T$. Gases expand more than liquids; liquids more than solids.

notes.title: 7.1 Temperature and our life: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.1

Temperature and our life

"Hot" and "cold" by touch are relative. Physics needs a reliable measure.

Outcomes: define temperature; daily effects; equator to poles

Key termTemperature. Degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Also: measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a sample of matter, on a standard scale.
  • Feeling is unreliable (hot then warm hand vs cold then warm hand). Wood can feel warmer than metal in the morning because metal conducts heat away faster.
  • Comfortable room temperature often about $18^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $22^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • Affects clothing, diet, health, and economy.
  • Earth: tropics hot (more direct sunlight); temperate moderate; poles cold (less solar energy).
Exam tip

Best definition often combines hotness/coldness and average molecular KE (not total KE of all molecules).

notes.title: 7.2 Extreme temperature safety: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.2

Extreme temperature safety
