Your body stays near $37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Extreme heat around you can overwhelm that control.

Outcomes: comfortable ranges; heat-safety precautions

Key termNormal body temperature. About $97^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ to $99^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ ($36.6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $37.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$); average often $98.6^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ ($37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$).
  • Without devices, surroundings near ~$28^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($82^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$) help maintain body temperature; real weather varies.
  • ~$32^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: heat cramps / exhaustion risk.
  • ~$40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $54^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: heat exhaustion more likely; limit activity.
  • Above ~$54^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: heat stroke risk.

Safety: drink water (do not rely on thirst alone); wear suitable clothing and loosen layers if overheating; use sunscreen; avoid extremely hot places.

Exam tip

Know body ~$37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and that high environmental heat causes cramps → exhaustion → stroke as temperature rises.

notes.title: 7.3 Temperature change and its effects: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.3

Temperature change and its effects

Global average temperature has risen. Greenhouse gases trap heat; human activity strengthens that trap.

Outcomes: global change; effects; causes; greenhouse gases

Key termGlobal warming signal. Average global temperature up about $1.4^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ ($0.8^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) over ~100 years (NOAA). Record hot years (e.g. 2016 in textbook data) show large jumps.
Key termGreenhouse effect. Greenhouse gases trap solar heat and warm Earth. Natural effect keeps a livable average (~$15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Extra gases from human activity (e.g. burning fossil fuels) enhance warming.
  • Gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour, fluorinated gases.
  • Local care of forests and natural resources can reduce warming pressure.
Exam tip

Natural greenhouse effect is useful; enhanced greenhouse effect from excess emissions drives harmful warming.

notes.title: 7.4 Measuring temperature with different scales: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.4

Measuring temperature with different scales

Thermometers use expansion (or another property) plus two fixed points to make a scale.

Outcomes: define thermometer; describe °C, °F, K; fixed points

Key termThermometer. Device that measures temperature (in degrees or kelvin). Many use liquid expansion in a narrow tube (mercury or alcohol).
Key termFixed points (at sea level). Lower: melting ice. Upper: boiling water.
  • Celsius (°C): ice $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, steam $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; 100 equal divisions.
  • Fahrenheit (°F): ice $32^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$, steam $212^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$; 180 divisions between them.
  • Kelvin (K): ice $273.15\,\mathrm{K}$, steam $373.15\,\mathrm{K}$; SI unit (no degree sign). Same size degree as Celsius.
Key termAbsolute zero. $0\,\mathrm{K}$ ($-273.15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$): lowest possible temperature; substance has no thermal energy in this limiting sense.

Reading: warmer → liquid expands up the tube; cooler → contracts down.

Exam tip

Room temperature ~$20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is Celsius, not Kelvin. °C and °F match numerically at $-40$.

notes.title: 7.5 Types of thermometers and their use: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.5

Types of thermometers and their use

Every thermometer needs a thermometric property that changes with temperature.

Outcomes: list types; describe uses and properties

Key termThermometric property. Physical property that changes with temperature (e.g. length of a mercury column; gas pressure; electrical resistance).
  • Mercury thermometer: mercury column length; household, lab, industry; about $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • Alcohol thermometer: alcohol expansion; non-toxic if broken; about $-115^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $78^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • Resistance thermometer: often platinum wire; resistance vs temperature; roughly $-270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $+700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • Thermocouple: two different metal wires (e.g. copper and constantan) forming hot and reference junctions; common in labs.
  • Also radiation thermometers (sense emitted radiation) for some high-temperature or remote uses.
Exam tip

Building a thermometer needs a substance that expands or contracts (or otherwise changes) with temperature.

notes.title: 7.6 Conversion between temperature scales: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.6

Conversion between temperature scales

Match fractions between ice and steam points, then rearrange.

Outcomes: convert °C ↔ °F ↔ K

Celsius ↔ Fahrenheit

$$T_C=\dfrac{5}{9}(T_F-32),\qquad T_F=\dfrac{9}{5}T_C+32$$

  • Example: $50^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ → $10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Room $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ → $68^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$.

Celsius ↔ Kelvin

$$T_C=T_K-273.15,\qquad T_K=T_C+273.15$$

  • Example: $72^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ → $345.15\,\mathrm{K}$; $573.15\,\mathrm{K}$ → $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
  • A change of $5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ equals a change of $5\,\mathrm{K}$ (same interval size).

Fahrenheit ↔ Kelvin: convert via Celsius (or derive from fixed points). Own scale: use the same fraction-of-interval idea between your ice and steam marks.

Exam tip

Minimum temperature in nature (ideal): absolute zero $0\,\mathrm{K}$.

notes.title: 7.7 Thermal expansion of materials: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
7.7

Thermal expansion of materials

Heat makes particles move farther apart. Most materials expand when heated and contract when cooled.

Outcomes: define linear expansion; compare rates; calculate $\Delta L$

Key termThermal expansion. Size increase on heating. In general: gases expand more than liquids; liquids more than solids. Different solids expand at different rates (lead more than Pyrex in table examples).
Key termLinear expansion. Increase in one dimension (length) of a solid.

$$\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T$$

Key termCoefficient of linear expansion ($\alpha$). Fractional length change per degree (unit $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$). Depends on the material.
  • Double $L_0$ → double $\Delta L$ (same $\Delta T$).
  • Example: gold rod $L_0=0.15\,\mathrm{m}$, $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $49^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\alpha=1.4\times 10^{-5}$ → $\Delta L=4.62\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$.
  • Hot water on a tight metal jar lid: metal expands more than glass → lid loosens.
  • Bimetallic strip: two metals with different $\alpha$ (e.g. brass and steel) bend when heated/cooled; used in thermostats and switches. The metal with larger $\alpha$ goes to the outside of the bend when heated.
  • Holes in solids expand with the material when heated (think of the hole as filled with the same material).
Exam tip

Iron inside a heated bimetallic bend usually means iron has the smaller $\alpha$ (expands less).

notes.title: Introducing Economics: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Economics · Unit 1

Introducing Economics

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Economics student textbook. What economics is, micro vs macro, how economists reason, and who makes decisions in an economy.

Study lessons 1.1 to 1.4. Be ready to define, compare micro/macro, and spot positive vs normative statements.

Learning competencies · Unit 1
  • Define economics (lesson 1.1)
  • Explain the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics (lesson 1.2)
  • Describe the methods used to study economics (lesson 1.3)
  • Explain the characteristics of the three decision-making units (lesson 1.4)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Economics: social science of efficient allocation of scarce resources to meet unlimited human needs.
  • Micro: individuals, firms, markets; central problem = price / resource allocation.
  • Macro: economy as a whole (GDP, employment, general prices); central problem = full employment of resources.
  • Methods: deductive (general → particular) and inductive (particular → general). Complementary.
  • Positive: what is / was / will be (facts). Normative: what ought to be (value judgments).
  • Decision units: households, business firms, government.

notes.title: 1.1 Meaning of economics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.1

Meaning of economics

From Greek oikonomia (household management) to a social science of scarcity and choice.

Outcomes: define economics; explain its nature (science and art)

Key termEconomics. Branch of social science that studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources so as to attain the maximum fulfillment of human needs. As a science of choice, it studies how people use limited productive resources (land, labour, equipment, technical knowledge, etc.) to produce commodities.
  • Studies scarce resources and their allocation.
  • Allocation should be efficient.
  • Human needs are unlimited.
  • Goal: satisfy unlimited needs as far as possible by using scarce resources efficiently.
Key termNature of economics. Definitions shifted over time (wealth, welfare, scarcity themes). Economics can be seen as both:
  • Science: systematic body of knowledge linking causes and effects; collects, classifies, analyses, and interprets facts to predict ("what is").
  • Art: techniques and procedures to solve problems such as unemployment, poverty, and inflation.
Exam tip

Best short definition stresses scarce resources + unlimited wants + efficient allocation / choice.

notes.title: 1.2 Branches of economics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.2

Branches of economics

Many specialised fields exist, but modern economics rests on two foundations: micro and macro.

Outcomes: distinguish micro and macro; state each field's fundamental problem

Key termMicroeconomics. Behaviour of individual decision-making units (households, firms, governments) and how they interact in specific markets. Examples: price of teff, income of one person, output of one firm. Central problem: price determination / resource allocation (what, how, for whom). Main tools: demand and supply of particular goods and factors.
Key termMacroeconomics. Aggregate behaviour of the economy as a whole. Examples: GDP of Ethiopia, total employment, national income, general price level, total investment and consumption. Central problem: full employment of resources / level of income and employment. Main tools: aggregate demand and aggregate supply.
  • Micro and macro are complementary, not rivals.
  • Other branches (development, environmental, monetary, health, etc.) grow from this foundation.
Exam tip

False: "Macro deals with individual units" or "Micro is the theory of income and employment." True: micro = individual markets; macro = whole economy.

notes.title: 1.3 Methods and approaches of studying economics: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.3

Methods and approaches of studying economics

Economists build theories with logic, then judge statements as fact-based or opinion-based.

Outcomes: explain study methods; distinguish positive and normative economics

Key termEconomic theory. Simplified picture of reality used for analysis.
Key termDeductive method. Reasoning from general principles to particular facts (general → specific). Conclusions checked against observation. Example: all humans are mortal; Abebe is human; therefore Abebe is mortal.
Key termInductive method. Reasoning from particular observations to a general rule (specific → general). Collect data, form a hypothesis. Example: grain prices fall at harvest when supply rises → "ceteris paribus, increase in supply leads to fall in price."

Deduction and induction support each other; they are complementary.

Key termPositive economics. Describes the world as it is: what is, was, or will be. Fact-based; disagreements settled by evidence. Examples: "Secondary schools in Ethiopia are increasing." "Inflation is 12 percent."
Key termNormative economics. Asks what the economy ought to be. Uses value judgments (good/bad). Opinion; often settled by voting or debate, not proof. Examples: "Government should introduce school feeding." "Poverty is something society should reduce." "Falling prices are good for consumers."
Exam tip

Words like should, ought, unfair, good/bad usually signal normative statements.

notes.title: 1.4 Decision making units: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
1.4

Decision making units

Three main economic agents: households, firms, and government.

Outcomes: identify the three units; explain each unit's role and objectives

Key termHouseholds. Chief owners of factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship). Sell factor services; earn rent, wages, interest, and profit. Spend most income on goods and services from producers; also save and pay taxes.
Key termBusiness firms (producers). Hire factor services from households; produce commodities sold to households, other firms, government, or abroad. Main buyers of factors and leading producers. Include private and government enterprises.
Key termGovernment (general government). Buys goods/services from producers and factor services from households to provide public services (police, education, health, sanitation, courts). Main income: direct and indirect taxes on households and firms. Taxes fund public expenditure and development.
Exam tip

Basic decision-making units = all three: households, business firms, and government. Firms = buyers of factors + producers of commodities.

notes.title: Basic Economic Problems and Economic Systems: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Economics · Unit 2

The Basic Economic Problems and Economic Systems

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Economics student textbook. Scarcity forces choice; choice has opportunity cost; societies answer what/how/for whom through an economic system.

Study lessons 2.1 to 2.3. Link scarcity → choice → opportunity cost → PPF, then name the three central questions and four systems.

Learning competencies · Unit 2
  • Describe the basic economic problem (lesson 2.1)
  • Recognize how basic economic problems affect individuals, firms, and society (lessons 2.1, 2.2)
  • Compare and contrast the main economic systems (lesson 2.3)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Scarcity: limited resources vs unlimited wants (universal). Not the same as short-term shortage.
  • Opportunity cost: value of the next best alternative forgone (in goods/services, not money alone).
  • PPF/PPC: max combinations given resources and technology. On curve = efficient; inside = inefficient; outside = unattainable. Growth = outward shift.
  • Central questions: what, how, for whom.
  • Systems: traditional, capitalist, command (socialist), mixed.

notes.title: 2.1 Scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.1

Scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost

Unlimited wants meet limited means. That imbalance is the fundamental economic problem.

Outcomes: define scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, PPF; contrast scarcity and shortage; calculate opportunity cost

Key termScarcity. Economic resources are finite relative to human wants. Imbalance between wants and means to satisfy them. If resources were fully abundant, there would be no economic problem.
  • Scarcity ≠ shortage. Scarce good: available amount < what people want at zero price (universal, endless). Shortage: cannot get the amount wanted at the prevailing price (specific, short-term).
Key termChoice. Because output is limited, we cannot satisfy all wants. Individuals, firms, and governments must choose what (and how much) to produce. Chain: scarcity → limited output → choice → opportunity cost.
Key termOpportunity cost. Value of the next best alternative sacrificed to obtain one more unit of a product. Measured in goods/services (not simply money). Example: resources that make 1 m cloth or 20 computers → opportunity cost of 1 m cloth = 20 computers.
Key termProduction possibilities frontier (PPF/PPC). Curve of maximum combinations of two outputs given fixed resources and technology (full employment, no tech change during the year, some specialization).
  • Points on the curve: attainable and efficient.
  • Points inside: attainable but inefficient.
  • Points outside: unattainable with current resources/tech.
  • Illustrates scarcity, choice (movement along the curve), and opportunity cost (downward slope).
  • Law of increasing opportunity cost: as you produce more of one good, opportunity cost per extra unit rises (resources not fully adaptable) → PPF concave to the origin.
  • Example (B→C): food $420\to 320$, computers $500\to 1000$ → opportunity cost of one more computer $=100/500=0.2$ tonnes of food.
Key termEconomic growth on the PPF. Outward shift from more/better resources and/or better technology. Growth in only one sector = asymmetric shift along one axis.
Exam tip

Outside the PPF is not maximum current output; it is currently unattainable. Growth needs resources and/or technology (not technology alone).

notes.title: 2.2 Central problems of economies: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.2

Central problems of economies

Every society, because of scarcity, must answer three basic questions.

Outcomes: describe basic problems; explain effects on individuals, firms, society

Key termCentral (basic) economic problems. Problems any economic system faces due to scarcity. Common to all systems.
  1. What goods and services to produce? (allocation of resources). Choose types and quantities: consumption vs capital; civil vs military; necessities vs luxuries.
  2. How to produce? (choice of technique). Labour-intensive (more labour relative to capital) vs capital-intensive (more capital relative to labour). Choice depends on factor supplies and relative prices.
  3. For whom to produce? (distribution of the national product). Who gets the output: few rich vs majority? Focus first on necessities for many, then luxuries, if the goal is broad benefit.

These questions shape daily choices of households, firms, and governments inside an economic system.

Exam tip

Memorise the trio: what / how / for whom = allocation / technique / distribution.

notes.title: 2.3 Economic systems: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
2.3

Economic systems

An economic system is how a society organises answering what, how, and for whom. Classified mainly by who owns resources.

Outcomes: define economic system; compare traditional, capitalist, command, mixed

Key termEconomic system. Set of organisational and institutional arrangements used to answer the basic economic questions.
Key termTraditional economy. Guided by customs and elders. Often farming, fishing, hunting, gathering; little surplus; barter; family/tribe centred. Common in parts of developing regions.
Key termCapitalist (market / free market / laissez-faire) economy. Private ownership of means of production; profit motive; consumer sovereignty; competition; limited day-to-day government role (defence, law and order); self-interest; often large income inequality.
Key termCommand (socialist) economy. Collective/state ownership; central planning; strong government control; little private property or profit motive; relatively greater income equality. Historical examples include early USSR and others; many later moved toward markets.
Key termMixed economy. Mix of capitalism and socialism: public and private sectors co-exist. Strategic industries (defence, power, heavy industry) often public; consumer/small-scale often private. Uses planning tools; allows private property with rules against extreme wealth concentration.
Exam tip

Ethiopia today is typically discussed as closer to a mixed economy (public + private). Capitalism ≠ no government at all; command ≠ no markets historically always forever.

notes.title: Economic Resources and Markets: Overview & summary
notes.bodyHtml:
Grade 9 · Economics · Unit 3

Economic Resources and Markets

Based on the MoE Grade 9 Economics student textbook. Free vs scarce resources, renewable stocks, markets, circular flow, and land in Ethiopian agriculture.

Study lessons 3.1 to 3.5. Match each factor to its payment, and real flows to money flows.

Learning competencies · Unit 3
  • Describe resources; types of resources and factor payments (lesson 3.1)
  • Distinguish renewable and non-renewable resources (lesson 3.2)
  • Define market types (goods, labour, financial) (lesson 3.3)
  • Explain circular flow of economic activities (lesson 3.4)
  • Recognize the role of land as a resource in Ethiopia (lesson 3.5)

Unit summary · Must remember

  • Free vs economic resources (test = price at zero demand).
  • Factors: land→rent, labour→wage, capital→interest, entrepreneurship→profit.
  • Renewable can replenish; non-renewable stocks are fixed (recycle helps but stock stays limited). Conserve: reduce, reuse, recycle.
  • Markets: goods/services, labour, financial.
  • Circular flow: real flows ↔ money flows; two-sector and three-sector models.
  • Ethiopia: agriculture depends on land, soils, agro-climates; state ownership with holding/lease rights.

notes.title: 3.1 Types of resources and factor payments: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.1

Types of resources and factor payments

Resources are inputs that make goods and services. Price tells free from scarce.

Outcomes: define resources; explain types and factor payments

Key termResources. Inputs used in production to make goods and services available to society.
Key termFree resources. Available amount > what people desire at zero price. Unlimited gifts of nature with no price. Examples: air, sunshine, solar energy, a mountain stream.
Key termEconomic (scarce) resources. Available amount < what people want at zero price. They have non-zero prices. Examples: human labour (all skill types), fertile land, minerals, clean water, forests, capital goods, entrepreneurship.

Four categories of economic resources and payments:

  • Labour: physical and mental human effort → wage
  • Land: natural resources / free gifts of nature used in production → rent
  • Capital: manufactured inputs (machines, equipment, infrastructure) → interest
  • Entrepreneurship: organising other factors and taking risk → profit
Exam tip

Labour is not only physical work; it includes mental/skilled effort too.

notes.title: 3.2 Renewable and non-renewable resources: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.2

Renewable and non-renewable resources

Some stocks refill naturally. Others sit fixed in the ground until we dig them out.

Outcomes: define and contrast renewable/non-renewable; describe conservation

Key termRenewable resources. Can be replaced over time by natural processes (fast like daily sunshine, or slow like soil formation). Examples: solar and wind energy, soil, trees, grass, geothermal pressure, groundwater.
Key termNon-renewable resources. Stock/reserve limited or fixed (often in the ground). Recycling can replenish usable supply somewhat, but overall stock stays relatively constant. Examples: natural gas, coal, oil, steel, aluminium.
  • Use all natural resources wisely. Even renewables can be depleted if overused or destroyed.
  • Protect from pollution (oil spills, toxic air, dumped garbage).
  • Conserve: reduce (lights off, walk/bike), reuse (jugs, bags), recycle (glass, paper, some plastics, aluminium, steel).
Exam tip

Conserve = not misuse/spoil/waste. Especially critical for non-renewables.

notes.title: 3.3 Types of markets: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.3

Types of markets

A market is where buyers and sellers meet to exchange. It can be a shop or an app.

Outcomes: define market; distinguish goods, labour, and financial markets

Key termMarket. Institution where two parties (usually buyers and sellers) meet to exchange goods and services. Physical (retail) or digital (online).
Key termGoods and services market. Households buy consumable goods/services; businesses sell them (stores, internet, peer trades). End products traded; money flows from consumers to firms.
Key termLabour market. Workers supply labour services; employers supply jobs. Ranges from daily labourers and domestic workers to skilled professionals. Viewed at both micro and macro levels.
Key termFinancial market. Place (physical or digital) where securities, currencies, bonds, and other financial assets are traded. Supports capital formation and liquidity (stocks, shares, bonds).
Exam tip

Classify local examples: shop = goods; hiring a guard = labour; buying a share = financial.

notes.title: 3.4 Circular flow of economic activities: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.4

Circular flow of economic activities

Income and spending loop continuously among households, firms, and (often) government.

Outcomes: define circular flow; explain models; interpret real vs money flows

Key termCircular flow of income. Visual model of how money (e.g. the Birr) flows through markets among decision-making units. Production, exchange, and consumption create continuous income and expenditure loops.
Key termReal flows. Factor services from owners to producers; goods and services from producers to buyers.
Key termMoney (financial) flows. Factor incomes (rent, wages, interest, profit) and spending on goods and services. Real and money flows are opposite sides of the same exchanges.
Key termTwo-sector model. Closed private economy: households + firms only. Households supply factors and spend all income on consumption; firms hire factors and sell all output to households. No saving, no government, no foreign trade.
Key termThree-sector model. Adds government: taxes/revenue and government expenditure join the household-firm loops (and saving via capital markets in fuller diagrams).
Exam tip

Inner circle often shows real flows; outer circle money flows. Payments for factors go households ← firms; payments for goods go firms ← households.

notes.title: 3.5 Land as an economic resource in Ethiopia: Notes
notes.bodyHtml:
3.5

Land as an economic resource in Ethiopia

Agriculture is the backbone. Land means area plus ability to grow food and other crops.

Outcomes: explain land's role; identify two main highland soil types

Key termLand in Ethiopian agriculture. Areal extent and productivity for food and other crops. Country area about $1{,}106{,}000\,\mathrm{km}^{2}$; about 35% considered suitable for agriculture (CSA, 2007). Potential rests on good soils and suitable climate.
  • Red-to-reddish brown soils: mineral-rich, good drainage, friable (easy to plough).
  • Brownish-to-grey and black soils (high clay): excellent potential with proper drainage and conditioning.
  • Altitude creates many agro-ecological zones → diverse crops and export potential (foreign currency).
Key termLand rights context. Feudal inequity ended 1975 ("Land to the Tiller") but led to state ownership. Since 1991, state still owns land; rural peasants/pastoralists have lifetime holding rights (not sale/mortgage). Urban land often on long lease (e.g. 99 years). Debates continue on access, freer holding rights, and fair compensation when land is taken.
Exam tip

Two highland soils to name: red-to-reddish brown, and brownish-grey/black clay soils.

questions.prompt: What is the basic unit of life?
questions.explanation: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is responsible for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts capture light energy in plant cells.

questions.prompt: adfa
Which method of asexual reproduction is correctly matched with the organism?
questions.explanation: Whip-tail lizards can reproduce by parthenogenesis. The other pairs are mismatched (e.g. yeast buds; stolons are vegetative, not sporulation).

questions.prompt: What is the correct sequence of events in human sexual reproduction?
options: Gamete formation -> fertilization -> meiosis -> zygote formation
Meiosis -> gamete formation -> fertilization -> zygote formation
Fertilization -> gamete formation -> zygote formation -> meiosis
Gamete formation -> zygote formation -> fertilization -> meiosis
questions.explanation: Meiosis produces gametes; then fertilization forms a zygote.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a major disadvantage of sexual reproduction compared to asexual reproduction?
options: It increases the number of offspring in a short time
It ensures exact copies of parents
It requires two individuals and more time
It does not allow any genetic diversity
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction usually needs two parents and takes more time/energy than asexual cloning.

questions.prompt: Which of the following sets correctly compares secondary sexual characteristics in males and females during puberty?
options: Males: Broadening hips -- Females: deep voice
Males: Increased muscle mass -- Females: increased fat in breasts
Males: Increased body hair -- Females: menstrual cycle begins
Males: Menstrual cycle begins -- Females: voice deepens
questions.explanation: Typical secondary traits include greater muscle mass in males and breast fat deposition in females. A and D reverse sexes.

questions.prompt: A teacher wants to create a supportive environment for students going through puberty. Which strategy best reflects an understanding of biological, psychological, and social changes during adolescence?
options: Ignoring physical differences to promote equality
Allowing students to avoid physical activities during puberty
Offering guidance counseling and normalizing developmental differences
Separating early and late developers into different learning groups
questions.explanation: Supportive practice acknowledges variation in puberty timing and offers guidance rather than isolation or denial.

questions.prompt: Which of the following features is NOT a secondary sexual characteristic in females?
questions.explanation: Ovaries are primary sexual organs. Secondary traits include hip broadening and pubic hair (voice deepening is typical of males).

questions.prompt:
This item is based on the parts of the male reproductive organ given below. Which of the following male reproductive structures are labeled by letters B and G respectively?

![Male reproductive organs schematic](figures/bio9-final-oeb2017-q07-male-repro.svg)
questions.explanation: In the schematic, B is the seminal vesicle and G is the testicle.

questions.prompt: If a couple wants to avoid pregnancy and STIs, which combination of methods would you recommend based on the advantages and effectiveness of each?
options: Male condom and fertility awareness methods
questions.explanation: Only barrier methods like the male condom reduce STI transmission as well as pregnancy risk among these choices.

questions.prompt: Which female reproductive structure is responsible for holding the developing embryo?
questions.explanation: The uterus (womb) is where the embryo implants and develops.

questions.prompt: During which phase of the menstrual cycle is an egg released from the ovary?
questions.explanation: Ovulation is the release of the egg from the ovary.

questions.prompt: If a woman's menstrual cycle were shortened from 28 to 21 days, what changes would you expect in the timing of ovulation and menstruation?
options: Ovulation would occur later, and menstruation would begin later.
Ovulation would occur earlier, and menstruation would start earlier.
Ovulation would occur on the same day but for a longer duration.
Ovulation would not occur at all in the shortened cycle.
questions.explanation: A shorter cycle typically advances ovulation and the next menses.

questions.prompt: A woman experiences a drop in hormone levels late in her cycle, leading to breakdown of the corpus luteum and shedding of the uterine lining. Which hormonal change is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Falling progesterone (and estrogen) after corpus luteum decline triggers menstruation.

questions.prompt: A woman's fertilized egg travels through the fallopian tube and attaches to the lining of her uterus. Which biological process has just occurred?
questions.explanation: Attachment to the uterine lining is implantation.

questions.prompt: Based on a table of female contraceptive methods (implants, diaphragm, spermicides, IUD, laparotomy/vas deferens), which option is CORRECTLY described?
questions.explanation: Row II (diaphragm covering the cervix to block sperm) is correctly described. Other rows mix wrong mechanisms, STI claims, or male sterilization with female methods.

questions.prompt: If a woman is using the temperature method of fertility awareness, when should she avoid sexual intercourse to prevent pregnancy?
options: 3-4 days before and 1 day after ovulation
1 day after the temperature returns to normal
questions.explanation: Fertile-window advice for temperature/ovulation awareness usually covers several days before ovulation and about a day after.

questions.prompt: Which of the following STIs is caused by a flagellated protozoan?
questions.explanation: Trichomoniasis is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellated protozoan.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most reliable way to prevent HIV transmission?
options: Taking medicine to slow down the disease
questions.explanation: Abstinence from sexual contact is the most reliable prevention; condoms reduce but do not eliminate risk. Antibiotics do not prevent HIV.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how food protects the body from diseases?
options: It helps the body become colder during hot weather
It provides energy for biological reaction
It increases the number of cells used to replace damaged cells of the body.
It provides nutrients that prevent deficiency diseases
questions.explanation: Adequate nutrients prevent deficiency diseases and support health.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines nutrition?
options: The process of eating food that only provides energy for the body.
The process by which living organisms obtain and use food substances.
The movement of macronutrients in the bloodstream to maintain health.
The process of breaking down food in the stomach and using it to repair the body.
questions.explanation: Nutrition is obtaining and using food substances for life processes.

questions.prompt: A table lists nutrients, uses, and deficiency diseases. Which row is correctly described?
options: Vitamin A: To build cell structure -- Night blindness
Vitamin C: Growth and repair -- Rickets
questions.explanation: Iron is needed for hemoglobin; deficiency causes anemia. Vitamin C deficiency is scurvy (not rickets); proteins are not mainly 'energy' nutrients.

questions.prompt: Which of the following nutrients are correctly matched with their sources?
questions.explanation: Calcium from milk is a classic correct match. Vitamin A is not primarily from citrus (citrus is rich in vitamin C).

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why water is an essential nutrient?
options: It functions as a solvent and transport medium in the body.
It aids in regulating metabolic activity and absorbing fat-soluble vitamins.
It is an essential nutrient that provide energy in human cell
It is an indigestible organic substance needed in small amount
questions.explanation: Water is a solvent and transport medium; it does not provide energy.

questions.prompt: Why are vitamins and minerals classified as micronutrients?
options: They provide a small amount of energy compared to macronutrients.
They are only found in very small food sources.
The body requires them in very small quantities.
They are less important for bodily functions than macronutrients.
questions.explanation: Micronutrients are needed in small amounts (they are still essential).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following food groups contain all the nutrients of a balanced diet?
options: Sucrose, glucose, vitamin C, iodine and Iron
Sugar, protein, fats, Vitamin A, Vitamin B and water
Sugar, Fats, proteins, fiber, water, vitamins and minerals
Starch, lipids, roughage, water, calcium, vitamin D and iodine
questions.explanation: A balanced set includes carbs, fats, proteins, fiber, water, vitamins, and minerals.

questions.prompt: You start experiencing fever, cough, sore throat, and shortness of breath at school. What is the most responsible action to prevent infecting classmates?
options: Use antibiotics to prevent the virus from spreading through your eyes, nose, and mouth.
Stay home, isolate yourself, and avoid contact with others until you recover.
Take over-the-counter medicine like Quartem without consulting a health professional.
Avoid attending school and staying in crowded indoor places.
questions.explanation: Isolation when infectious respiratory symptoms appear reduces spread. Antibiotics do not treat viruses.

questions.prompt: Which group of people needs the most energy based on age, sex, and activity level?
questions.explanation: Heavy physical work raises daily energy needs the most among these options.

questions.prompt: If a child is not properly exposed to morning sun and lacks nutrients from fish oil, milk, and butter, what would be the likely consequence?
options: Bleeding gums and poor wound healing
Deformed bones in the legs and stunted growth
Dry or flaky skin, swelling of legs and abdomen
Reduced oxygen transportation and less energy production
questions.explanation: Low vitamin D / related nutrients lead to rickets: soft/deformed bones and poor growth.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions of malnutrition is CORRECTLY described?
options: Stunting: low weight-for-height caused by lack of vitamins and minerals
Underweight: low height-for-age caused by adequate food and recurrent illness
Wasting: low weight-for-height caused by frequent or prolonged illness
Micronutrient deficiency: low height-for-age caused excess sugar and fat
questions.explanation: Wasting is low weight-for-height, often linked to recent severe illness or acute food shortage.

questions.prompt: Sifan, 15, eats many sugary and fatty foods and rarely exercises, and has gained a lot of weight. Which action would most likely help prevent obesity?
options: Increasing exercise and eating a balanced diet with fewer high-energy foods
Eating high energy foods only once a day to avoid weight gain
Drinking more water to speed up digestion and taking fatty foods
Sleeping longer and eating more fruits with sugar
questions.explanation: Energy balance via activity and a less energy-dense balanced diet is the sound approach.

questions.prompt: If a person drinks excess alcohol for a long time, what would be its long-term effect?
options: Causes false beliefs, hallucination and psychosis
provide relief when the body experiences pain or stress
Causes stomach ulcers, heart disease and cirrhosis
questions.explanation: Chronic heavy alcohol use damages organs (e.g. liver cirrhosis, heart disease, ulcers).

questions.prompt: All of the following health problems are associated with smoking cigarettes EXCEPT?
options: Reducing the development of tumor in the lining of the lungs
Increases the heart rate and blood pressure.
Increases the stickiness of blood platelets
Reduction of the volume of oxygen in blood.
questions.explanation: Smoking increases (not reduces) lung cancer risk. The other effects are associated with smoking.

questions.prompt: Why does heroin reduce the feeling of pain in the body?
options: It increases blood flow to the brain to produce hallucinations
It blocks pain signals by binding to endorphin receptor sites
It removes damaged neurons and activate the nervous system
questions.explanation: Opioids such as heroin bind opioid/endorphin receptors and reduce pain signaling.

questions.prompt: Suppose an Ethiopian athlete plans to take a performance-enhancing drug for medical reasons. What should they do to avoid violating anti-doping rules?
options: Apply for a therapeutic use exemption from WADA
Avoid telling your history to anyone
questions.explanation: A Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) from WADA/anti-doping authorities is required for banned medicines used for legitimate treatment.

questions.prompt: From this list: AIDS, Tuberculosis, Anemia, Malaria, Diabetes, Trichomoniasis, Chronic bronchitis, Covid-19 -- which diseases are non-infectious?
questions.explanation: Anemia (III), Diabetes (V), and Chronic bronchitis (VII) are non-infectious. The others are infectious diseases.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between monozygotic twins and dizygotic twins?
options: Monozygotic twins come from two separate eggs, while dizygotic twins come from one egg.
Dizygotic twins share the same placenta and have always same sex, while Monozygotic twins have separate placentas can be different sex.
Monozygotic twins are genetically identical, while dizygotic twins are not identical and come from two separate zygotes
Dizygotic twins resemble each other while Monozygotic twins are strikingly different
questions.explanation: Monozygotic (identical) twins come from one zygote; dizygotic (fraternal) twins come from two zygotes and are not genetically identical.

questions.prompt: Which disease is correctly associated with its main route of transmission and its prevention?
options: Tuberculosis is spread by airborne droplets, prevented by using antiretroviral drugs
HIV is spread through mosquito bites and prevented by antibiotic.
Covid-19 is a viral disease spread through droplets and prevented by using antibiotics.
Malaria is spread by mosquito bites and prevented by insecticide-treated nets.
questions.explanation: Malaria is mosquito-borne; ITNs help prevent bites. Antibiotics do not treat viruses; ARVs are for HIV, not TB prevention as stated.

questions.prompt: Which represents the correct sequence of ecological levels from the smallest to the largest?
questions.explanation: Levels build from organism up through population, community, ecosystem, then biome.

questions.prompt: Which list includes only biotic components of an ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Only living components: plants, fungi, bacteria, pathogens. The others mix in abiotic factors (sunlight, humidity, salinity, rainfall).

questions.prompt: How does the availability of light influence the distribution of photosynthetic organisms in aquatic ecosystems?
options: Light penetrates equally in all parts of the water, supporting photosynthesis at any depth
Light is irrelevant in aquatic ecosystems as organisms derive energy from other sources
Light only affects photosynthesis near the water's surface, limiting photosynthesis to shallow areas
The absence of light in deep waters supports the growth of plants and algae
questions.explanation: Light attenuates with depth, so most photosynthesis occurs in shallow/photic zones.

questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate about the effects of biotic and abiotic factors on species distributions?
options: Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors
Biotic factors, like predators, have a greater impact than abiotic factors
Both biotic and abiotic factors work together to determine species survival
Abiotic factors, like temperature, don't affect species distributions
questions.explanation: Distribution is shaped by both living interactions and physical/chemical conditions.

questions.prompt: Fertilization in humans occurs when:
options: A sperm meets an egg inside the oviduct.
The ovum moves from ovary to uterus.
A sperm cell sinks into the lining of the uterus
The sperm swims through the cervix to the uterus
questions.explanation: Fertilization normally occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube).

questions.prompt: Which of the following best defines a biome?
options: A large area with different climate and varied vegetation types
A large group of population found in different ecosystem
A large group of ecosystems that shares the different type of climax community
A large group of ecosystems that share the same types of climates and climax community
questions.explanation: A biome groups ecosystems with similar climate and climax community/vegetation type.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches fauna and flora of the savanna biome?
questions.explanation: Savannas are grassland with grazing megafauna such as elephants.

questions.prompt: What is a common plant adaptation found in desert biomes?
options: Broad leaves for maximum water loss
Reduced leaf surface and water storage in tissues
questions.explanation: Desert plants often reduce leaf area and store water (e.g. succulents).

questions.prompt: Deforestation is an ongoing threat to tropical rain forests. Which of the following is its likely effect?
questions.explanation: Fewer trees mean less CO2 uptake; diversity and soil fertility typically fall, not rise.

questions.prompt: Why should students develop love and respect for fauna, flora, and their biomes?
options: Because they are expensive to replace
To ensure sustainable use and biodiversity conservation
Because they are the only source of income in tourism
questions.explanation: Respect supports sustainable use and conservation of biodiversity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following aquatic biomes is the most productive among the others?
questions.explanation: Estuaries (and wetlands) are among the most productive aquatic systems; estuaries are a common best-answer for 'most productive' in exam items.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes secondary succession?
options: It begins when organisms grow on cooled, solidified lava.
It starts with pioneer species like lichens and mosses growing on bare rock
It results in a climax community that never change
It begins from an ecosystem that was disturbed but the soil is still present
questions.explanation: Secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains. Bare lava/rock is primary succession.

questions.prompt: Match: I kills and eats another; II feeds on a plant but usually does not kill it; III one benefits, other neither helped nor harmed; IV both benefit. Correct sequence for I-IV?
questions.explanation: I predation, II herbivory, III commensalism, IV mutualism.

questions.prompt: Which pair best represents a parasitic relationship?
questions.explanation: Blood flukes are parasites of humans. Caterpillar-plant is herbivory; mycorrhizae mutualism; many epiphytes are commensal.

questions.prompt: If $\sin A = \dfrac{2}{3}$ for an acute angle $A$, then which of the following is equal to $\tan A$?
Which of the following is NOT correct about a right-angled triangle?
options: If base, height and hypotenuse are $a$, $b$ and $c$, then $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
If $3$, $4$, $\sqrt{7}$ are sides of a triangle, then this triangle is a right-angled triangle.
If $\theta$ is an angle of a right-angled triangle, then $\sin\theta$ can be greater than $1$.
For an isosceles right-angled triangle, two sides are equal in length.
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta$ cannot exceed 1. (Note: $3^2+(\sqrt{7})^2=16=4^2$, so option B is actually a valid right triangle.)

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined, not 0.

questions.prompt: Two men A and B lie on level ground on opposite sides of a 120 m tower. A observes the top at $60^\circ$ and B at $30^\circ$. How far apart are the two men?
questions.explanation: Distances: $120/\tan 60^\circ=40\sqrt{3}$ and $120/\tan 30^\circ=120\sqrt{3}$. Sum $=160\sqrt{3}$ m.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the measures of interior angles of a decagon?
How many lines of symmetry does a regular nonagon have?
questions.explanation: A regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry; nonagon has 9.

questions.prompt: Which of the following defines a regular polygon?
questions.explanation: Regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

questions.prompt: The four interior angles of a pentagon are $120^\circ$, $95^\circ$, $100^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. What is the smallest exterior angle of this pentagon?
questions.explanation: Fifth interior $=540^\circ-385^\circ=155^\circ$. Exteriors $=180^\circ-$ interiors: $60^\circ,85^\circ,80^\circ,110^\circ,25^\circ$. Smallest is $25^\circ$.

questions.prompt: For an n-sided regular polygon, each interior angle is 5 times each exterior angle. What is the measure of each interior angle?
questions.explanation: Let exterior $=e$. Then $5e+e=180^\circ\Rightarrow e=30^\circ$, interior $=150^\circ$.

questions.prompt: What is the area of a regular hexagon with side length 12 cm?
questions.explanation: Area $=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 144=216\sqrt{3}$.

questions.prompt: The perimeter of a square inscribed in a circle of radius 8 cm is equal to:
questions.explanation: Diagonal $=16$. Side $=16/\sqrt{2}=8\sqrt{2}$. Perimeter $=32\sqrt{2}$.

questions.prompt: One interior angle of a polygon is $100^\circ$ and each of the other angles is $110^\circ$. What is the name of this polygon?
questions.explanation: $100+(n-1)110=(n-2)180\Rightarrow n=5$ (pentagon).

questions.prompt: If $\triangle ABC \equiv \triangle DEF$, then which of the following is NOT true?
questions.explanation: Under A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, angle C corresponds to F, not D.

questions.prompt: Two plane figures are congruent if
options: Corresponding angles congruent and corresponding sides proportional
Corresponding angles congruent and corresponding sides congruent
Corresponding sides congruent and corresponding angles proportional
Corresponding angles proportional and corresponding sides proportional
questions.explanation: Congruence requires equal corresponding sides and equal corresponding angles.

questions.prompt: What is the length of DF that makes $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ if $AC=8$, $BC=x-1$, $DF=3x+3$, $EF=18$ and $\angle C\equiv\angle F$?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{8}{3x+3}=\dfrac{x-1}{18}\Rightarrow x=7$, so $DF=24$.

questions.prompt: Perimeters of similar triangles ABC and DEF are 14 cm and 8 cm. The ratio of the area of $\triangle DEF$ to $\triangle ABC$ is:
questions.explanation: Side ratio $8/14=4/7$; area ratio $(4/7)^2=16/49$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true while constructing similar figures?
options: If scale factor > 1, the new figure is smaller than the original
If scale factor < 1, the new figure is larger than the original
If scale factor = 1, the new figure is congruent to the original
If scale factor = 1, the new figure is smaller than the original
questions.explanation: Scale factor 1 preserves size: the figures are congruent.

questions.prompt: A 6 m ladder leans against a building 4 m above the ground. At what height would a 12 m ladder touch the building if both form the same angle with the ground?
questions.explanation: Similar triangles: heights scale with ladder length, $4	imes(12/6)=8$ m.

questions.prompt: If $A=(10,1)$ and $B=(2,7)$, then the magnitude of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ (in units) is:
questions.explanation: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-8,6)$, magnitude $\sqrt{64+36}=10$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has magnitude and direction.

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have areas $441$ cm$^2$ and $1764$ cm$^2$. What is the scale factor from the first triangle to the second triangle?
questions.explanation: Side scale factor $=\sqrt{1764/441}=2$. Among the given options, $\dfrac{1}{2}$ matches the reciprocal ratio of first:second sides (21:42).

questions.prompt: Two vectors are parallel if
options: They are orthogonal to each other
One vector is a scalar multiple of the other
It has no magnitude and no direction
questions.explanation: Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other.

questions.prompt: Let $A=4i-2j$ and $B=6i-9j$. Then $\dfrac{1}{2}A-\dfrac{1}{3}B$ equals:
Suppose $\overrightarrow{AB}$ has initial point $A=(1,2)$ and terminal point $B=(4,6)$. If the initial point moves to the origin, where is the terminal point?
questions.explanation: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(3,4)$; from the origin the terminal point is $(3,4)$.

questions.prompt: Given vector $a=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\end{pmatrix}$, which of the following is NOT true?
options: $-a$ has the same magnitude and opposite direction to $a$
questions.explanation: Halving a vector reduces its magnitude.

questions.prompt: If each central angle of a regular polygon is $72^\circ$, how many sides does it have?
Let $\vec{u}=(1,2)$ and $\vec{v}=(-3,-1)$. What is the magnitude of $4\vec{u}+3\vec{v}$?
questions.explanation: $4u+3v=(-5,5)$, magnitude $\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$.

questions.prompt: A boat moves 8 km South then 8 km West. What is its displacement from the start?
questions.explanation: Resultant is southwest: $8\sqrt{2}$ km at S $45^\circ$ W.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is quantitative data?
questions.explanation: Age is numerical (quantitative).

questions.prompt: Which is NOT true about the population: 4, 9, 2, 3, 9, 1, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 7, 2, 5, 9, 3, 5, 8, 9?
questions.explanation: With 20 values, median is the average of the 10th and 11th ordered values: $(4+5)/2=4.5$, not 4.

questions.prompt: A fair die is tossed once. What is the probability of getting a factor of 6?
If you toss a coin four times, what is the size of the sample space?
questions.explanation: $2^4=16$ outcomes.

questions.prompt: What is the probability of a certain event?
questions.explanation: A certain event has probability 1.

questions.prompt:
Given the following histogram for some data.

![Histogram of values 1 to 5](figures/math9-final-oeb2017-q34-histogram.svg)

Which of the following is NOT true about this data?
questions.explanation: Frequencies are 5,6,1,3,7 for values 1-5 (N=22). Mode is 5 (freq 7). Median is (2+3)/2=2.5. Range is 5-1=4, not 6, so D is NOT true.

questions.prompt: For the frequency table v: 5,6,7,8,9 with f: 5,2,4,6,3, what is the median?
questions.explanation: N=20; 10th and 11th values fall in class 7, so median = 7.

questions.prompt: What is the mode of this data (v: 5,6,7,8,9; f: 5,2,4,6,3)?
questions.explanation: Highest frequency is 6 at value 8.

questions.prompt: The range of this data is equal to:
questions.explanation: Range = 9 - 5 = 4.

questions.prompt: The standard deviation of this data is equal to:
questions.explanation: Mean = 7; population variance = 2; SD = $\sqrt{2}$.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that a value is greater than or equal to the mean?
If each data value is multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{2}$, which is NOT true?
questions.explanation: Variance scales by $(1/2)^2$: new variance $=2\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{1}{2}$, not 1.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red, 2 blue and 3 black balls. Probability of a blue ball at random?
Which of the following defines a probability?
options: The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment
A numerical value that describes the likelihood of an event occurring
A subset of a sample space
A trial whose outcome cannot be predicted in advance
questions.explanation: Probability is a number describing likelihood of an event.

questions.prompt: Two dice are thrown. Probability that the sum equals 9?
Mean score of 40 students was 72.5. One score was copied as 52 instead of 88. What is the correct mean?
A coin and a die are tossed together. Probability of tail and a prime number?
questions.explanation: $P(T)=\tfrac{1}{2}$, $P(\text{prime})=\tfrac{3}{6}=\tfrac{1}{2}$ -> product $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a measure of location?
questions.explanation: Median is a measure of central location; the others measure spread.

questions.prompt: Group I ages: 2,1,4,3,9,6,3,2,6. Group II: 6,5,7,5,6,7,5,6,7. Which is true?
options: The two groups have the same mean
Group I shows more variation than group II
The mean of group I is closest to each value than group II
The range of group I is less than the range of group II
questions.explanation: Group I mean 4, range 8; Group II mean 6, range 2. Group I varies more.

questions.prompt: Which pair of vectors are parallel?
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}=-2\vec{u}$ for option D.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Congruent figures are similar with scale factor 1.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT correct about a regular nonagon?
options: From one vertex we can draw only 7 diagonals
The sum of all interior and exterior angles is $1620^\circ$
The sum of all its central angles is $360^\circ$
questions.explanation: Diagonals from one vertex $=n-3=6$, not 7.

questions.prompt: Two cities report their temperatures as 0°C and 32°F. What conclusion can you draw?
options: The first city is colder than the second
The second city is colder than the first
It's impossible to compare temperatures in different scales
Both cities have the same temperature
questions.explanation: 0°C = 32°F, so both report the same temperature.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a common characteristic of all waves?
options: They all require a medium to travel through
They all require a source of electricity to be generated
They all move at the same speed
They all transfer energy without transferring matter
questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy; not all need a medium (electromagnetic waves).

questions.prompt: Why does a longer ramp make it easier to push a heavy object up to a higher place?
options: It increases the weight of the object
It spreads the effort over a longer distance
It reduces the amount of work required
It uses gravity to help lift the object
questions.explanation: A longer ramp reduces required effort by increasing distance (work against gravity is similar, ignoring friction).

questions.prompt: In a simple pendulum, what is the primary factor that determines the period of oscillation?
options: The mass of the pendulum bob
questions.explanation: For small angles, $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ depends mainly on length.

questions.prompt:
If the efficiency of the pulley system in the figure below is 80%, then what is the AMA of the pulley system?

![Pulley system](figures/phys9-final-oeb2017-q05-pulley.svg)
questions.explanation: Four supporting rope segments give VR = 4. AMA = efficiency × VR = 0.80 × 4 = 3.2.

questions.prompt: An echo was received after 3 s by a sonar system. Speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. How deep is the ship?
Which simple machine is commonly used in an office chair to allow easy movement across the floor?
questions.explanation: Chair casters are wheel-and-axle systems.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of sound in air at temperature $50^\circ$C? (Use $v_0=331$ m/s at $0^\circ$C)
questions.explanation: Approximate $v \approx 331 + 0.6\times T = 331 + 30 = 361$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A force-multiplier simple machine occurs when:
options: Force of load is greater than force of effort
Distance moved by load is greater than distance moved by effort
Force of effort is greater than force of load
Distance moved by load equals distance moved by effort
questions.explanation: Force multipliers have MA > 1: load force > effort force.

questions.prompt: If VR = 3 and MA = 2, what can be said about the efficiency of the machine?
options: The machine is more efficient than ideal
The machine is less efficient than ideal, with some energy lost
questions.explanation: Efficiency = MA/VR = 2/3 < 100%, so energy is lost to friction etc.

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason we feel hot when the temperature rises?
options: The body can no longer regulate its internal temperature
The body produces too much sweat
The air becomes too dense for breathing
Heat is absorbed by the skin and the body's temperature increases
questions.explanation: Higher air temperature increases heat transfer to the body.

questions.prompt: A copper pipe expands more than a plastic pipe when both are heated equally. What does this suggest?
options: Copper expands more with heat than plastic does
The plastic pipe remained unaffected by the heat
questions.explanation: Copper has a larger effective expansion response in this comparison.

questions.prompt: A pendulum is released from a certain height. If the length of the string is tripled, what happens to the period?
options: The period will remain the same
The period will decrease by a factor of three
The period will increase by a factor of the square root of three
The period will increase by a factor of three
questions.explanation: $T\propto\sqrt{L}$, so tripling L multiplies T by $\sqrt{3}$.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a simple machine?
questions.explanation: Simple machines make work easier by trading force and distance.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best defines periodic motion?
options: A motion that continues to increase in speed over time
A motion that repeats itself at regular intervals of time
A motion that moves in a straight line and then stops
A motion that depends on the mass of the object only
questions.explanation: Periodic motion repeats in equal time intervals.

questions.prompt: The diameter of the wheel is 20 times greater than the diameter of the axle. What is the velocity ratio of this wheel and axle system?
questions.explanation: VR ≈ D_wheel / D_axle = 20.

questions.prompt: Why is the temperature at the equator much warmer than at the poles?
options: The poles are closer to the Sun
The equator receives more direct sunlight year-round
The equator is farther from Earth's core
questions.explanation: Near-vertical solar rays at the equator deliver more heating per area.

questions.prompt: A tuning fork placed in water produces ripples. What does this demonstrate about energy transmission?
options: Energy can only move through air
Sound waves create heat, not motion
Vibrations transfer energy through a medium
questions.explanation: Mechanical vibrations transfer energy through the water medium.

questions.prompt: Which factor most influences human perception of thermal comfort besides air temperature?
questions.explanation: Humidity strongly affects how hot or cold we feel.

questions.prompt: A student stretches a spring. To double the elongation (within Hooke's law), what should they do?
options: Double the force applied to the spring
Halve the force applied to the spring
questions.explanation: Hooke's law: $F=kx$, so elongation doubles if force doubles.

questions.prompt: What is the primary cause of global warming?
options: The buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Enhanced greenhouse effect from greenhouse gases.

questions.prompt: Why does sound travel more slowly in a gas than in a liquid or solid?
options: Particles in solids are far apart
Particles in a gas are farther apart
Particles in a gas are close together
Particles in a liquid are farther apart
questions.explanation: Gas particles are farther apart, so energy transfers more slowly.

questions.prompt: Efficiency of a machine: slope length 40 m raises an object 8 m; effort 80 N pushes a 240 N object up the plane. Efficiency?
In a ripple tank, where wave crests from two sources meet, higher peaks are seen. Conclusion?
options: The sources are out of phase
questions.explanation: Crest + crest meeting produces constructive interference.

questions.prompt: Which thermometer uses expansion of a liquid to measure temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury (or alcohol) thermometers use liquid expansion.

questions.prompt: A louder echo is heard when clapping in a hallway than in an open field. Why?
options: The air is denser in the hallway
Hallway surfaces reflect sound more effectively
The open field produces higher-frequency waves
questions.explanation: Reflective walls return more sound energy as an echo.

questions.prompt: What temperature range can an alcohol thermometer typically measure?
questions.explanation: Alcohol freezes near -115°C and boils near 78°C, limiting the range.

questions.prompt: How does a wedge make it easier to split or cut objects?
options: By changing the direction of the applied force
questions.explanation: A wedge redirects and concentrates force to split materials.

questions.prompt: If a car's engine coolant temperature rises a lot in hot weather, what should you do to avoid overheating?
options: Increase the air intake to cool the engine
Add more fuel to lower the engine temperature
Increase the engine speed to release heat more quickly
Turn off the engine and allow it to cool down
questions.explanation: Stop and cool the engine to avoid damage.

questions.prompt: Why is the Kelvin scale used in scientific experiments instead of Celsius or Fahrenheit?
options: It is based on the freezing point of water
It starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature
It is easier to use than other scales
It is the most widely used in everyday life
questions.explanation: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, useful for gas laws and thermodynamics.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has effort 50 N and lifts load 150 N. What is the MA?
questions.explanation: MA = load/effort = 150/50 = 3.

questions.prompt: What is one major effect of rising temperatures on agriculture?
options: Crop failures due to heat stress and drought
Improved productivity of all crops globally
questions.explanation: Heat stress and drought often reduce crop yields.

questions.prompt: What happens to the velocity ratio of a pulley system when the number of pulleys is increased?
questions.explanation: More supporting strands increase VR.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is incorrect about nodes and antinodes of a wave?
options: Distance between a node and an adjacent antinode equals $\lambda/2$
Distance between a node and an adjacent antinode equals $\lambda/4$
questions.explanation: Node to adjacent antinode is $\lambda/4$, not $\lambda/2$. So C is incorrect.

questions.prompt: When comparing Celsius and Kelvin scales, which is true?
options: Both scales start at the same zero point
A change of 1°C equals a change of 1 K
Kelvin is always higher by 100 units
questions.explanation: Celsius and Kelvin degree sizes are equal; zeros differ.

questions.prompt: Pitch of a screw is 0.2 cm; effort moves in a circle of radius 15 cm. Velocity ratio?
Which set of temperatures are equivalent?
The power of a machine measures:
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work.

questions.prompt:
A mass on a spring oscillates with the displacement-time graph shown. Which statement is correct?

![Displacement-time graph](figures/phys9-final-oeb2017-q39-oscillation.svg)
options: The amplitude of the oscillation is 0.04 m
The frequency of the oscillation is 2 Hz
The mass achieves maximum speed at 0.5 s
The period of oscillation is 1 s
questions.explanation: Amplitude is 0.04 m. Period is 2 s (f = 0.5 Hz). At 0.5 s the mass is at an extreme (speed minimum).

questions.prompt: An electromagnetic wave has wavelength 10 nm. What are its frequency and period respectively? ($c=3\times 10^8$ m/s)
questions.explanation: $\lambda=10\times 10^{-9}$ m; $f=c/\lambda=3\times 10^{16}$ Hz; $T=1/f\approx 3.3\times 10^{-17}$ s.

questions.prompt: How do solids, liquids, and gases respond to an increase in temperature?
options: Gases expand the most because particles are far apart and move freely
Solids expand the most because particles are tightly packed
questions.explanation: Gases typically show the largest expansion for a given temperature rise.

questions.prompt: A 2 m second-class lever moves a 400 N load. Distance between load and effort is 160 cm. Effort if 100% efficient?
questions.explanation: Load arm = 2.0 - 1.6 = 0.4 m. Effort = (400×0.4)/1.6 = 100? Wait: second class: effort at end, load between fulcrum and effort. Fulcrum--load--effort. Effort arm=2m, load arm=2-1.6=0.4m. E=400*0.4/2=80 N.

questions.prompt: A fishing pole is a compound machine. Which simple machines make it up?
options: Wheel and axle, inclined plane, pulley
questions.explanation: A fishing rod/reel commonly combines lever, wheel-and-axle (reel), and pulley-like line guides.

questions.prompt: What happens to the pitch of a sound if the frequency increases?
questions.explanation: Higher frequency means higher pitch.

questions.prompt: The distance which a compression or rarefaction travels per unit time gives:
questions.explanation: That is the wave speed.

questions.prompt: Best difference between a fixed pulley and a movable pulley?
options: Fixed changes force direction; movable changes the amount of force needed
Fixed reduces force needed; movable changes direction
Both reduce force needed in different ways
Both change only the direction of the force
questions.explanation: Fixed pulley mainly redirects effort; movable pulley reduces effort (MA≈2).

questions.prompt: Which characteristic of a sound wave determines its loudness?
questions.explanation: Loudness relates to amplitude.

questions.prompt: Steel bridge segments 20 m long; built at 20°C; 4 cm gap. Using $\alpha\approx 1.1\times 10^{-5}$ °C$^{-1}$ (steel), max temperature before buckling?
questions.explanation: $\Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T\Rightarrow 0.04=20\times 1.1\times 10^{-5}\times\Delta T\Rightarrow\Delta T\approx 182$; $T\approx 202^\circ$C ≈ 200°C. (Paper table lists $10^{-6}$; intended key matches $10^{-5}$.)

questions.prompt: At what temperature do Fahrenheit and Celsius scales read the same value?
questions.explanation: They coincide at -40.

questions.prompt: What principle do thermocouples work on?
options: Temperature affects electrical resistance of metals
Two wires of the same metal form two junctions
Temperature causes a metal wire to expand
A voltage is created when two different metals are heated at a junction
questions.explanation: Seebeck effect: voltage from a junction of dissimilar metals.

exams.title: Grade 11 Natural Biology · 2nd Semester Final Exam
exams.subtitle: OEB 2017/2025 · 50 MCQs · 75 min

questions.prompt: Galgalo and Soreti are husband and wife who had 3 children. One of their male children, Bona, is hemophilic while Chaltu and Gadisa were normal. What explanation can you make from a pedigree for this heritable trait?
options: Hemophilia is an autosomal dominant trait
Bona carries the hemophilic trait on his Y chromosome
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive; an affected son with unaffected parents implies the mother is a carrier.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of pedigree analysis? It shows
options: Inheritance patterns of social diseases in humans
The genotypes of the neighbors of family members
Who will marry whom in human society
Whether a trait is sex-linked or autosomal
questions.explanation: Pedigrees help determine inheritance patterns such as sex-linked vs autosomal.

questions.prompt: A karyotype shows an individual with an extra copy of a chromosome. Which chromosomal mutation is most likely present, and why?
options: Missing part of a chromosome, because partial deletions are more common
Down syndrome, because it results from trisomy 21, a change in chromosome number
Inversion, because part of a chromosome appears reversed
Translocation, because chromosomes are exchanged between non-homologous pairs
questions.explanation: An extra chromosome is aneuploidy (e.g. trisomy 21 / Down syndrome).

questions.prompt: What is the main feature that differentiates autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked single-gene disorders?
options: Their patterns of inheritance in humans
Their existence on X and Y chromosomes of humans
Their ability to affect both male and female parents equally
Their being much bigger events than chromosomal disorders
questions.explanation: They are distinguished mainly by inheritance pattern.

questions.prompt: Design a breeding program to develop disease-resistant maize. Which two genetic-based selection methods would you combine, and how would you justify their use over natural selection?
options: Mass selection and random mating, for faster trait loss
Mass selection and natural selection, for random variation
Pure line and bulk selection, for controlled genetic improvement
Inbreeding and indigenous observation, for unknown results
questions.explanation: Pure-line and bulk selection allow controlled improvement for desired traits.

questions.prompt: How do we benefit from bioinformatics software to understand evolutionary processes?
options: Through the analysis of nucleotide or amino acid sequences
Through screening databases for pathogen genomes
Through saving large amounts of abiotic data
Through editing defective genes and reading CT scan results
questions.explanation: Sequence comparison is central to evolutionary bioinformatics.

questions.prompt: Which description of the human musculoskeletal system is correct?
options: Made up of muscles and glands that provide body coordination
Made up of muscles and skeletons that provide excretory functions
The organ system that gives humans respiratory functions
The organ system that gives humans the ability to move
questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal system enables movement and support.

questions.prompt: If you create a model of the musculoskeletal system, what components must it include to show function and structure?
questions.explanation: Bones, muscles, and joints are the core structural/functional parts.

questions.prompt: Identify the correctly matched type of muscle with its description.
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated.

questions.prompt: What can you predict if the human skeleton were one big single bone instead of 206 bones joined by joints?
options: No blood cell production in bone marrow
questions.explanation: Joints between many bones allow flexible movement.

questions.prompt: What is the role of calcium when released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during muscle contraction?
options: It allows actin and myosin to bind and form a cross-bridge
It breaks the link between actin and myosin
It allows troponin and tropomyosin to bind
It makes tropomyosin block the actin binding site
questions.explanation: Ca2+ exposes myosin-binding sites so cross-bridges can form.

questions.prompt: Identify the INCORRECTLY matched male reproductive structure with its function.
options: Testes: produce sperm cells and testosterone
Seminiferous tubules: produce immature sperm cells
Vas deferens: matures and stores sperm cells
Seminal vesicle: secretes fructose into the semen
questions.explanation: Maturation/storage is mainly epididymis; vas deferens transports sperm.

questions.prompt: In humans, fertilization and gestating a fetus occur respectively in:
questions.explanation: Fertilization in fallopian tubes; gestation in uterus.

questions.prompt: Gametogenesis cells: 1 spermatozoa, 2 spermatogonia, 3 primordial germ cells, 4 spermatids, 5 primary spermatocytes, 6 secondary spermatocytes. Which numbers are all diploid?
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia, primordial germ cells, and primary spermatocytes are diploid.

questions.prompt: Which explanation about menstruation and the menstrual cycle is correct?
options: The menstrual cycle includes uterine changes but not ovarian changes
Menstruation occurs when a matured ovum is fertilized in the uterus
Menstruation is monthly discharge from puberty to menopause without interruption
Menstruation occurs when the corpus luteum dies, progesterone drops, and the uterine lining breaks down
questions.explanation: Menses follows progesterone drop after corpus luteum degeneration (if no pregnancy).

questions.prompt: How does the hypothalamus influence the menstrual cycle?
options: It directly releases eggs from the ovaries
It regulates the pituitary gland that controls the ovarian cycle
It has nothing to do with the menstrual cycle
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic GnRH controls pituitary FSH/LH.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is correct about contraception?
options: Chemical barriers such as spermicides are often used by males
Condoms are the only contraceptive methods that help prevent STIs
Condom, diaphragm and cervical cap are sexual practices used as contraceptives
Intrauterine devices and contraceptive ring are barrier contraceptive methods
questions.explanation: Among common methods, condoms uniquely help prevent STIs as well as pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Female infertility is inability to get pregnant after unprotected sex. What does male infertility refer to?
options: Production of inadequate/unhealthy sperm or prevention of ejaculation
questions.explanation: Male infertility relates to sperm quality/quantity or delivery problems.

questions.prompt: Which stage of syphilis is correctly matched with its symptom?
options: Primary: rash on hands and soles
Secondary: gummatous lesions or syphilitic tumor
Tertiary: formation of non-itchy painless chancres on genitals
questions.explanation: Latent syphilis has no clinical symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which is the most preventive method for STIs caused by bacteria and viruses?
options: Regular use of bed nets and vaccinations
questions.explanation: Safer/protective sex (e.g. condoms, mutual monogamy) is key STI prevention.

questions.prompt: In a community where FGM is widely practiced, how can you help protect children?
options: Encourage the practice as removing dirt
Accept local practices to live safely
Create awareness about risks to the reproductive system
questions.explanation: Awareness and education against harmful practices is the constructive approach.

questions.prompt: Which is a benefit of good family planning?
options: Equal numbers of male and female children
Ensuring resources required for raising children
Putting infant and maternal health at risk
questions.explanation: Family planning helps match family size to available resources and health.

questions.prompt: If a woman shifts from IUD to oral contraceptives, what risk has she avoided?
questions.explanation: IUDs can increase menstrual bleeding; switching avoids that IUD-related risk.

questions.prompt: After consuming alcohol, Bikila decides to engage in unprotected sex. Likely consequence of this decision?
options: Confusion and higher desire of sleepiness
Higher risk of violence, traffic accidents and death
Increased risk of sexually transmitted infections
questions.explanation: Unprotected sex raises STI risk; alcohol impairs judgment.

questions.prompt: What is a side effect of chewing khat as a recreational stimulant?
options: High sexual drive in libido among male users
J-shaped legs, coma and death immediately
questions.explanation: GI inflammation (stomatitis/esophagitis/gastritis) is a known adverse effect; alertness is a desired effect not a side effect in this framing.

questions.prompt: How do drugs such as cocaine, khat, and alcohol change users' lifestyles?
options: Lead to impulsive actions that may result in unprotected sex
Affect health that never alters lifestyle
Have a positive impact on lifestyle
questions.explanation: Psychoactive drugs can increase impulsivity and risky sexual behavior.

questions.prompt: Why is the cranium considered among the strongest bones?
options: Because it protects the soft and delicate brain
Because it is located at the top of the body
Because it protects the soft spinal cord
questions.explanation: Cranial bones form a protective case for the brain.

questions.prompt: You hand a 2 kg bag to a friend by extending your arm slowly. Which muscle contraction are your arm muscles performing?
questions.explanation: Lowering/controlled lengthening under load is eccentric contraction.

questions.prompt: How does the musculoskeletal system protect internal organs?
options: Bones create a hard outer shell around the body
Ligaments prevent excessive movement of organs
Bones form protective cavities for vital organs
questions.explanation: Examples: skull, rib cage, pelvis enclose vital organs.

questions.prompt: Which part of the musculoskeletal system benefits most from weightlifting for strength?
questions.explanation: Weightlifting primarily builds muscle strength.

questions.prompt: Identify the correctly matched body part to its joint type.
options: Ball and socket joint: the skull
questions.explanation: The knee is a classic hinge joint.

questions.prompt: A city has area 500 km² and 50,000 people. What is the population density?
questions.explanation: Density = 50,000/500 = 100 people/km².

questions.prompt: Two ecologists must report the number of plants in Yayo forest. Which method should they use?
